Imperial Japanese Army telegrams in which two digits stand for one kana: the vowel row, then the consonant column counted backwards. Harumi-Matsuba found them in the JACAR files and rebuilt the table from one telegram against the readings pencilled on its outgoing draft. Four telegrams read, one of them with no translation: a request of January 1904 for maps of Korea. Where National Institute for Defense Studies, via JACAR: C09122911500, C09122909900 (General Staff telegram file, 1902), C09123116600 (General Staff, 1904), C03020059400 (Army Ministry 満密大日記, January 1904). The cipher A coordinate table: the first digit is the vowel row of the syllabary, the second the consonant column counted backwards; 10 is ン. How it was solved The table was inferred from one telegram’s twelve pairs against the readings pencilled on its outgoing draft, then tested on telegrams found later, one of them with no translation at all. Credit Harumi-Matsuba, with Claude, Codex and Sonnet ( issue #58 , kagigo1901-public , October 2026). What it says “Until I return to Tokyo, please handle the business of the General Staff as you see fit”; “please lend the required maps of Korea”, six days before the Russo-Japanese War began. Still open C09122909900 enciphers a noun phrase, not prose. In C03020059400 two of the twelve pairs are one digit off the table, and three characters of its filed translation are illegible. Three pairs that are one digit off the translations, probably slips by the writer; a 1901 telegram in another method; which Army cipher this table belongs to. No person has checked the transcriptions.

Each kana is two digits. The first gives the vowel, the second the consonant: ア 9 カ 8 サ 7 タ 6 ナ 5 ハ 4 マ 3 ヤ 2 ラ 1 ワ 0 a 0 ア 09 カ 08 サ 07 タ 06 ナ 05 ハ 04 マ 03 ヤ 02 ラ 01 ワ 00 i 1 イ 19 キ 18 シ 17 チ 16 ニ 15 ヒ 14 ミ 13 リ 11 u 2 ウ 29 ク 28 ス 27 ツ 26 ヌ 25 フ 24 ム 23 ユ 22 ル 21 e 3 エ 39 ケ 38 セ 37 テ 36 ネ 35 ヘ 34 メ 33 レ 31 ヱ 30 o 4 オ 49 コ 48 ソ 47 ト 46 ノ 45 ホ 44 モ 43 ヨ 42 ロ 41 ヲ 40 A voiced kana adds 5 to the first digit and takes the column of its voiced row: ガ 9, ザ 8, ダ 7, バ 6, so ガ = 59, ジ = 68, デ = 37 + 50 = 87, ブ = 76. ン is 10, and a final 80 closes the message. The consonant columns run backwards through the syllabary, from ア at 9 to ワ at 0. The Army’s coordinate ciphers of 1874 and 1894 described on Cryptiana use iroha order instead. The same table is used unchanged from Osaka in March 1902 to Kokura and Moji in January 1904. It may be the Army’s 鑰号 (Yakugō, in use 1901–04) written without its key, or the numeric part of 特号; nothing found so far settles which.

The letters of 31 May and 8 June 1482 are nos. 10 and 12 in Magyar Diplomácziai Emlékek III (1877), the 8 March 1486 passage is in the 1878 supplement, and 2 May 1486 is III no. 75, with decipherment slips beside the cipher. What it says Matthias offers an intervention against Venice with ten thousand Swiss and six thousand cavalry, provided the league sends money to Milan. Still open The printed March decipherment keeps some unexplained editorial markers, left in.

Record Date and origin Earlier source Result R1140 31 May 1482, Pozsony MDE III, no. 10, pp. 13–14 Printed cipher reading R1141 8 June 1482, Pozsony MDE III, no. 12, pp. 16–17 Printed cipher reading Both are to Beatrice’s sister Eleonora d’Aragona, Duchess of Ferrara. The edition gives the plaintext of the cipher: Matthias offers an intervention against Venice, provided the league sends money to Milan. The proposed force comprises ten thousand Swiss and six thousand cavalry; five hundred more cavalry, including a hundred hussars, also need a safe route. He does not intend to declare himself openly against Venice before his relationship with the league is settled. uno expediente optimo et necessario per lo favore et salute de tuta la lega Dece milia Svizari et sei milia cavalli del Signor Re di Hungaria. These are excerpts of the 1877 decipherment . The manuscript’s cleartext and cipher boundaries match the edition’s roman and italic sections. The editorial note states that the italic words were written in secret signs. MDE III (1877), p. 13: an earlier decipherment in print. This is a crop of the public-domain edition, not an archive photograph. Image: Magyar Diplomácziai Emlékek III (1877), p. 13, via MTAK REAL-EOD.

Beatrice relays Matthias’s criticism of the league’s reluctance to spend. The king repeats the troop offer, requires payment at Milan, and asks for decisive cooperation. The published text has the proverb: ali avari che per sparagnare uno grosso perdeno lo ducato Misers save a grosso and lose a ducat. Near the end the decipherment describes endless negotiations as “uno Jocare de balla cum retornare sempre ali principij” —playing ball and always returning to the starting point. The printed page has balla ; the OCR text gave holla . The edition and manuscript both date the letter 8 June, despite a secondary citation giving July.

The evidence is the agreement of dates, salutations, clear passages and cipher boundaries with the edition. No full transcription of the symbols was made, no key was recovered and no percentage was measured. The method is existing decipherment : printed decipherments found and matched to the images. The letter-by-letter accuracy of the older decipherment has not been tested. The 1482 alphabet looks different from those of the 1486 letters. Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana index has no article on Beatrice; his other publications were not searched. Archive photographs remain local because DECODE states that their publication requires archive permission.

Translation R1140_en.md <!-- English translation of readings/R1140_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): the decipherment printed in MDE III (1877) no. 10, with the same holes. --> # R1140, Beatrice of Aragon to Eleonora, Duchess of Ferrara, Pozsony, 31 May 1482: English translation Most Illustrious Lady, most honoured Sister, after due recommendation. I am writing more fully on behalf of His Majesty the King my consort to His Majesty the Lord King our father about the matters below, for fear these letters might miscarry, the road being dangerous; and I shall leave long words aside and come to the conclusion. Having understood the danger you are in, the Lord King of Hungary, notwithstanding the great business he has in being at war on two sides, one against the Turk, the other against the attack that the Emperor with the whole Empire seeks to make on him, has nevertheless decided on an excellent and necessary expedient for the favour and safety of the whole league. His Majesty, after he understood the preparations of the Pope and of the Venetians against the league, and above all against your state, sent to the Swiss, who are his confederates, and an answer has come with some captains of the said Swiss, and [?] and the matter arranged, that if the league is willing only to spend a hundred thousand ducats and send them to Milan, and the Lord King of Hungary to bear the rest of the expense, and that it be soon, he will bring it about that by the end of the month of August there will be sixteen thousand fighting men in the territories of Brescia and Verona against the Venetians: ten thousand Swiss and six thousand horse of the Lord King of Hungary. Furthermore His Majesty holds 500 horse ready to send you, among them a hundred hussars; but he must be told by what route he is to send them to you: you must send us a commissary of yours. Besides that, the Lord King of Hungary is sending Megrebal [Magyar Balázs] to the Croatian border to raise men, likewise in your favour; but he declares to you that, not being otherwise considered in your league, he does not wish to declare himself openly an enemy of the Venetians, but that the said Swiss should make war as soldiers of the league, and he would gladly have Don Federico as their captain; and when the King of Hungary has entered your league, he intends to show himself openly an enemy of the Venetians. And beyond this he further offers that, if the league will help him with only a hundred thousand ducats more, His Majesty will spend on his side a much greater sum, and will raise another army and fall upon the Venetians from the other side, so that everyone would see that the way would be good. So that when the league is minded in earnest to help itself, it will find the right way not only to divert the Venetians from attacking it, but not to be attacked by them. Encourage the Most Illustrious Lord Duke to do his diligence and duty about the above, and meanwhile to resist steadfastly; for, as I said above, when the league is willing to make the said expense, whatever it wishes will be easy for it. The Lord King of Hungary is willing to put in much more than as much again, to make the Venetians feel more damaged than they think to damage others. All I write above is by the will and order of the Most Serene Lord King my consort and your brother, with compassionate and affectionate help, and to put it into effective execution. Pozsony, the last of May 1482. Your Most Illustrious Ladyship's most devoted and obedient sister, the Queen of Hungary. To the Most Illustrious Lady Eleonora, Duchess of Ferrara etc., Lady and most honoured sister. I have understood what Your Ladyship [?writes] [?to] me in your letter of the 14th of last month, and with great displeasure; all of which I have made known to the Most Serene Lord King my consort, who has had no less displeasure at it; but in part he lays the blame on the whole league, which, had it been willing to spend, would have had plenty of help at small cost, and such that it would not only have taken [them], but would have reduced them to scarcity in defending themselves; and he rightly says that so it usually happens to misers, who to save a groat lose the ducat. [?Now], things standing thus, and His Majesty finding himself with two armies, one against the Turk, the other against the Emperor and the Germans, he has thought of the expedient that I write in the other letters enclosed here, which is prompt and excellent. It remains for the league to make diligence in sending money to Milan; and when His Majesty is assured of it, so as not to lose time, he will order some captains of the Swiss to come with a commissary of His Majesty to take the payment for the 10,000 foot and six thousand horse; for he does not intend to make or send a smaller army, so that whatever event or opposition may arise, it may be sufficient by itself. His Majesty has been waiting for the ambassadors of the Most Serene League, who it has been said for a long time, and confirmed more from day to day, were coming; which has been the reason for keeping Messer Francesco Fontana from being [?despatched]. When the league is willing to [?help] itself with the Lord King of Hungary, and do what is fitting and what reason requires, we believe, Your Most Illustrious Ladyship, that he alone will be enough to save the state of the league and to punish the Venetians. But that league must come to a different understanding with His Majesty, and the conditions be brought to their true duty; for if it should be necessary to make an army of a hundred thousand persons, being helped with money in no too great a sum, he will do it quickly, and with men of his life. When the league comes to an understanding with His Majesty in earnest, His Majesty will find a good way to settle the wars he has here, so as to join with the league in the oppression of the Venetians; but he means to go into it in deed and not with negotiations; and so His Majesty will put his kingdom and his life at risk, once and for all, to remove such [?rivals]; for otherwise, he says, it is a game of [?ball] that always returns to the beginning. I always commend myself to Your Ladyship. Pozsony, 8 June 1482. Your Most Illustrious Ladyship's obedient sister, the Queen of Hungary etc. To the Most Illustrious Lady Eleonora, Duchess of Ferrara etc., Lady and most honoured sister.

Ten letters of the Avignon pope to his agent in Barcelona with ciphered passages in a simple substitution of invented signs, reported by Meister in 1906 with no decipherment. Canon Puig y Puig deciphered and printed them in 1920. His decipherment was checked against his one facsimile page, and his unprinted key rebuilt from it (91% of the page’s cipher letters confirmed). The letters of the pope’s circle, whose key is not shown to be his, have their own pages. Five letters of men of his circle, deciphered by the same editor, have their own pages. Where Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona, the Schism papers Climent left to the chapter (Puig’s “Documentos inéditos del obispo Çapera”, today the paper part of the series Cisma d’Occident). Not digitised. Catalogue entry 334 here. The cipher Clear Latin with ciphered words and passages. The cipher is a plain substitution, one sign per letter, 20 letter values, signs joined without word breaks, with a dotted V for the King of Aragon and groups of null signs at sentence breaks. How it was deciphered By Sebastián Puig y Puig, canon of Barcelona, in 1920. He rebuilt the key “a fuerza de paciencia” from lines Climent had deciphered on three of the letters, and printed the letters with the deciphered passages in italics. He never printed the key. It is rebuilt here from his one facsimile page (section 05). What it says Money for a pope under siege, embassies to Paris, and whom to trust. One passage gives his three reasons for refusing the “submission” France demanded: it would bring gravior capcio et mors manifesta , a harsher captivity and plain death. Key Rebuilt from the facsimile against Puig’s text. It decrypts every legible cipher run on the page: 755 of 826 letters confirmed sign by sign (91%), none against it. It corrects Puig three times, for example te sicudum to tenendum . Still open Puig’s printed text of the ten letters is not copied into the repository (Google Books refuses scripts); what is held and checked here is the p. 475 facsimile page, word by word (reading audit, 22 October 2026). One overwritten stretch of the facsimile page, and the ciphertext of the other letters, which is not imaged. Credit The decipherment is Puig’s (1920); the key table is new here. Meister (1906) reported the documents on information from Franz Ehrle.

In his history of papal cryptography, Aloys Meister wrote that Benedict XIII kept to the cipher practice of his predecessor Clement VII. Examples, he said, were in the cathedral archive of Barcelona, in a box labelled Documentos referentes a la familia Luna I : a letter in Benedict’s own hand with some lines in cipher, and an instruction of about three folio pages, a large part of it in cipher. His footnote says the information came from Father Ehrle, who assured him the texts were “mixed with signs”. Meister had not seen them and printed neither. That made it the project’s best lead for a ciphertext from before 1425 with no known decipherment, and possibly 1,500–3,000 signs of papal cipher from about 1400. The archive scan of 23 September 2026 found no decipherment of it. One check was left: Puig y Puig’s 1920 book on Pedro de Luna, which HathiTrust would not serve to this machine.

Sebastián Puig y Puig, canon of Barcelona, found the papers while working on his history of the bishops of Barcelona. They were Climent’s own. Francesc Climent, called Çapera, was Benedict’s chamberlain and treasurer, nuncio to Castile, later bishop of Barcelona and patriarch of Jerusalem, and he left his books and papers to the chapter when he died in 1430. Puig sorted the paper documents under the working title Documentos inéditos del obispo Çapera , and from them wrote Pedro de Luna, último papa de Aviñón (Barcelona, 1920). In the preface he says he printed the most important of them, “especially the ten or eleven written in an unknown key, which after laborious trials we had the good fortune to decipher”. A note at the first of them explains how. Puig’s note: italics in the appendix mark the deciphered passages. He got the key “by patience” from lines Climent had left on documents 1063, 461 and 463. Document 595 holds two keys of Climent that fitted none of the letters. Image: S. Puig y Puig, Pedro de Luna (Barcelona 1920), p. 466 n. 2, via Google Books (University of Wisconsin copy). So Climent had deciphered some lines himself, on three of the letters, and Puig used those lines as a crib to recover the key and decipher the rest. Because the cipher is mixed into clear Latin, a ciphered word is usually framed by clear context, which is the situation Puig describes. Puig’s borrowing had a cost. When the archive was catalogued in the 1970s, Josep Baucells quoted a note by the archivist Josep Mas: between 1920 and 1930 Canon Puig studied a large part of the Schism documents at home, “but many were not returned”. Some of the cipher originals may now survive only in Puig’s print.

Puig’s appendix calls fourteen items carta cifrada . Ten are Benedict XIII’s own, and this page is about them. The other four, and a deciphered sentence of a fifth letter quoted in a note, come from other men of his circle; Puig speaks of “la clave o claves”, and nothing shows that they used Benedict’s key, so each has its own page: Santa Cruz, October 1399 , Jafet, September 1400 , Exea, August 1408 , Comuel, December 1415 and Comuel, June 1416 . Every page of the fourteen was checked for gaps. He leaves no gap in the deciphered text, and a handful of odd forms inside the italics (“mi. i ur”, “ot.o”, “cer ificari”) look like one-letter slips of decipherment or print. The word counts are estimates from Puig’s printed lines. Benedict’s own letters, from the siege of the Avignon palace to his escape in March 1403, carry about 2,200 deciphered words. That is more than Meister’s “three folio pages”, which is probably letter XXVII, and one letter with “some lines” in cipher. Letter XXVII as Puig printed it: roman type was written in clear, italics were in cipher. The ciphered part gives Benedict’s three reasons for refusing the submission. Image: S. Puig y Puig, Pedro de Luna (Barcelona 1920), p. 467, via Google Books (University of Wisconsin copy).

Puig printed no key and no sign table, but on p. 475 he inserted, sideways and without a caption, a photogravure of the last page of letter XXXV (22 June 1400). His printed text of the same passage runs in a narrow column beside it, so every cipher run on the plate comes with its plaintext. The last page of Benedict XIII’s letter of 22 June 1400, rotated upright. Clear Latin alternates with runs of cipher signs. Lines 8 to 16 are almost all cipher: et presertim scribe quo modo se habet in negociis nostris … Image: S. Puig y Puig, Pedro de Luna (Barcelona 1920), p. 475, facsimile of Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona, Documentos inéditos del obispo Çapera no. 1068; via Google Books (University of Wisconsin copy), rotated and deskewed here. The signs are small invented shapes, several of them joined by hair-lines, written into the line of ordinary Latin. Two runs were aligned with Puig’s text to see what kind of cipher it is and whether his italics fit: End of line 1: Negocium convencionis , then a dotted V̇ , then signs for cum duce Burgundie . Puig prints “Regis Arag.” in roman here, so V̇ is a name sign for the King of Aragon that he expanded. In the letters that follow, u is the same sign three times, and d , e and c each repeat. Start of line 8, et presertim scribe qu… : e repeats four times, s twice and i twice. The value for m matches the one found for cum in line 1, and the values for b , c and u match those in Burgundie . It is a letter-for-letter substitution in invented signs, with name signs mixed in, and Puig’s decipherment fits where it was tested. Google serves the page at 1826 × 2500 pixels, about forty pixels per manuscript line of a reduced halftone, and a first attempt on the long run broke down at quo modo se habet . A second pass over the whole page did better.

No sharper image could be found. The Google scan is the largest served, the second Google copy is snippet view, and HathiTrust would not serve its copy. So the plate was cut from the page, turned upright, straightened by 0.7°, and split into its 26 lines. Each cipher run was then examined at three to five times magnification with the contrast stretched, word by word against Puig’s text. At that scale the signs separate once the plaintext fixes where each word falls. One key decrypts the whole page: Plain Sign on the plate Plain Sign on the plate a open hook, like a δ with no bowl n n b T with a bar p inverted T with a stroke (⊥) c, i a small o q double-barred upright d double cross (‡) r a single upright stroke e δ s T f σ with a flag t c with a stroke above (c′) g a 4-like sign u, v cb, written as one joined sign h a 2-like sign x an α-like sign o a double loop (ꝏ) l a looped d V̇ = the King of Aragon ( Rex , Regis , Regi Aragonum , four times) m ε with a foot groups of λ- and ʒ-like signs = nulls at sentence breaks It is the simplest kind of cipher: one sign for each letter, no alternatives, no word breaks. Many of the signs are ordinary letters used for other letters ( n is n, but T is s and δ is e ), so a run looks like scrambled handwriting. The letter o is written as a double loop, so modis is m ꝏ d o s in signs. c and i share a single small o on the 1920 halftone, and d and p are hard to tell apart. The original may separate them with a tick or a dot the reproduction lost. Four groups of λ- and ʒ-like signs stand where Puig prints a semicolon or a dash, and he gives no text for them. They are nulls marking punctuation. Top: the end of line 3, …negocium , then line 4, c′ δ n δ n ‡ cb ε = tenendum , then o n = in . Puig printed te sicudum . Bottom, line 24: detinent , then the six signs of absque (Puig: abique ), then o o n, the start of congedio (Puig: congerio ). Image: S. Puig y Puig, Pedro de Luna (Barcelona 1920), p. 475, facsimile of Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona doc. 1068; via Google Books (University of Wisconsin copy), cut, deskewed and contrast-stretched here. How much it decrypts. The cipher runs on the page carry 148 words, 826 letters of Puig’s plaintext. 125 words were confirmed sign by sign. Sixteen have one to three signs too blurred to confirm. Seven, in line 4, fall in a stretch that the writer underlined and overwrote, which the halftone cannot resolve. That makes 755 of 826 letters confirmed (91.4%), or 96.3% of the legible runs, and not one sign contradicts the key. The word-by-word record is plate475_check.tsv , and the key is key.md . Three corrections to Puig. In line 4 the cipher says tenendum , not Puig’s te sicudum , which is not a Latin word. The sentence is et ideo est sic negocium tenendum in suspenso : “so the business is to be kept in suspense”, repeating the clear in suspenso tenendum just before it. In line 24 the Prior of Portaceli, the Pope’s messenger, frightened off by the besiegers, left absque congedio , “without leave”, not abique congerio . And necesaria is written necessaria . Otherwise Puig’s decipherment of the page stands. The key is a known-plaintext reconstruction. The decipherment is Puig’s; the key he worked out in 1920 is now on record.

Line 4 of the facsimile , non approbando nec reprobando; de cardinali catan- , is underlined and overwritten in the original and cannot be transcribed sign by sign on the halftone. Neither can the sixteen blurred signs elsewhere (blocker: needs a photograph of doc. 1068 or a 600-dpi scan of p. 475). The other letters’ ciphertext. The key should decrypt all of Benedict’s letters of 1399–1403, but none of them is imaged (blocker: needs the originals, some of which Puig may not have returned). Not this cipher: a line of 4 December 1398 in a key Puig calls unknown ( Vico to Carbonell, 1398 , its own page), and two keys of Climent in document 595 that Puig could apply to nothing and did not print. The material Meister reported, a long papal cipher of about 1400, was deciphered and printed by Puig in 1920. The project’s oldest-cipher search goes on with the other candidates, all of which also need photographs from the archives.

Français 3252 — 5 April 1571 f36r Illustrissimo et Eccellentissimo Signor mio. Il signor Biagio quale è gionto al primo di questo, m'ha detto che 'l Commesso di Monsignor il Thesauriere le havera mandato per ricevere li danari in Averna per le due paghe quale s'hano da dar alle fanterie Italiane, quando saranno riscosse, ha detto a Monsignore et le Maesta che alli cinq di questo essi sarano in essere fuora di [?] franchi de quali n'haveva avertito detto Thesauriere le febvere, per vedere dove vorra di modo che mancavano detti [?] franchi, quali non s'haveranno con li [?] però come s'esquire questo dell'altre cose simile, restiamo ancho confusi et in quella parte. Quanto alli [?] franchi quali s'hano da esigere in Provenza per pagar le compagnie ch'erano a tenere là da qui, in Lion non s'haveva né lingua se fosero pronti o no, di modo che ci può altrettanto dubitare, e più de ciò c'habbino a tardare che altrimente. A talche sempre restiamo in difficulta bisogni, onde ogni hora trovar modo da intertenere quelle che vi sono, sin tanto che li altri vengano, dove non bastando gli che si ha dalle terre come non basta, è forza che ogni giorno m'impegni de più in più. Detto signor Biagio ha lassato il Mastro di Campo et il Sergente di battallia de dette compagnie, quali se ne vengono a giornate, de modo che non si vedevano esser dove elle sono, che non sia alle sette o otto di questo, che potrano poi col far mostra et venire da là qui esser dove si ha. Como? penso al Valenza, overo alla fine del mese se pur vi sarano anchor. Monsignor de la Motta ha tolto cura di mandar l'uomo espresso per intendere che cosa è de questi danari, et avvisarne. Io credo che questa resolutione della lega per sua occasione da farne quietare un poco più di quello mi credeva. ? a la E.S. uostra tenghi certo che ci e s [t] ato d'il pensiero et de le pratiche grande et ui sono ancho fa per leuare il ? re da questo paese et forsi ance piu ? auanti ? Et in questo proposito gli vuò dire che quando il signor Biagio a Turino ove capitò prima che venisse qui, andò a vedere l'ambasciatore Ferrarois, chiamato il Cavallier Gucino?, de lui è molto familiar, ove retirati soli in camera, doppo havere ragionato delle cose di Francia et domandatone che prouisione si faceua a questo paese gli dise: Signor Biagio, io ui asicuro che se'l re non prouede di altra maniera a questo paese et ben presto ne ? reus [c] ira fuori et lo perdera forsi con qualche altra cosa ? dauanta [g] io et racordateui di lloco doue siamo et dil tempo che io ui dico questo il ? hauendomi riferto ? l'ho rimandato a Turino per uedere se li e posible di cauarne qualche particolarita ma la E.sa Vostra creda a me, se questa lega non se ? f36v Parlandone il signor ? quasi come sde [gn] ato dise questi co ? ioni ? hano f ? opart ? et lo rilieuano di spesa i ? di uno milione d'oro la ? sarebe seguito desordeni e qua e altroue et bisogna et si guardi ? et ? come noi ? Pero chi ha termine ha vita. Forsi sara detto per noi quello, che noi istessi non si curiamo de fare. Supplico ben l'Eccellenza Vostra di fare che le cose ch'io gli scrivo non si sappia, se non da chi si deve, et non si puo di meno, et supplicar anch'essi, si per il beneficio loro presente come l'avvenire, d'andar riservati nel parlar; et in oltra dir al signor Presidente, che de questi particolarmente ch'io le scrive? (come scrive? anche medesimamente all'E.V.) non habb[ino] mai a sapere nulla delle cose mie, per esser genti doppie di pessima natura et che per danari venderebbero Christo non che suoi patroni. Io ringratio la E.V. infinitamente della recetta, et acque mandatami per conto di Genavera; e vero che dove dice Sterco di cino?, io tengo vogli dire Visco Quercino, per esser materia propriatissima a detto male, con laudato dal Diascoride, Theofrasto Paracelso, et altri principali della medicina. Aspettaro la polvere, et poi ne faremo prova, qual spero con la gratia d'Iddio, et il favore che V.E. m'ha fatto, debbia sperare bonissimo frutto ? signor ? giosi ha deto et si pensaua di mandare il capitan ? Mirandola ? conducent ? soldati ? La Eccellenza Vostra havra visto, et per vie mie, et per la lettera che gli mandai ultimamente del gentilhuomo ? la dificulta et si ? a in nel lasare pasar ? alaso ? Pero io non so come si possa esequire questo effetto senza porre a grosso rischio di perderne una gran parte, perche dal canto di Savona e di Genova non bisogna pensarci, continuando essi sopra la prattica del Finale, di la quale n'ho scritto piu volte, et hora ne so meno che mai; di maniera che questa parte e dil tutto rinchiusa, et l'altra e molto difficile. Et in questo proposito del Finale gli vo' dire che un gentilhuomo haver suo servitore? me disse che 'l Conte di Millesimo parlando seco quando fu domandato a Milano dal Duca d'Alberche per vedere se voleva pigliar carico dal Re Filippo, volendosi servire di lui et dil loco suo, fra l'altre particularita gli disse, ch'esso Duca d'Alberche li haveva detto che voleva operar con tutte le forze, et auttorita c'haveva dal Re Filippo, affine che 'l Re di Francia non pigliasse il possesso de detto Finale. Queste sono le precise parole ch'esso m'ha detto, di modo che si puo considerare dil resto, qual sij l'animo loro, et questi non sono f37r sogni ne imaginationi. Le diece compagnie della cavalleria legiera partita di Fiandra, alloggio hiersera a Luvimborgo, hoggi passa la montagna, et tiens[i] si fermera alle frontiere verso noi. Il signor Duca di Savoia a quest'hora debb'esser a Nizza, havendo per andarli pigliato la strada di Savona. Circa a quegli heretici intendero se vi sono, et essendoli non li staranno. In questi doi giorni, sono avisato che in due case, l'una a Verzolo, et l'altra a Tellio, in Valle di Magna vi sono doi ministri che predicano secretamente. Credo saro sforzato di farli fare compagnia a quegli doi che sono qua prigione di longhissimo tempo. Mandai i saluti di V.E. al signor Cavalliero Guasco, et hieri ne ricevei l'alligato plico, quale gli mando. Scrivo a loro Maesta quel tanto che la vedra per la coppia qui annessa, affine non si persuadano, che le cose quando vengono comandate, restano subito esequite, et Dio vogli che queste compagnie francese siano qua alla fine dil presente. Quegli di Pinarolo gia qualche giorni, et hieri li di Carmagnola mi mostrarono lettere delli suoi, dove scrivano l'E.V. haverli accordato, che non faccino piu prestiti che per il mese passato, et fondandosi sopra loro scritti, fanno sempre maggiore difficulta, di modo che li fastidij ogn'hor piu moltiplicano, et come dice il proverbio, mancando la robba cresce il rumore. Circa al Cordero ho mandato a Granoboli per haver la evocazione sottoscritta, quale subito havuta, la mandaro all'E.V. Fra tanto qua non se gli puo procedere, et come li ho scritto per altre mie, il processo e mandato a detto Granoboli, d'onde credo che quegli del parlamento ne siano in pena, per ritrovarsi il processo diverso dil tutto alla supplica fatta, d'onde n'e seguito l'evocazione, quale converra sia revocata et di nuovo rimessa qua, che gli dovra procedere, pero non sara che bene che l'E.V. ne dica un motto al signor Presidente, et fargli intendere le triste, anzi pessime opperationi di costui, affine non resti inganato nell'oppenione sua, et m'assicuro come che Iddio e Iddio ? et di subito sarebe ? consilio di Belagarda Che sara il fine con pregar Iddio la renda felice. Da Saluzzo li 5 Aprile 1571. Di V.E. ? Lodovico Birago. Il signor Duca di Ferrara e andato in diligenza alla Mirandola et fatto li mutare la guarnigione a causa d'un trattato quale se dice li haveva il signor Duca di Fiorenza. Monsignor di Bellegarda quale veneva di giornate? giunse hier a Turino per le poste. Where Printed in figures in the 1819 Mémoires of Catinat, vol. 2, pp. 295–342, from the Bavarian State Library’s OCR; the originals at Vincennes were not consulted. The cipher A three-figure group code. Le Bouyer de Saint-Gervais printed it in 1819 unread. How it was read Étienne Bazeries reconstructed the code from these pages in 1893 and printed only two letters and the opening of a third. His published table decodes all seven, recovering 12,362 groups. What it says Louvois orders Bulonde shut up at Pignerol “avec un masque”. The longest letter, 14 September, has the King choose the solid course: bring the army back over the Alps, hold the passes, keep Carmagnole then burn it, and take Coni in winter. Still open Six groups misprinted above the table’s range in 1819, and an OCR error rate near one group in seventy. Credit The code is Étienne Bazeries’s (1893).

The 1691 campaign in Piedmont opened with the failed siege of Coni (Cuneo), abandoned by Bulonde on 28 June against orders, and closed with the French army still in the plain between Turin and Pignerol, unable to take Coni or to winter. Catinat commanded; Louvois, secretary of state for war, died on 16 July; his son Barbezieux succeeded him and the King wrote to Catinat himself. The court’s ciphered despatches to Catinat survived among the marshal’s papers and were printed in figures in the second volume of the 1819 Mémoires , pp. 295–342, with the clear passages the clerk had left in clear. Bazeries states that except for the 19 August letter, whose minute is at the Dépôt de la guerre, these despatches “n’ont pas été enregistrées”: if so, the 1819 print is the only text of the other six.* Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat , t. II (1819), p. 320: the end of the 6 September letter and the first lines of the King’s letter of 14 September, which runs to p. 342 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, bsb10720287, scan 354). The Grand Chiffre de 1691 is a two-part code of 587 groups: two or three homophones for each letter, consonant-vowel syllables, word stems ( Envoi , Trouv , Expliqu ), whole words ( Sa Majesté , Pignerol , Carmagnole ), a dozen nulls that mark the ends of sentences, and one group that cancels the group before it. Bazeries rebuilt it from these letters over three years and printed his table, with 91 entries left blank, at the end of Le Masque de fer ; that table, transcribed from the Gallica scan for the Feuquières letter , is used here unchanged. The figures were taken from the Bavarian State Library’s hOCR of the volume, word by word with their boxes. Specks the OCR read as a stray “1” (which would decode as Passage ) were dropped by box size, show-through glyphs stripped, the editor’s footnote markers and running heads removed, and the letters cut at their printed headers. Each group was looked up, the units concatenated between nulls, and the result word-segmented with a lexicon drawn from the three Catinat volumes, Rousset’s Louvois , Feuquières’ memoirs and Bazeries’ book, so that sa maj este vou loit sca voi r comes out as sa majesté vouloit scavoir . The word division is an aid to the reader; the group-level decoding is what is checked. Controls. Bazeries printed the 8 July and 19 August letters in clear. Our decoding of the OCR’d figures matches his text at 2,640 of 2,690 characters (98.1 %) and 3,204 of 3,233 (99.1 %) after normalising accents and i/j, u/v. The residue is single groups the OCR misread (26 Vous as 24 Le ), a few places where his clear text departs from the printed figures, and his free rendering of two table entries. Every stretch that could not be divided into words, 137 in all, was then cropped from the page image and checked by eye: seven OCR errors were found and corrected, six groups turned out to be misprinted above 587 in the 1819 edition itself, and the rest were seventeenth-century spelling correctly transcribed.

Louvois, 9 July. The more the King reflects on Coni, the more he is touched, for the reputation of his arms and for what the place will cost the winter quarters; a siege with the whole army is no longer possible. Two tasks: fortify Carmagnole so the enemy “n’osent le regarder”, and destroy every post the enemy could hold in winter against the roads to Casale and Pignerol: Villeneuve d’Ast and Quiers “vous les devriez brusler absolument”, sparing the churches, and the castles between Turin and Asti likewise, all done “de manière qu’il ne paroisse point qu’elles vous aient esté prescrites”. Seize Bene; burn Carignan if the enemy could winter in it. Seek battle before the Germans arrive and avoid it after, to let them fall sick and desert for want of pay. Oblige the peasants to bring their grain into the King’s garrisons, with commissaries to hold the governors to it. The Duke of Savoy’s talk “mériteroit bien” two thousand bombs into Turin, and the bridge of Turin would be worth breaking, “mais ce sont des vues que Sa Majesté vous met devant les yeux et non des ordres”. Louis XIV, 24 August. Chamlay carries the King’s thoughts on every course still open in the war. Will the enemy march into Savoy, or mass by Turin to eat the forage and force Catinat back over the mountains first? The negotiation at Rome makes it very desirable to stay beyond the Alps as long as possible. Casale: palisades, money for eighteen months, grain, more cavalry, gunners. Some at court think Villefranche fortified and Saluces, Savillan and Fossano garrisoned would let the army winter in Piedmont; the King does not tire of saying so, but Catinat is not to let the King’s wish override his judgement. Pignerol is “le premier objet” in any plan. And the King would greatly wish Coni taken at the close of the campaign. Louis XIV, 29 August and 6 September. A treaty offered by the people of Mondovì is good but can only serve to sound them, since the army can no longer take quarters there. The resident at Geneva reports the enemy has asked the city for passage into Savoy and would go by the Valais into the Chablais. Larray has thrown an Irish battalion into Briançon for fear the Barbets would seize it. If Catinat crosses the Po, let it be before the enemy moves. Chamlay has arrived. Louis XIV, 14 September, Fontainebleau. Chamlay has reported, and the King has seen “avec peine” that the upshot is to withdraw the army of Piedmont over the mountains at the end of the campaign and not to bring it back. He sets out both sides at length. Against withdrawal: the enemy masters of Italy, the allies and neutral princes forced to declare against him, Casale lost from view, the reputation of his arms damaged and his enemies encouraged by an appearance of weakness “quoyque fausse dans le fonds”. For it: the impossibility of subsisting in Piedmont without Turin; a country “fort estroit et extrêmement couvert”, cut by torrents that rise in hours and cannot be bridged; the distance of Casale; the sickness of the troops every campaign, with no hospitals to hold them; the enemy’s freedom to engage or refuse behind the Doire and the Po. Then Catinat’s plan for the defensive: the cols of Provence, Dauphiné and Savoy held, the heights of Saint-Pierre by Pignerol and of Suze occupied, cheaper subsistence, fewer sick, the surplus cavalry on the Saône ready to go to Germany, and the Duke of Savoy left to choose between keeping the allied army idle in his ruined country or sending it away and seeing the French return. “J’ay comparé les inconvénients et les avantages d’un parti avec ceux de l’autre … et je me suis déterminé à préférer le parti solide à l’honorable.” The orders follow. Prolong the campaign to All Saints or even Saint-Martin, and keep Carmagnole to the last, because both cover the negotiation with the Pope and the Italian princes that might extricate him from Casale “et mesme peut-estre de la guerre de Piedmont”; the enemy must not learn that he means to quit Piedmont for good, so the works at Carmagnole go on, “avec un peu moins de vivacité et de dépense”. When the order comes, carry off what can be carried, the grain on the cavalry’s cruppers to Pignerol, throw the rest in the water, tear up the works, burn palisades, gates, hay and grain. Secure Pignerol’s magazines against a bombardment, which “me donneroit beaucoup de mortification en présence de mon armée”. Hold the valleys of Pragelas and Pérouse for the Briançon road. After recrossing, take Coni in the winter; the artillery and stores are ordered to Lyon and Grenoble. Fortify Briançon and the frontier against the valleys of Luzerne, Saint-Martin and Angrogne. Winter quarters by Catinat’s memoir. And retreat with such precaution that the enemy can attempt nothing. The full decoded texts, divided into words, with the groups as printed and page breaks, are in the repository under targets/catinat1691/letters .

Six groups stand above 587 in the 1819 print (654, 593, 855, 942, 854, 595) and one glyph on p. 326 is damaged; they are flagged and left without a value. The OCR error rate measured on the two controls is about one group in seventy. Errors that break the French were caught by the image check; a substitution that leaves plausible French (24 for 26, 8 for 587) can survive at that rate, so a passage to be quoted should be checked against the page image; every group’s box is recorded. About a hundred groups fall on entries Bazeries left blank and are decoded from context. Where his clear text of the 8 July letter departs from the figures as printed, either the 1819 compositor or his table is wrong, and only the originals at Vincennes can say which. Whether the minutes of the five unpublished letters survive at the Service historique de la Défense, and whether their substance was already known to Rousset and Catinat’s biographers from other papers, is not checked.*

Il n'est pas necessaire que je vous explique avec quel desplaisir Sa Majesté a appris le desordre avec lequel, contre vostre ordre et sans necessité, Monsieur de Bulonde a pris le parti de lever le siege de Coni, puisque Sa Majesté, en connoissant mieux que personne les consequences, connoist aussi combien est grand le prejudice que l'on recevra de n'avoir pas pris cette place, dont il faudra tascher de se rendre maistre pendant l'hiver. Elle desire que vous fassiez arrester Monsieur de Bulonde et le fassiez conduire à la citadelle de Pignerol, où Sa Majesté veut qu'il [?vo] gardé enfermé pendant la nuit dans une chambre de ladite citadelle, et le jour, ayant la [?juge]berté de se promener sur les remparts, avec un masque. Le Roy est en peine de Monsieur de Vins; et quoyque [?le] ne m'en ayez rien mandé, je suis persuadé que vous n'avez pas oublié de luy mander par des courriers ce qu'il aura à faire, et que vous ne m'en ayez envoié copie en mesme temps. Je doute pas que vous ne fassiez avancer les ouvrages de Carmagnole avec toute la diligence [?posrble], afin de pouvoir vous esloigner de cette place sans en avoir d'inquietude. Sa Majesté demande ce que vous projettez de faire en vous avançant à Poirin et à Quiers. Si vous ne croiez pas pouvoir garder Quiers et Villeneuve d'Ast pendant l'hiver, ne conviendroit-il point de les destruire, pour empescher les ennemis de s'y mettre et de s'en servir à incommoder vos quartiers? Sir, the ordinary post has delivered to me the letters you took the trouble to write me on the [1st!] of this month, about which the King was surprised to see that you did not send by an express courier the bad as well as the good news [?], which must be sent with diligence. His Majesty orders me to repeat to you what I have already told you, which is that His Majesty wished to learn from you who was the author of the proposal for the general assault on the outworks of Cuneo. I beg you to let me know as soon as possible; you [?] are in a position to know it now, since the army is to be reunited. There is no need for me to explain to you with what displeasure His Majesty learned of the disorder with which, against your orders and without necessity, Monsieur de Bulonde took the decision to raise the siege of Cuneo; for His Majesty, knowing the consequences better than anyone, also knows how great is the harm that will come from not having taken that place, which we shall have to try to master during the winter. He wishes you to have Monsieur de Bulonde arrested and taken to the citadel of Pinerolo, where His Majesty wants him [?] kept shut up at night in a room of the said citadel, and by day having the [?li]berty of walking on the ramparts, with a mask. As the governor of Pinerolo is under your orders, you will please send him these [orders] for the [?execution] of His Majesty's will. The King is anxious about Monsieur de Vins; and although [?you] have told me nothing of it, I am persuaded that you have not forgotten to send him word by couriers of what he is to do, and that you have [not] sent me a copy at the same time. I [do not] doubt that you are pushing on the works at Carmagnola with all [?possible] diligence, so as to be able to move away from that place without anxiety about it. His Majesty asks what you plan to do in advancing to Poirino and Chieri. If you do not think you can hold Chieri and Villanova d'Asti during the winter, would it not be advisable to destroy them, to prevent the enemy from settling there and using them to harass your quarters? If the same thing could be done at Asti, you would gain a great advantage from it. You must by now be informed of the orders the King is meanwhile sending to Monsieur de la Hoguette to send you four battalions and fifteen squadrons; as soon as the King has had news [19?] of the success Monsieur de la [?] Mirabouc has had, His Majesty will send him orders to send you two more. I told you in my last the days on which the troops of the Emperor and of the Elector of Bavaria left the neighbourhood of Philippsburg. I am sending orders to the Sieur du Pile to countermand the thirteen thousand setiers of wheat he is to send to Nice, in view of the six thousand already there. You will have learned from Monsieur d'Herleville the talk that Monsieur de Savoie has held, since the news he had of the raising of the siege of Cuneo, about the negotiations of the advocate Perraquin. If you can send money to Casale, I beg you that it be up to a million livres. You may keep the Sieur Olri's mules as long as you think fit, but after that I beg you to send them back to Dauphiné. I am, Sir, your very humble and very devoted servant. M. Louvois. Monsieur, plus le Roy fait reflexion à ce qui s'est passé à Coni, plus Sa Majesté en est touchée, non seulement pour la reputation de ses armes, mais encore par la consideration des obstacles que cette place pourra apporter à l'establissement des quartiers d'hiver en Piedmont; et Sa Majesté, qui eust desiré que vous eussiez pu remarcher à cette place pour en faire le siege avec toute l'armée, connoist bien que cela n'est plus possible presentement. Sa Majesté juge que vous devez vous appliquer à deux choses: l'une, à si bien fortifier Carmagnole que les ennemis n'osent le regarder, et l'autre, à destruire tous les lieux que les ennemis pourroient occuper pendant l'hiver qui pourroient troubler vostre communication avec Cazal et avec Pignerol. Villeneuve d'Ast et Quiers paroissent de cette nature: Sa Majesté estimeroit qu'en marchant pour changer la garnison de Cazal vous les deuriez brusler absolument, epargnant les eglises autant que faire se pourra. S'il y avoit des chasteaux qui puissent ou resserrer vos quartiers ou faciliter la communication de Turin à Ast, Sa Majesté croiroit encore que, pendant que vous estes maistre de la campagne, vous deuriez encore leur faire subir le mesme sort; et vous devez faire ces sortes de choses de maniere qu'il ne paroisse point qu'elles vous aient esté prescrites, et qu'au contraire vous les faites de vous mesme. Ce seroit encore une chose utile de se saisir de Bene, si cela est praticable; et si Carignan [?homme] pouvoit estre occupé par les ennemis pendant l'hiver, vous ne devez pas hesiter à le brusler. Et autant que vous deuriez chercher un combat avant l'arrivée des Allemands, autant devez-vous l'esviter aprés qu'ils seront arrivez, afin de leur donner le temps de devenir malades et de deperir faute de payement [?parti]. Quand je dis esviter, le Roy n'entend pas vous prescrire de vous retirer devant l'ennemi, mais bien d'essayer de vous bien poster, de ne point hesiter à vous retrancher, en sorte que si les ennemis vous veulent attaquer ce soit à leur desavantage. Sur tout ce que dessus le Roy ne vous prescrit rien, mais Sa Majesté vous ouvre seulement des veues sur lesquelles vous ferez ce que vostre bon esprit et vostre affection à son service vous inspirera. Vous pourrez, en renvoiant Monsieur le marquis de Vins sur la frontiere de Provence, disposer des deux [?batails] de [?Montcas], [?elles] mettant en garnison dans les places de derriere, ce qui vous donnera moyen de vous fortifier d'autant. Vous veillerez seulement que vous ne les devez pas mettre dans Pignerol, où il y a deja deux bataillons irlandois. Je vous conjure de presser les ingenieurs de m'envoier un plan de Carmagnole et de m'expliquer sur icelui les pentes des eaux. Comme la [?reisson] doit estre à peu prés faite lorsque vous recevrez cette lettre, rien n'est plus important que d'obliger les peuples à refugier leurs bleds dans les places où le Roy a garnison; et cela est d'une telle importance que vous et Monsieur Bouchu devez y envoier des commissaires qui y tiennent exactement la main, et empescher que les gouverneurs, pour leur propre compte, ne dispensent les peuples d'executer les ordre qui leur seront envoiez pour cet effet. Je ne suis point d'avis que vous obligiez les peuples à livrer leurs bleds presentement, mais seulement de les refugier dans les places, où on leur promettra de ne les point prendre sans payer. Je vous suplie d'aviser Monsieur Bouchu de me faire envoier toutes les semaines des estats de ce qu'il y entrera de bleds et de ce qu'ils se vendront aux marchez. Monsieur d'Herleville vous aura donné part des discours de Monsieur de Savoye sur les negociations que vous avez eues avec luy; il meriteroit bien que, si vous en avez le temps, vous jettassiez deux mille bombes dans Turin. S'il estoit possible de rompre le pont de Turin, ce [?sepaoit] une chose fort utile; mais, ainsi que je vous l'ay marqué ci-dessus, ce sont des veues que Sa Majesté vous met devant les yeux, et non des ordres qu'elle vous donne. Vous [?povaz] compter qu'il sera le quinse aoust avant que la pluspart des troupes allemandes puissent entrer en Piedmont, qu'elles y marchent avec une repugnance infinie, et qu'un grand nombre en desertera. Je ne vous recommende [?fois] de faire entrer beaucoup de fourrages dans Carmagnole, parce que [?de meur] suis persuadé que vous en connoissez [?ne] importance. [?ou] Si les troupes que vous envoi[?]z à Cazal pouvoient passer Montafie, il ne pourroit estre que tres à propos qu'elles s'y fissent [243?] feu, aussi bien que la garnison de Suze à Pianesse quand elle pourra pousser. Je suis, Monsieur, votre très humble et très affectionné serviteur, M. LOUVOIS. Sir, the more the King reflects on what happened at Cuneo, the more His Majesty is affected by it, not only for the reputation of his arms, but also in consideration of the obstacles that this place may put in the way of establishing winter quarters in Piedmont; and His Majesty, who would have wished that you could have marched back to that place to besiege it with the whole army, well knows that this is no longer possible at present. His Majesty judges that you should apply yourself to two things: the one, to fortify Carmagnola so well that the enemy dare not look at it; and the other, to destroy all the places the enemy might occupy during the winter that could disturb your communication with Casale and with Pinerolo. Villanova d'Asti and Chieri seem to be of that kind: His Majesty would think that, when marching to change the garrison of Casale, you should burn them completely, sparing the churches as far as can be done. If there were castles that could either hem in your quarters or facilitate communication from Turin to Asti, His Majesty would further think that, while you are master of the field, you should make them suffer the same fate; and you must do this kind of thing in such a way that it does not appear that it was prescribed to you, but on the contrary that you are doing it of yourself. It would also be useful to seize Bene, if it is practicable; and if Carignano [?] could be occupied by the enemy during the winter, you should not hesitate to burn it. And as much as you should seek a battle before the arrival of the Germans, so much should you avoid one after they have arrived, so as to give them time to fall sick and waste away for want of pay [?]. When I say avoid, the King does not mean to prescribe that you retreat before the enemy, but rather that you try to post yourself well and not hesitate to entrench, so that if the enemy wish to attack you it is to their disadvantage. On all the above the King prescribes nothing to you; His Majesty only opens views to you, on which you will do what your good sense and your devotion to his service inspire. On sending Monsieur the Marquis de Vins back to the Provence frontier, you may dispose of the two [?battalions] of [?Montcas], putting them [?] in garrison in the places behind, which will give you the means of strengthening yourself by as much. Only take care that you must not put them into Pinerolo, where there are already two Irish battalions. I beg you to press the engineers to send me a plan of Carmagnola and to explain to me on it the slopes of the waters. As the [?harvest] must be about finished when you receive this letter, nothing is more important than to oblige the people to take refuge with their wheat in the places where the King has a garrison; and this is of such importance that you and Monsieur Bouchu should send commissaries there to see to it strictly, and to prevent the governors, on their own account, from excusing the people from carrying out the orders that will be sent them for this purpose. I am not of the opinion that you should oblige the people to deliver their wheat now, but only to take refuge with it in the places, where they will be promised that it will not be taken without payment. I beg you to advise Monsieur Bouchu to have sent to me every week statements of how much wheat comes in and at what price it sells in the markets. Monsieur d'Herleville will have told you of Monsieur de Savoie's talk about the negotiations you have had with him; he would well deserve that, if you have time, you should throw two thousand bombs into Turin. If it were possible to break the bridge of Turin, it [?would be] a very useful thing; but, as I told you above, these are views that His Majesty puts before your eyes, not orders he gives you. You [?may] count on its being the fifteenth of August before most of the German troops can enter Piedmont, that they march there with infinite reluctance, and that a great number will desert. I do not [?once more] recommend you to bring a great deal of forage into Carmagnola, because I [?] am persuaded that you know its importance. If the troops you are send[ing] to Casale could pass Montafia, it could only be very proper that they should [243?] fire there, as well as the garrison of Susa at Piossasco when it can push forward. I am, Sir, your very humble and very devoted servant, M. LOUVOIS. Catinat, j'ai reçu les deux lettres que vous m'avez écrites le [?g] de ce mois au camp de Faule. Dans l'une vous me parlez du voyage que vous avez fait à Carmagnole et de l'estat où vous avez trouvé cette place. Il seroit à souhaitter qu'elle fust en meilleur estat, et que ce fust un poste qui pust occuper longtemps les ennemis. Dans l'autre je vois que leur armée est toujours à Montcalier et que les troupes qui viennent d'Allemagne arrivent tous les jours. Le general Caraffa, [?connorsant] la petitesse du pais où il [?mioit] aller et le manque[e] de fourrages [?ay], a fait voir sa prevoyance en faisant avance[r] [?r] grains dans les lieux d'où il croira les pouvoir tirer s'il en a besoin. Je vois avec peine ce que vous me mandez du peu de fourrages que vous trouvez où vous estes et dans les lieux circonvoisins. L'inegalité des [?rivies] me donne beaucoup d'inquietude, et j'aprehende qu'elle ne vous mette en estat de ne pouvoir pas marcher aussi promptement que vous le desireriez dans les lieux où vous croirez devoir faire marcher mon armée. S'ils s'approchent de Pignerol, vous [?co] devant noissez le parti que vous devez prendre pour les empescher de rien faire. Je suis bien aise d'aprendre qu'ils ne pensent point à envoier personne du costé de la Val d'Aost pour essayer de penetrer en Savoye; ce seroit une diversion qui, quoyque peu considerable, ne laisseroit pas de pouvoir nous embarasser. J'ai reçu vos deux lettres du 13 de ce mois du camp de Pancalier, sur lesquelles j'aurois bien des choses à vous dire [?sii] en avois resolu de vous envoier le sieur de Chamlay, instruit de mes intentions et de tout ce qui regarde la continuation de la guerre de Piedmont, celle de Savoye, et en un mot ce qui concerne toute ma frontiere. J'ay pris cette resolution ne pouvant vous expliquer assez bien par escrit mes pensées sur tout ce que je croi que vous devez faire, et pour sçavoir les vostres encore plus en destail que vous ne pouvez me les expliquer par escrit, quoyque vous le fassiez avec grande netteté et exactitude. Vous pouvez parler avec confiance sur tout audit sieur de Chamlay; vous le trouverez bien instruit, et quand vous l'aurez entretenu quelques jours, il pourra repasser dans les lieux où la guerre se fera apparament l'année prochaine, pour me rendre compte des mesures qu'il y aura à prendre, tant pour accommoder les lieux où les ennemis pourront venir que pour y faire des preparatifs pour que les troupes qui y seront destinées s'y puissent vivre. Le voyage dudit sieur Chamlay me donnera des connoissances que je n'en ay point, et il en prendra aussi qui dans la suite pourront estre utiles. Cependant [?essay] [?personnz] de vivre le plus longtemps que vous pourrez où vous croirez estre le mieux pour le bien de mon service. N'hesitez point à tirer les bleds qui sont dans Saluces, Savillan et Fossan, et touts les autres grains, tant les miens [?cependant] ceux des particuliers, que vous ferez remettre soit à Carmagnole soit à Pignerol. Je ne vous marque sur cela mes intentions que pour gaigner quelques jours d'avance, ledit sieur de Chamlay estant instruit de mes intentions; il part demain sans faute, et arrivera apparament deux ou trois jours aprés cette lettre, que j'envoie par un courrier exprés. Je suis contant de la franchise avec laquelle vous me parlez; continuez à en user de mesme, et me dites toujours le veritable estat des choses et ce que vous pensez. Vous me parlez dans une de vos lettres du 13 [?e] du peu de fourrages que vous trouvez, et de ce que vous aprehendez que les ennemis ne s'aprochent de Pignerol pour ravager les environs de cette ville et ruiner les establissements que l'on y a faits. Vous vous reglerez sur les mouvements des ennemis, et ferez là-dessus ce que vous croirez le mieux. Vous envoiant le sieur de Chamlay, qui, comme je vous l'ay deja dit ci-dessus, est pleinement instruit de mes intentions, qu'il vous expliquera, il seroit inutile de vous en dire davantage. Et la présente n'étant pour autre fin, je prie Dieu qu'il vous ait, M. de Catinat, en sa sainte garde. Écrit à Versailles ce 19 août 1691. M. Catinat, I have received the two letters you wrote me on the [?] of this month from the camp at Faule. In the one you tell me of the journey you made to Carmagnola and of the state in which you found that place. It would be desirable that it were in better condition, and that it were a post that could occupy the enemy for a long time. In the other I see that their army is still at Moncalieri, and that the troops coming from Germany arrive every day. General Caraffa, [?knowing] the smallness of the country into which he [?] go and the lack of forage [?], has shown his foresight by bringing forward [?] grain to the places from which he thinks he can draw it if he needs it. I see with regret what you tell me of the little forage you find where you are and in the places round about. The unevenness of the [?] gives me much anxiety, and I fear it may put you in a state of not being able to march as promptly as you would wish into the places where you think you should march my army. If they approach Pinerolo, you [?know] beforehand the course you must take to prevent them from doing anything. I am very glad to learn that they are not thinking of sending anyone towards the Val d'Aosta to try to penetrate into Savoy; that would be a diversion which, though of small consequence, would not fail to be capable of embarrassing us. I have received your two letters of the 13th of this month from the camp at Pancalieri, on which I should have many things to tell you [?had I not] resolved to send you the Sieur de Chamlay, instructed in my intentions and in everything regarding the continuation of the war in Piedmont, that in Savoy, and in a word whatever concerns my whole frontier. I have taken this resolution, not being able to explain to you well enough in writing my thoughts on all that I believe you should do, and in order to learn yours in still more detail than you can explain them to me in writing, although you do so with great clarity and exactness. You may speak with confidence on everything to the said Sieur de Chamlay; you will find him well instructed; and when you have talked with him for a few days, he can go back through the places where the war will probably be waged next year, to report to me on the measures to be taken, both to prepare the places the enemy may come to and to make preparations there so that the troops destined for them can live there. The said Sieur Chamlay's journey will give me knowledge I do not have, and he will also gain some that may be useful in future. Meanwhile [?try] to live as long as you can where you think best for the good of my service. Do not hesitate to take the wheat that is in Saluzzo, Savigliano and Fossano, and all the other grain, mine as well as [?] that of private persons, which you will have deposited either at Carmagnola or at Pinerolo. I tell you my intentions on this only to gain a few days in advance, the said Sieur de Chamlay being instructed in my intentions; he leaves tomorrow without fail, and will probably arrive two or three days after this letter, which I am sending by an express courier. I am pleased with the frankness with which you speak to me; continue to use it in the same way, and always tell me the true state of things and what you think. You speak to me in one of your letters of the 13th [?] of the little forage you find, and of your fear that the enemy may approach Pinerolo to ravage the surroundings of that town and ruin the establishments made there. You will regulate yourself by the enemy's movements and do what you think best in the matter. As I am sending you the Sieur de Chamlay, who, as I have already told you above, is fully instructed in my intentions, which he will explain to you, it would be useless to say more. And this letter being for no other purpose, I pray God, M. de Catinat, to keep you in His holy care. Written at Versailles, 19 August 1691. Je ne répondrai point en détail à tout ce qu'elles contiennent, ayant chargé le sieur de Chamlay de vous expliquer mes pensées sur tous les partis que nous pouvons prendre dans la suite de cette guerre. Vous aurez bien examiné tous [?sdcix] ensemble ce qui est praticable de faire, sçachant comme vous sçavez tous deux l'estat de mes affaires, de mes negociations, celui du pais et la force des ennemis. Vous saurez apparemment, quand vous serez ensemble, le parti qu'ils auront pris: s'ils auront marché en Savoie, ou s'ils se seront mis tous ensemble du côté de Turin pour revenir à vous, ou pour vous obliger, aprés avoir consommé tous les fourrages, de vous retirer le premier, de passer la montagne et de leur laisser une liberté entiere dans tout le pais qui est entre Turin et Pignerol. J'envisage toujours avec peine ce qui vous obligera par force à quitter ce pais. Je suis très aise de voir, dans la lettre où vous me parlez de la negociation de Rome, que vous n'oublierez rien de tout ce qui sera possible pour allonger la demeure de mon armée au delà des montagnes. J'ai ordonné au marquis de Barbesieux d'écrire au marquis de Crenan de faire planter les palissades autour de la ville et citadelle de Casal et de faire tout ce qu'il croira nécessaire pour bien défendre la place; et j'ay ordonné en mesme temps que l'on y fist remettre de l'argent, pour qu'il y en eust au moins pour un an et demy. Le marquis de Crenan a aussi ordre de preparer les bleds, les grains et autres choses necessaires pour le mesme temps. Il seroit à souhaitter que la garnison fust plus forte, surtout en cavallerie, pour qu'elle pust inquieter les ennemis et se faire porter plus de respect qu'elle ne fait. Je voudrois bien aussi qu'il y eust plus d'officiers d'artillerie et de canonniers; mais je n'[?esc]ay comme le [?sy] faire entre[r]; et j'ay fait mander au marquis de Crenan de dresser des soldats à bien remuer l'artillerie. Par ce que vous me mandez de Carmagnole, je ne vous voy plus si resolu à l'abandonner depuis avoir veu le memoyre du sieur de Chamlay. Je souhaite que vous [?reso] [?courrier] viez ensemble de le garder, et qu'il soit possible de le faire. Ce que je vous mande ne changer[a] [?ie] [?nace] que vous doit dire le sieur de Chamlay de ma part. Je ne croi pas vous aprendre rien de nouveau quand je vous diray qu'il y a des [654!] cy qui croient que, s'il on pouvoit fortifier Villefranche, y mettre un gros corps d'infanterie dedans, et emplir Saluces, Savillan et Fossan de troupes, l'on pourroit demeurer en Piedmont; vous verrez avec le sieur de Chamlay sur cette proposition ce qu'il sera possible de faire. Je ne me rebute pas de vous parler de ce qui pourrait faire demeurer mes troupes en Piedmont; par l'envie que j'en aurais, cela ne vous doit pas faire passer par dessus ce que vous croirez qui sera le plus utile au bien de mon service. L'on a envoyé au sieur Peletier de Souzy des mémoires par lesquels il paraît que l'on travaille fort et ferme aux fortifications de Carmagnole; cela me fait croire que l'on pourroit le garder. N'oubliez rien pour cela, si nous sommes assez heureux pour que cela se puisse; fait[es] y mettre ce que vous y croirez necessaire. Il n'y a rien que je souhaite tant que la conservation de Pignerol dans tous les partis que nous prendrons. Ce doit être le premier objet, et quand vous le pourrez je serai très aise que vous examiniez bien tout ce que vous croirez que l'on pourra faire [593!] me tirer de l'inquietude où la seule pensée de son siege me met. Si nous sommes assez heureu[x] [507?] pour ne point sortir de Piedmont, dont je doute fort, cela [?aucun] [16?] enlever à tout à fait; si au contraire nous nous mettons l'année prochaine sur la deffensive, il faut, à force de précautions et de travail dans les lieux où vous le croirez nécessaire et d'infanterie, empescher les ennemis d'y pouvoi[r] mesme penser: ce costé-là bien gardé, celui de Suze dans l'estat où vous dites que [855!] le devra mettre, les passages de Savoye garnis de troupes, et les petites villes de Dauphiné et de Provence bien fermées. Je crois que les ennemis seront bien embarrassés. Ce que vous proposez pour les estapes de la Maurienne et de la Tarentaise me paroit bien pensé, et que, n'y ayant plus de cavallerie à passer, il faut oster les fourrages. J'ordonne au marquis de Barbesieux d'écrire que l'on se conforme sur cela à ce que vous manderez. J'attends que le sieur de Chamlay soit revenu pour me déterminer sur toutes choses. Aussitôt que j'aurai pris ma dernière résolution, je donnerai tous mes ordres pour que toutes choses soient en l'état que je pourrais le désirer la campagne prochaine. [?tie] souhaiterois fort qu'en finissant la campagne vous pussiez prendre Coni. Rien ne serait si bon pour le bien de mon service, par toute la raison que vous me dites. Si vous croyez le pouvoir faire, songez aux preparatifs à faire, tant pour ce qui regarde l'artillerie que les vivres. M. Catinat, I have received by the last two couriers the three letters you wrote me from Pancalieri dated the 20th of this month, for I believe the one dated the [16?] is so only by mistake. I shall not answer in detail everything they contain, having charged the Sieur de Chamlay with explaining to you my thoughts on all the courses we can take in the rest of this war. You will have examined well, the two of you [?] together, what is practicable to do, knowing as you both know the state of my affairs, of my negotiations, that of the country and the strength of the enemy. You will probably know, when you are together, what course they have taken: whether they have marched into Savoy, or whether they have all gathered on the side of Turin to come back at you, or to oblige you, after consuming all the forage, to withdraw first, cross the mountains and leave them entire freedom in all the country between Turin and Pinerolo. I still contemplate with regret what will force you to leave that country. I am very glad to see, in the letter in which you speak of the negotiation in Rome, that you will neglect nothing possible to lengthen the stay of my army beyond the mountains. I have ordered the Marquis de Barbezieux to write to the Marquis de Crenan to have palisades planted round the town and citadel of Casale and to do everything he thinks necessary to defend the place well; and I have ordered at the same time that money be sent there, so that there should be enough for at least a year and a half. The Marquis de Crenan also has orders to prepare the wheat, grain and other things necessary for the same period. It would be desirable that the garrison were stronger, above all in cavalry, so that it could harass the enemy and make itself more respected than it is. Francesc Climent, called Çapera, was Benedict XIII’s chamberlain and treasurer and later bishop of Barcelona; he left his papers to the cathedral chapter. Among them Sebastián Puig y Puig found fourteen letters partly or wholly in cipher, deciphered them, and printed them in the appendix of Pedro de Luna, último papa de Aviñón (1920). This is one of them: Pedro Comuel to Climent, 21 Dec 1415 (appendix CXVII, CXVI in the index, pp. 562–563; Çapera no. 669). Of its 822 words Puig prints 308 in italics as his decipherment. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 found no text of the letter in the repository; on 23 October Puig’s pages were fetched as images from Google Books and transcribed ( texts/comuel1415_reading.md , with an English translation). The deciphered passages name Diego de Vadillo, “the cooking-pot of these dealings and tribulations against the Pope”, who led the King of Aragon to his league with the Emperor; set out the King’s new road against Benedict, that Clement VII was not the true pope; and tell Climent to have the Queen of Castile warned by her confessor, “secret, and more than secret”, that her marriage dispensation and her son’s legitimacy hang on Benedict’s title, and to beware of the Archbishop of Toledo (translation). The originals are not digitised, and the archivist Josep Mas noted that Puig studied many of the Schism papers at home in 1920–30 and did not return them all. Puig’s print may be the only witness.

Puig never printed a key, and the only image of any of these ciphers is his facsimile of one page of Benedict XIII’s own letter of 22 June 1400. From that page the key of Benedict’s letters was rebuilt here: a plain substitution, one sign per letter. Puig writes of “la clave o claves”, the key or keys, he recovered, and nothing shows whether this letter, from another writer, used the same one. So it has its own entry. Benedict XIII’s letters are on Benedict XIII to Climent, 1399–1403 (a different or unverified cipher, with its own page); the other letters of his circle each have their own page for the same reason: Santa Cruz to Climent, 1399 , Jafet to Climent, 1400 , Exea to Climent, 1408 , Comuel to Climent, June 1416 .
The ciphertext. No image of the letter exists, so its cipher, its key and Puig’s reading cannot be checked. Blocker: needs the original in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona.

Humili recomendacione premissa post cursorem dni. toletan. misit vobis domino julianus de loba bullas illas de quibus in ultimis literis meis feci mencionem novit deus quo brevius potui expedicionem bullarum illarum procuravi quibus expeditis cum vobis scribere et cursorem facere vellem dictus dns iulianus de loba sciens quod tam de his quam de innovatis et ocurrentibus negociis vobis scriberem tanto bullas accepit et cum eis cursorem velocem vobis destinavit graciam vestram sibi procurare voles quod sine dubio displicuit mi valde non quare bullas misit, ymo placuit, sed quare per eumdem cursorem poteramus omnia expedire et modo illa de causa oportet hunc mittere vobis cursorem cuius expensas et salarium racionabiliter ipse dns. julianus solvere debere precat sibi deus. — Item per dictum cursorem dni. totelani scripsi vobis satis late tam circa prorogationem petitam per ipsum d. toletan. quam de ocurrentibus aliis circa negocia ecclie. et de innovatis et quo modo Ambaxatores dni. Regis Aragon. venerant ad dnm. nrm. et fecerant jam sibi aliam terciam requisicionem, cui statim dns nr. suam fecit responsionem satis copiosam cuius copiam mitto vobis cum presentibus alligatam quamvis scripseram quod illa mitterem per certam notabilem personam etc. sed in brevi, dante dno., ibunt ad presentes partes ipsas due. notabiles persone cum literis et cum quodam compendio in quo ordinatum expressa erunt omnia acta per dum. nrm. et alios in negociis ecclesie unionis et publicabitur. Item. placeat quod v. r. p. responsionem huiusmodi dno. Toletano primo et depost una cum eo vel als. dne. Regine intimari et cum eis bonum quod poteritis in negociis et tribulacione ecclie. procurare presenti, quod domina Regina et Archiepiscop. rescribat forcius illis quibus nuper scripserunt mandan. Ambaxatoribus Castelle perpinian. exeuntes quod statim protestentur contra Regem, quod in factis per Regem non consentiant et hoc facto revertantur sicut jam scripsi et super omnia faciatis quod dns. toletanus scribat suos _didaco de vadillo qui est olla istorum tractatuum et tribulacionum contra Papam; iste proditor est malus homo et iste principaliter induxit regem ad faciendum ligam et tractatus cum imperatore._ — Postquam scripsi vobis per ultimum cursorem multa per dominum _Regem Aragon sunt innovata_ que ut melius sciatis mitto vobis copia litere mi de perpiniano superinde misse presentibus interclusa; credo dum legeritis viscera vestra conmovebuntur, et ut videbitis in copia litere huiusmodi _ad hoc non habuisti capitula seu copiam capitulorum concordie regis cum imperatore, veritas est quod ante concordiam istam rex atemptaverat substraccionem facere sed quia determinatum fuit locum non habere nec illam facere posse, deliberavit per aliam viam contra Papam intrare et procedere recipiendo pro fundamento quod papa Clement predecessor suus [?non] fuit verus papa et Rex sibi non est obediendum etc. et quedam corolaria iniqua, scilicet ex quo potestis dicere domine Regine in quantum periculum ponit eam Rex Aragonum et filium suum regis et regnum Castelle, nam dicta dna Regina ut scitis non poterat contrahere cum rege Castelle patre istius etc. et Papa ut scitis dispensavit cum eis in matrimonio ex quibus procreatus est rex Castelle qui nunc est. Videat ergo domina regina periculum quod si dominus noster non est verus papa non valet dispensationem eum cum rege et regina facta ut prefertur et per consequens Rex Castelle non est legitimus sed bastardus et si non est legitimus, Regnum non pertinet ad eum sed ad regem Aragonum et per istam Rex Aragonum dispossidebit regem Castelle de regno et ipse erit Rex Spanie amore dei. De istis secretissime avisabitis dominam reginam sicut scribo et forcius ita ut impremptetur in ea aliquid diabolicum contra regem Aragon. et provocetur contra eum et faciatis omnino quod confessor domine regine sibi dicat in confessione et foro consciencie ita quod hoc sit secretum inter eos et caveatis quod non senciat hoc sed sit secretum et plus quam secretum inter vos et confessorem et reginam._ Ideo faciatis omnino quod hec _confessor dicat regine et non vos sed caveatis de Archiepiscopo toletano et cum istis iuduci facietis reginam contra regem, postquam Rex iam est discopertum contra Papam terribiliter._ — Mercurii preteriti que fuit XVIII Decembris in publico consistorio fuit petitum pallium pro vobis quod illico concessit dns. nr. Et subsequenter in eodem consistorio secreto tamen filius dni. Didaci de Astunyega fuit factus Episcopus placentinus in form. et dns pacen translatus ad ecclesiam Cartaginen et de ecclia. pacen. contemplacione dne. regine fuit provisum dno. archidiacono de gordon capellano maiori dni. Regis Castelle. Nichilominus de ecclia. dertusen. fuit provisum dno. Othoni de Montecatheno. Hec q. hucusque ocurrere. dum ulteriora ocurrent quamvis peiora statim rescribam V. R. P. quam Altissimus dei filius feliciter et votive conservare dignetur in longitudine dierum. Script. festinanter paniscole XXI Decembris. — Cursor lator presentium vocatus Alfonsus Dalmasanci debet ire ad vos in sex diebus. Arripit iter hodie sabbati XXI decembris hora IX ante meridiem rescribatis si compleverit etc. — V. R. P. filius et servitor humilis. — P. Comollis etc. subdiaconus etc. — Reverendisimo in xpo pr. et dno. meo metuendissimo dno. ff. archiepo. Cesaraugust. in partibus Castelle nuncio Ap.
