Item. placeat quod v. r. p. responsionem huiusmodi dno. Toletano primo et depost una cum eo vel als. dne. Regine intimari et cum eis bonum quod poteritis in negociis et tribulacione ecclie. procurare presenti, quod domina Regina et Archiepiscop. rescribat forcius illis quibus nuper scripserunt mandan. Ambaxatoribus Castelle perpinian. exeuntes quod statim protestentur contra Regem, quod in factis per Regem non consentiant et hoc facto revertantur sicut jam scripsi et super omnia faciatis quod dns. toletanus scribat suos _didaco de vadillo qui est olla istorum tractatuum et tribulacionum contra Papam; iste proditor est malus homo et iste principaliter induxit regem ad faciendum ligam et tractatus cum imperatore._ — Postquam scripsi vobis per ultimum cursorem multa per dominum _Regem Aragon sunt innovata_ que ut melius sciatis mitto vobis copia litere mi de perpiniano superinde misse presentibus interclusa; credo dum legeritis viscera vestra conmovebuntur, et ut videbitis in copia litere huiusmodi _ad hoc non habuisti capitula seu copiam capitulorum concordie regis cum imperatore, veritas est quod ante concordiam istam rex atemptaverat substraccionem facere sed quia determinatum fuit locum non habere nec illam facere posse, deliberavit per aliam viam contra Papam intrare et procedere recipiendo pro fundamento quod papa Clement predecessor suus [?non] fuit verus papa et Rex sibi non est obediendum etc. et quedam corolaria iniqua, scilicet ex quo potestis dicere domine Regine in quantum periculum ponit eam Rex Aragonum et filium suum regis et regnum Castelle, nam dicta dna Regina ut scitis non poterat contrahere cum rege Castelle patre istius etc. et Papa ut scitis dispensavit cum eis in matrimonio ex quibus procreatus est rex Castelle qui nunc est. Videat ergo domina regina periculum quod si dominus noster non est verus papa non valet dispensationem eum cum rege et regina facta ut prefertur et per consequens Rex Castelle non est legitimus sed bastardus et si non est legitimus, Regnum non pertinet ad eum sed ad regem Aragonum et per istam Rex Aragonum dispossidebit regem Castelle de regno et ipse erit Rex Spanie amore dei. De istis secretissime avisabitis dominam reginam sicut scribo et forcius ita ut impremptetur in ea aliquid diabolicum contra regem Aragon. et provocetur contra eum et faciatis omnino quod confessor domine regine sibi dicat in confessione et foro consciencie ita quod hoc sit secretum inter eos et caveatis quod non senciat hoc sed sit secretum et plus quam secretum inter vos et confessorem et reginam._ Ideo faciatis omnino quod hec _confessor dicat regine et non vos sed caveatis de Archiepiscopo toletano et cum istis iuduci facietis reginam contra regem, postquam Rex iam est discopertum contra Papam terribiliter._ — Mercurii preteriti que fuit XVIII Decembris in publico consistorio fuit petitum pallium pro vobis quod illico concessit dns. nr. Et subsequenter in eodem consistorio secreto tamen filius dni. Didaci de Astunyega fuit factus Episcopus placentinus in form. et dns pacen translatus ad ecclesiam Cartaginen et de ecclia. pacen. contemplacione dne. regine fuit provisum dno. archidiacono de gordon capellano maiori dni. Regis Castelle. Nichilominus de ecclia. dertusen. fuit provisum dno. Othoni de Montecatheno. Hec q. hucusque ocurrere. dum ulteriora ocurrent quamvis peiora statim rescribam V. R. P. quam Altissimus dei filius feliciter et votive conservare dignetur in longitudine dierum. Script. festinanter paniscole XXI Decembris. — Cursor lator presentium vocatus Alfonsus Dalmasanci debet ire ad vos in sex diebus. Arripit iter hodie sabbati XXI decembris hora IX ante meridiem rescribatis si compleverit etc. — V. R. P. filius et servitor humilis. — P. Comollis etc. subdiaconus etc. — Reverendisimo in xpo pr. et dno. meo metuendissimo dno. ff. archiepo. Cesaraugust. in partibus Castelle nuncio Ap. Translation comuel1415_en.md # Pedro Comuel to Francesc Climent, Peñíscola, 21 Dec 1415: English Translation of `comuel1415_reading.md` (Puig y Puig 1920, app. CXVII). The passages Puig deciphered are in _italics_. Names modernised here only. Holes: one doubtful word, [?not], as in the reading. ## Translation Most reverend father in Christ and my most dread lord. With humble commendation first made: after the courier of the lord of Toledo, Don Julián de Loba sent you those bulls I mentioned in my last letters. God knows I procured the dispatch of those bulls as quickly as I could; once they were dispatched, when I meant to write to you and send a courier, the said Don Julián de Loba, knowing that I would write to you both about these and about the new and current business, took the bulls and sent them to you by a fast courier, wishing to win your favour for himself. This certainly displeased me greatly, not because he sent the bulls (indeed that pleased me) but because we could have dispatched everything by that same courier; and now for that reason I must send you this courier, whose costs and wage Don Julián himself should in reason pay, God pray for him. — Item, by the said courier of the lord of Toledo I wrote to you at length both about the prorogation the lord of Toledo asked for and about other current matters of the Church and the news, and how the ambassadors of the lord King of Aragon had come to our lord and had already made him another, third, requisition, to which our lord at once made a full answer, a copy of which I send you attached to this, although I had written that I would send it by a certain notable person, etc.; but shortly, God granting, those two notable persons will go to your parts with letters and with a compendium in which all the acts of our lord and of others in the business of the union of the Church will be set out in order, and it will be published. Item, may it please Your Reverend Paternity to make this answer known first to the lord of Toledo and afterwards, together with him or otherwise, to the lady Queen, and with them to procure what good you can in the business and tribulation of the present Church: that the lady Queen and the Archbishop write more strongly to those to whom they lately wrote, ordering the ambassadors of Castile leaving Perpignan to protest at once against the King, that they do not consent to what the King has done, and, this done, to come back, as I wrote before; and above all see to it that the lord of Toledo writes to his people _[about] Diego de Vadillo, who is the cooking-pot of these dealings and tribulations against the Pope; this traitor is a bad man, and he above all led the King to make a league and treaties with the Emperor._ — Since I wrote to you by the last courier much has been _changed by the lord King of Aragon_; so that you know it better I send you, enclosed with this, a copy of a letter of mine sent from Perpignan on it. I believe your heart will be stirred when you read it, and as you will see in the copy of that letter, _you have not had the chapters or a copy of the chapters of the King's concord with the Emperor. The truth is that before this concord the King had tried to make the withdrawal [of obedience], but because it was decided that there was no ground for it and that he could not do it, he resolved to go against the Pope by another road and proceed, taking as his foundation that Pope Clement his predecessor was [?not] the true Pope and that the King need not obey him, etc., and certain wicked corollaries; that is, from which you can tell the lady Queen into what danger the King of Aragon puts her and her son the King and the kingdom of Castile: for the said lady Queen, as you know, could not marry the King of Castile, this one's father, etc., and the Pope, as you know, gave them a dispensation for the marriage from which the present King of Castile was born. Let the lady Queen therefore see the danger: if our lord is not the true Pope, the dispensation granted to the King and Queen, as said, is not valid, and consequently the King of Castile is not legitimate but a bastard; and if he is not legitimate, the kingdom does not belong to him but to the King of Aragon, and by this the King of Aragon will dispossess the King of Castile of his kingdom and be King of Spain, for the love of God. Advise the lady Queen of this most secretly, as I write and more strongly, so that something diabolical against the King of Aragon is imprinted in her and she is roused against him; and by all means see that the lady Queen's confessor tells her this in confession and in the court of conscience, so that it stays secret between them; and take care that it is not sensed, but that it is secret, and more than secret, between you, the confessor and the Queen._ Therefore by all means see that _the confessor, and not you, tells the Queen; but beware of the Archbishop of Toledo; and with these [arguments] you will bring the Queen to act against the King, since the King has now come out terribly against the Pope._ — Last Wednesday, 18 December, in public consistory the pallium was asked for you, and our lord granted it at once. Then in the same consistory, but in secret, the son of Don Diego de Zúñiga was made bishop of Plasencia in form, the lord of Pax [Badajoz] was translated to the church of Cartagena, and the church of Pax was, in regard of the lady Queen, provided to the lord archdeacon of Gordón, chief chaplain of the lord King of Castile. Moreover the church of Tortosa was provided to Don Otto de Montcada. This is what has happened so far; when more happens, even worse, I will write back at once to Your Reverend Paternity, whom may the Most High Son of God deign to keep happily and as you wish for length of days. Written in haste at Peñíscola, 21 December. — The courier bearing this, named Alfonso Dalmasanci, is to reach you in six days. He sets out today, Saturday 21 December, at the ninth hour before noon; write back whether he did it, etc. — Your Reverend Paternity's son and humble servant, P. Comollis, etc., subdeacon, etc. — To the most reverend father in Christ and my most dread lord, the lord Fr. [Francesc], Archbishop of Zaragoza, nuncio of the Apostolic See in the parts of Castile.

The rest of the work is the project’s own: Daniel Bourdeau chose and checked the targets, and the transcription, cryptanalysis and write-ups were done with Anthropic’s Claude models in Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, claude-opus-5, Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), agents run by Brice Dudout, chatgpt-astra-6). Of 711 profiled targets, 468 are the project’s own results, and 98 of them recovered a key by cryptanalysis. 243 targets came wholly or partly from outside contributors and are marked as such: they are left out of the LLM-performance figures. Three ciphered despatches of the Dutch ambassador to the Porte to Van de Spiegel. R2120 was deciphered at the time: its clear decipherment is filed as R2121 and concerns an Ottoman loan. The letters of 1789 and 1793 use a heavily homophonic word code with no surviving key. Feyseel Nur showed from the deciphered siblings that it is alphabetical within blocks of 500 groups, and a table of 354 values decodes both letters in part, 41% of their groups firmly. 2504 2604 2704 2526 336 3131 381 1124 238 541 2004 2263 … a homophonic word code, alphabetical within blocks of 500 Constantinople → The Hague · numerical code · 1788–1793 Van Dedem at Constantinople, 1788–1793 from Frederik Gijsbert van Dedem → to Van de Spiegel Go to the full text ↓ Nationaal Archief, 3.01.26 (L.P. van de Spiegel) inv. 212 (DECODE R2120, R2122, R2131). These are ciphered despatches from the Dutch ambassador to the Porte to Grand Pensionary Van de Spiegel. One was deciphered at the time; the other two were deciphered here with the legation’s own codebook, found in the Nationaal Archief. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method · R2120, read from its contemporary decipherment (R2121): read from existing decipherment (complete) · R2122 and R2131, read with Kroll's codebook (NA 1.02.20 inv. 785): read after matching with key from external sources (complete) · On the map With Feyseel Nur (solution) and EscalatorStudios (key corrected) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Not solved · text not obtained (clear decipherment of R2120 exists) The letters Ciphered despatches from the Dutch ambassador Van Dedem at Constantinople to Grand Pensionary Van de Spiegel (1788–1793) and, in 1799, to the Agent van Staat Van der Goes. The 22 December 1788 despatch concerns an Ottoman loan of seven or eight million. Where Nationaal Archief, 3.01.26 inv. 212 and 2.01.08 inv. 346 (DECODE R2120, R2122, R2131, R1895), all listed with no decipherment. R2120 was in fact deciphered at the time: its pages were rephotographed as R2121 with the clerk’s full clear decipherment. The cipher A heavily homophonic code: one group stands for about one word, and a common word has several groups. R2122 (15 January 1789, 258 groups) and R2131 (9 February 1793, 50 groups) use it; the 1799 despatch (R1895) uses marks over the digits and was not attempted. How it was tried Three deciphered siblings (R2121, R1947, R2053, about 1,300 groups) were transcribed and aligned; only about half of the target groups occur in them and no consistent values came out. The Fagel codebooks are a different, alphabetical system. What it says Only the clerk’s R2121 text is read: the Porte pledges the revenues of several provinces for the loan, and Van Dedem suggests the Directors of the Levant Trade or Hope & Co. take it up. Still open R2122, R2131 and R1895 are unread. Needed: the legation codebook (NA 1.02.04) or Croiset’s working sheets, or more deciphered letters in the same code. R2122, 15 January 1789: the opening groups 2504 2604 2704 also begin R2120 and R2053. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.26 inv. 212, despatch of 15 January 1789, via DECODE R2122.

Record Date What it is State R2120 22 Dec 1788 Two cipher pages, 633 groups. The same pages appear as R2121 P5 and P1. Read at the time: the decipherment is R2121 pp. 2–4 R2122 15 Jan 1789 A “Duplicaat”: two cipher blocks, 258 groups, inside clear Dutch Deciphered with Kroll’s codebook (23 Oct 2026); about ten groups give no sense R2131 9 Feb 1793 One cipher paragraph of 50 groups, framed by 701 … 301 Deciphered with Kroll’s codebook (23 Oct 2026); two groups give no sense, and 87.2% of the words read as sense, under the 95% bar R1895 26 Aug 1799 No. XVIII to the Burger Agent: two- and three-digit groups with ×, ″, ¯ and ~ marks A different system: its own page

This is the clerk’s decipherment (R2121). Van Dedem reports a conference with the Reis Effendi, the Kaymakam and the Kâhya Bey. He told them that the States would not take on the Porte’s proposed loan directly, but might allow it to be raised quietly. The Porte then set out its security: om speciaal voor de geheele Leening en de interest tot de geheele aflossing toe te verbinden al de inkomsten van de Provincie Morea, Negropont, Salonique, Volos, Urfan en Cara Agatz, als ook die van de Landen van Damascus, Sorien en Rodosto … het geheel vast jaarlijks tribut van Jenischeher “to pledge, specially for the whole loan and the interest until full repayment, all the revenues of the provinces of Morea, Negropont, Salonica, Volos, Urfan and Cara Agatz, and those of the lands of Damascus, Sorien and Rodosto … the whole fixed yearly tribute of Jenischeher.” The Porte also offered cotton and wool from Salonica and Smyrna at preferential prices. Van Dedem suggests that the Directors of the Levant Trade, or failing them Hope & Co., should take the loan up. Some place names were left in clear inside the cipher.

Keys. DECODE’s notes link these records to fourteen others in the same code: Kroll 1784–85, Van Haeften 1776, Schenck 1777, and Van Dedem 1789 and 1809. None of them is a key. The undated Fagel series “Cijffers zonder bestemming” (R2842–R2852, before 1793) is made of large alphabetical Dutch codebooks. In R2843 the words from a to ad alone run past 670, so it is not this code. The code. In plain numerical order it is not alphabetical (the second pass below finds the order). For example, welke falls near 2888, landen near 1277 and als near 17. It is also strongly homophonic: in R2121’s clear text de occurs 36 times, but no group occurs more than 11 times, and 541, 641, 841 and 941 are all frequent. The fixed opening 2504 2604 2704 and the frames 701 801 … 301 401 501 601 look like nulls. Cribs. R2121 (Dutch, 633 groups), R1947 (8 Nov 1789, French, 498) and R2053 (1 Dec 1789, French, 196) were transcribed together with their solutions. Only 58% of R2122’s groups and 52% of R2131’s occur anywhere in them. The French and Dutch cribs share only 17% of their groups. Alignment. Word aligners (hard EM and leave-one-out) were run with restarts, and a variant that treats the hundreds digit as a dummy was also tried. None converged to consistent values: the same group came out as different words in different places. Without reliable values the first pass decoded nothing in the two letters.

Feyseel Nur’s second pass (4 October 2026, pull request 21 , with Claude and Codex) re-indexes each group within its block of 500: thousands, then whether the hundreds digit is 5 or more, then the last two digits as a row, then the hundreds digit modulo 5 as a column. In that order the crib values follow the alphabet. Frequent words fill whole rows: en is 541, 641, 741, 841 and 941; nearby are 537 egter , 837 eindelijk , 543 engagement , 643 engager , 644 entrer . The test: on 95 re-aligned crib pairs the rank correlation within blocks is 0.799 for this layout, against 0.351 for plain numerical order, and no shuffled assignment of words reaches 0.368 in 10,000 trials. An independent re-derivation by OpenAI Codex gives the same layout. The resulting table has 354 values, graded by how they are attested. In R2122 (255 groups) 107 have a firm value, and in R2131 (46 groups) 16 do. The decoded words fit the loan of R2121 in R2122: ENVOYÉ het verlangen en van PORTA ontrent het doen een … negociatie . In R2131, a reading about the Porte keeping neutral in the war with the French is suggested by the values but not established. The groups without a value keep only an alphabetical bracket. With holes in nearly every clause, neither letter built sentences on that table, and the reading audit of 22 October 2026 classed both decoded, not read. The codebook found the next day (section 05) settled them.

On 23 October 2026 the inventory of the Constantinople legation (Nationaal Archief 1.02.20, legatie Turkije) turned up, under the chargé Kroll (1784–85), inv. 785, “Sleutel geheimschrift”. Its six scans on the Nationaal Archief site are the codebook itself, headed “Kroll. Un Chiffre”: pages of 500 groups in five columns of 100, the words alphabetical across the rows, letters and syllables at the foot of each column, titles in 3001–3500, and a note on noun and preterite forms. It is this code: Feyseel Nur’s layout above is its layout, and the firm values of the second pass recur in it. Every group of R2122 and R2131 was looked up on the scans ( key/kroll785_values.tsv ) and the cipher re-read on the DECODE images (in R2131, 2261 is 2262). Both letters now give Dutch sentences, with about fourteen groups that give no sense where they stand. 9 February 1793 (R2131). The whole cipher paragraph: Ik heb de eer UwHoEdGestr: te informeeren [?als dat] de Ottomanische Porta sig op eergister volkomen aan de Envoyé van Pruissen [?verbonden] heeft, om gedurende deze oorlog met de Franschen sig in [?alle] [?deelen] neutraal te houden, zonder eenige alliantie meer [met] meergemelde Natie aan te gaande. “I have the honour to inform Your Honour [?that] the Ottoman Porte, the day before yesterday, [?bound] itself fully to the Prussian envoy to keep itself neutral in [?all] [?respects] during this war with the French, without entering into any further alliance [with] the aforesaid nation.” The group 319 (Son Altesse) stands where alle is needed, and 591 gives a stray g . The paragraph builds coherent sentences but reads at 87.2%, under the 95% bar. 15 January 1789 (R2122). Van Dedem’s démarches after the resolution of 2 October; the Porte’s wish for a loan negotiation in the Republic, which he has let the Prussian envoy know of; and a portrait of the English ambassador: Ik [heb] het zelfde omtrent de Engelsche Ambassadeur niet durven observeeren, wijl daar hoogenaamt geen staat op te maaken is, en hij een allergevaarlijkst sujet en vol intrigues is, en hij zo ras het met zijn particulier belang strookt, steets gewoon is van zijn eigen woorden die van een ander te maaken, en om tot zijn doel te geraaken, zig met duijzenderley leugens op te houden en zijn beste vrienden te compromitteren “I [have] not dared to observe the same towards the English ambassador, since no reliance at all can be placed on it and he is a most dangerous subject and full of intrigues; and as soon as it suits his particular interest he is always used to making his own words those of another, and, to reach his end, to busy himself with a thousand lies and to compromise his best friends.” The letter ends on a new Swedish subsidy.

Fourteen groups whose codebook value gives no sense where they stand: 1230, 1330 (twice), 80, 760 (twice), 3928, 1605, 1463, 2622 in R2122; 319 and 591 in R2131; and 4414 in R2122, which is no code in the book. Each occurs once or twice, too few to settle a different value or a slip. An English translation of R2120’s contemporary decipherment is not yet written.

Missive of Mr van Dedem van de Gelder. Right Honourable Sir! In a subsequent negotiation with the Reis Effendi, the Kaymakam, and the Kâhya Bey, lieutenant of the Grand Vizier, of State, I gave him to understand, first, that however much I could assure him that Their High Mightinesses continue to be most strongly attached to the interests of this Court, and show themselves inclined on every occasion to give tokens of their true sentiments and sincere friendship, I must nevertheless forewarn him that I did not at all believe that Their High Mightinesses could or would charge themselves with the direct execution of the proposal he had made; that the only thing which I flattered myself could possibly take place, and at the same time serve to do this Court a direct advantage and give a telling proof of goodwill, would be for Their High Mightinesses to facilitate the carrying out of this negotiation, either directly or by connivance, as the circumstances of the time would best allow, and [?] it solely by their tacit consent. Secondly, that the Porte should first fix and state at what rate the annual interest would run, and in what manner and by what fixed and certain funds — apart from the general obligation of this whole Ottoman Empire — it intends to make the lenders entirely safe and easy, both for the sum lent and for the promised annual interest and its further discharge; and within or after what time and in what manner the actual repayment will finally be made. But since the Ministry does not know what is required in the Republic on such occasions, though it is absolutely inclined to accept all reasonable conditions, the request is that I should first hand over a plan in which all the conditions on which a loan of 7 or 8 millions could take place are specified. But at my instance it has been provisionally settled that, specially for the whole loan and the interest until full repayment, all the revenues of the province of the Morea, Negroponte, Salonica, Volos, Urfan and Kara Ağaç shall be pledged, as also those of the lands of Damascus, Syria and Rodosto, which nine lands each yield the Porte annually fifty thousand kilos of wheat, Constantinople measure. Further, for greater security and for payment of the interest, they wish in addition to pledge the whole fixed annual tribute of Yenişehir, which brings the Porte four hundred and fifty thousand piasters in money a year. Moreover the Ministry will undertake every year to cede by preference to the Republic a quantity of cotton and a portion of the produce of the lands of Yenişehir and Smyrna, as also a portion of the wool that comes from Salonica, at the current (price) or a fixed sum; and if (the) money is transported with one or more warships or other large ships which one would [?find] for the war, the Ottoman Porte [?...] [?the same] at a moderate sum […] buy. And since I consider this moment a good time to obtain for the Republic in general, and for commerce and navigation in particular, privileges of great importance which otherwise could not be hoped for, and since I would moreover already dare to answer that, if the management of it were entrusted to me, I would engage the Ottoman Empire to set the interest so high that one could count on at least 6 per cent clear, I consider myself obliged to commend the matter anew to Your Honour's serious consideration, and to put it to you whether, for the reasons given, it would not be the business of the Directors of the Levant Trade to take its execution upon themselves, so as by that means to give new lustre to commerce in that part of the world. If so, I beg Your Honour to communicate the contents of this letter to them, since, having no cipher with those gentlemen, I neither can nor dare write to them directly about it. Hoog Edele Gestrenge Heer! Van begrip zijnde, dat het belang en politique systema van Haar Hoog Mogenden en dat van [1230] derzelve twee nieuw geallieerden en [1330] tegenwoordig toestand van zaaken, door de resolutie van den twee October, meer als ooit vooraf voor een en het zelfde moet gehouden worden, zijn zo bij de Porta als elders al mijn demarches, welke tot de ontfang van die resolutie door het manqueeren van de [?troupes] instructie genoegsaam werkeloos hebben moeten blijven, daarna, in allen deele geregeld, en het avantage hebbende bij elke gelegendheyd ten klaarsten te bespeuren [dat] het gantsch Ministerie een bijzonder vertrouwen in mij steld, kan ik UHoogEd: Gest: (na waarheyd) versekeren [dat] mijne insinuaties niets van goed effect geweest zijn, en ik niet twijfel of dezelve zullen bij continuatie van aanbelang genoeg gerekent worden, om ingang te vinden. Uyt eerst voormelden hoofde, heb ik mede dienstig geoordeeld de Envoyé van Pruissen het verlangen van de Ottomanische Porta omtrent het doen eener Negociatie in de Republiek niet geheel te moeten laaten ignoreren, ten einde de Koning zijn Meester, wie zijn belang zeker mede is [dat] de Porta tegenwoordig niet verleegen gelaaten, noch aan eenig ongepaste vernedering bloot gesteld word, daar van tot deszelfs narige opening te geeven. Ik [heb] het zelfde omtrent de Engelsche Ambassadeur niet durven observeeren, wijl daar hoogenaamt geen staat op te maaken is, en hij een allergevaarlijkst sujet en vol intrigues is, en hij zo ras het met zijn particulier belang strookt, steets gewoon is van zijn eigen woorden die van een ander te maaken, en om tot zijn doel te geraaken, zig met duijzenderley leugens op te houden en zijn beste vrienden te compromitteren, durvende ik mij ter overlegging van dien gerust beroepen en verlaaten op het getuygenis dat Zijne Majesteit de Koning van Pruissen en alle andere hoven welke alhier een minister hebben daarvan kunnen geeven. En zonder [80] minst moeite zou ik het verleenen van een nieuw subsidie aan Zweeden geheel tegen konnen [1330], doch bedenkende [?de Middellandsche Zee] aan de volvoeren [760] der desseinen van de drie geallieerde Mogenheden zou kunnen schadelijk zijn, heb ik daar aan in [?Maison] reeds voordeel gedaan. En zal ik, ofschoon de Minister van Zee omtrent alles zeer agterhouden [760] handeld en nooit iets daarvan [4414] te kennen ge [?de Keizer van Rusland], egter bij continuatie dat point aanraaden. High Noble Honourable Sir! Being of the view that the interest and political system of Their High Mightinesses and that of [1230] their two new allies and [1330] the present state of affairs, through the resolution of the second of October, must more than ever before be held to be one and the same, all my démarches, both at the Porte and elsewhere, which until the receipt of that resolution, for want of the [?troops'] instruction, had to remain largely idle, have since then been regulated in every respect; and having the advantage of perceiving most clearly on every occasion [that] the whole Ministry places a particular trust in me, I can assure Your Honour (in truth) [that] my insinuations have been of no good effect, and I do not doubt whether, if continued, they will be reckoned of enough importance to find acceptance. For the first-mentioned reason I have also thought it useful not to let the Prussian envoy wholly ignore the Ottoman Porte's wish concerning the making of a negotiation in the Republic, so that the King his master, whose interest it certainly also is [that] the Porte be not now left embarrassed nor exposed to any unseemly humiliation, may be given notice of it for its further opening. I [have] not dared to observe the same towards the English ambassador, since no reliance at all can be placed on it and he is a most dangerous subject and full of intrigues; and as soon as it suits his particular interest he is always used to making his own words those of another, and, to reach his end, to busy himself with a thousand lies and to compromise his best friends; for the proof of which I dare confidently appeal to and rely on the testimony that His Majesty the King of Prussia and all other courts that have a minister here can give of it. And without [80] least trouble I could wholly oppose [1330] the granting of a new subsidy to Sweden, but, considering [?the Mediterranean] could be harmful to the execution [760] of the designs of the three allied powers, I have already made an advantage of it in [?Maison]. And although the Minister of the Sea [the Kapudan Pasha] acts very reservedly [760] about everything and never [4414] makes known anything of it [?the Emperor of Russia], I shall nevertheless, continuing, recommend that point. And what would do that matter no little good is the success of the known negotiation, since a sum could then be used directly in that direction. Not wishing to detain Your Honour's attention further this time, I refer for the public news to my letters of yesterday and today to the Griffier, with which, assuring you of my respect, I have the honour to remain with all due esteem, High Noble Honourable Sir, Your Honour's humble and obedient servant. Thurloe’s office intercepted this letter from Brussels in June 1656 and Thomas Birch printed it in 1742 in English. The writer has received White’s letter of 14 April, brought by the footman of monsieur de Barrière (the Prince of Condé’s agent in London), and suspects that others were intercepted. Then: “The enclosed paper is a new direction to write to me by the way”, and the cipher. White is probably one of the White brothers, Richard, Ignatius or Andrew, whom Cryptiana discusses; du Gard is not identified. The top of p. 79: the new direction, in figures and letters. Image: Thomas Birch, A Collection of the State Papers of John Thurloe (1742), vol. 5 p. 79, via the Internet Archive. This letter was one of four short pieces with no known decipherment in Birch’s volumes that Cryptiana lists together. They share only the printed source and each is in its own cipher: Beverning and Vande Perre to Boreel, 1653 , Brussels to Copinger, 12 August 1656 and Waddall to “Vanyeare”, 22 August 1656 each have their own page.

As printed: 18, 15, 4, 20, 87, q, t, 20, y, 1. and 12, m, 17, 24, 15, 8, 15, 17, f, 20, 18, 15, 9, 7, 6, 13, 20. That is 27 signs, 19 of them distinct; 15 and 20 occur four times each. The letters among the figures may be plain or may be signs in their own right; at this length nothing settles it. Every royalist and Commonwealth key of 1653–60 that Cryptiana publishes (Marshall 1656–58, Barwick–Hyde 1659–60, Stamford 1655, Butler 1656, the Charles II key intercepted in 1655, Kingston 1658, Westrope 1655, the Hague agent and Blake) was applied and scored with an English quadgram model. The best results are strings like “edaewQTeYa”: no name, no place.
The address (27 signs): not read. Blocker: too short. No key online; the ciphers of the Bruges and Brussels royalist agents of 1656 would be in the Clarendon manuscripts, which are not online.

My cousin, having been informed that you give all possible support to my affairs, I wished to write and ask you to continue in the future, considering the extreme need in which I now find myself after obeying certain commands of the king, which caused me to enter this war. You will learn more fully from the commander of Saint John, my ambassador, whom I have instructed to communicate everything to you. Please give him such assistance as he needs and believe what he tells you on my behalf. By doing this you will oblige me increasingly to you, as our Lord knows. Having commended myself to your good grace, I pray that he keep you in his protection. From Arnhem, this eighteenth day of July [year absent]. This translates the apparent sense, not every literal anomaly. “Certain” interprets the unexpanded aulc ; “eighteenth” interprets dih[u]itieme . The cipher gives titles, not the personal names of the recipient or ambassador.

Short French, German and Italian substitution probes on rough transcriptions gave no reliable decryption. Extending the transcript to all sixteen lines gave French fragments under a five-gram model. Image comparison then corrected compound signs and nulls: the paired looped stems labelled DD give s, and the paired arches CE give r. Tall looped f forms, small circles and several other shapes are nulls. Early drafts had confused m/n zigzags, seven/b with corner/f, and angular u with a plain cross/g. The address and body share letter values and null behaviour. Their coherent decryptions cross-check each other, but are not independent known plaintext. A synthetic 180-letter French substitution control was recovered exactly by the probe; it checks the solver implementation only. The searches recorded in the notes found no earlier decipherment, but one existed. George Lasry had recovered the key in 2023. His reconstructed key for the Duke of Guelders’ cipher (BnF fr. 3015) is published in section 2 of S. Tomokiyo’s “George Lasry’s codebreaking” . It notes that many symbols in the ciphertext are needlessly doubled. The work on this page is therefore an independent re-solution. It has not yet been checked symbol by symbol against Lasry’s table. The catalogue of BnF Français 5190 lists no. 171 as d’Émery’s cipher letter of 25 January 1636 and no. 172 as Rohan’s reply. D’Émery was the king’s ambassador to Victor Amadeus I of Savoy in these months; in May 1636 the duke names him as party to the plan sent to Rohan. A letter on the 1804 settlement of the House of Orange’s claims, with 128 groups of a French numerical nomenclator reaching at least 2510 (DECODE R2238). Every key reachable online (Euler’s Grand Chiffre in all its variants, the KHA and Fagel family keys, British Library and Uppsala French codes) was tested and ruled out; the passage is too short for a ciphertext-only attack. The key is most likely in the undigitised KHA packet A31-902. 1087, 638, 1193, 1083, 1531.18.536.503t, 537.788e, 2510, 1114.137 … key not found: the codebook reaches at least 2510 The Hague → William V in exile · French numerical nomenclator · 18 June 1804 Robert Fagel to William V, 18 June 1804 to William V Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V (old inv. nr. 337), DECODE R2238: three pages, the middle one a coded passage of 128 numerical groups between clear French sentences about the Orange compensation talks with the Batavian Republic. The code groups were transcribed from the DECODE images and the letter was dated and placed in its negotiation. No key was found. Every key that can be reached online, in DECODE and in the digitised Royal Collections and Fagel papers, was tested and ruled out, and the passage is too short for the key to be recovered from the ciphertext alone. No decipherment is known; the key has to come from the archive. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter Robert Fagel to the exiled Stadholder, The Hague, 18 June 1804, on the final liquidation of the House of Orange’s claims. Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V (old inv. nr. 337); DECODE R2238, which records no decipherment. The cipher 128 numerical groups, 99 distinct (12 to 2510), a large syllabic nomenclator for French; dots join groups inside a word. How it was tried The key was sought in the Stadholder’s 1782 Grand Chiffre (R1024), all four KHA keys, the Fagel family keys R2842–R2852, the British Library French codes of 1798–1805, the Uppsala key R5160 and the sibling book cipher. None gives French. Why it resists A text this short from a code of about 2,500 values has no unique ciphertext-only solution. Still open The text. The likeliest key is KHA A31-902, a packet with no scans; an archive request is drafted.

The first page (P2) is in clear: a letter from the Hereditary Prince of the 6th announces the Stadholder’s departure; the courier Gaebel arrived on the 9th; the Commissaires of the House kept him so that d’Yvoy could be briefed; a note went to the Batavian side, whose answer was that he hoped to speak with Damen. The second page opens in clear, “Dès lors il n’a plus fait entendre parler de lui, et l’on ne tardera pas à connaître la déclaration, sur laquelle les instructions de V. A. S. et celles du ministre du Roi sont parfaitement d’accord”, then goes into figures. The last page closes “La Haye 18 Juin 1804 … R. Fagel”. The context is established from print. Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken IV prints the surrounding papers: d’Yvoy’s appeal to Talleyrand of February 1804, his promise of 500,000 guilders for payments in Paris, Berlin and The Hague, Princess Wilhelmina’s letter of 14 June saying the arrangement was decided, and Fagel and d’Yvoy’s return with the signed convention on 7 August. It does not print this letter.

128 groups, 99 distinct, two to four digits; 1531, 1731 and 2510 were checked at high resolution and are genuine four-digit groups. Commas separate words and dots join groups inside a word. The words & , car and que are in clear, and a boxed insertion adds a line between the rows. Small superscript marks (c, 3, 6, 9, fractions) follow some groups; their reading is uncertain. The full transcription is targets/fagel1804/ciphertext.txt .

Key What it is Result R1024, Grand Chiffre (Euler, 1782) KHA code of 4,732 transcribed entries, 51–5000, with an optional additive table Direct lookup is nonsense; all 187 row and 187 column starts of the table fail; so do all 5,000 cyclic shifts, affine maps, complements and digit permutations, scored with a French language model (best −10.2 per character against −8.5 for the letter’s own clear French). The table also requires a start letter at the head, which the letter lacks. R2233, R2235, R2240 The other KHA keys in DECODE (1793–1801) Small homophonic or name systems; cannot produce the groups R2842–R2852 Fagel family keys, Nationaal Archief 1.10.29 Every range audited page by page; none goes above about 1055 R1035, R1891 Dutch legation codebooks, 1798 and 1803 Dutch-language; the plaintext is French R8963/R8964, R8984, R8987 British Library French codes, 1798–1809 Numbered only to 750 or less; nonsense, also modulo 1000 R5160 (Uppsala) French nomenclator, Chiffre François, de M. de Lacy Numbered 210–841 only R2237, R2239, A32-630 Sibling letters and deciphered file of 1795–97 Euler/Boyer small book cipher, references to about 334; a different system DECODE holds no second message in this code, so there is no parallel text to crib from either.

With 128 groups from a code of about 2,500 values, no statistical attack can give a unique decoding; only the codebook or a deciphered copy can. The modern KHA inventory does not match DECODE’s old number 337; the subject belongs with A31-2306–2308, the 1802–1804 compensation negotiations. The best target is A31-902 , a packet of court cipher papers of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, which the Royal Collections’ catalogue backend confirms has no scans. After it come A31-2307 and A31-2308 (1804), A31-2292–2293, and Robert Fagel’s negotiation file, Nationaal Archief 1.10.29 no. 1909. A research request to the Koninklijke Verzamelingen is drafted as targets/fagel1804/ARCHIVE_REQUEST.md .

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (81% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Harumi-Matsuba (transcription, solution) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (81% of the cipher) The letters Scipion de Fiesque (Scipione Fiesco), French envoy to Emperor Maximilian II, to Catherine de’ Medici and Charles IX, October 1567 to November 1569: 23 letters with cipher passages, 44 pages, 29,707 signs. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 15919, via Gallica (btv1b90573568). No DECODE record. The cipher A homophonic alphabet of letters, digits and invented signs, two to five per letter, with doubled-letter signs, about a dozen word codes and null groups. How it was deciphered Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed the key for this volume; Harumi-Matsuba transcribed every cipher page with AI models and decoded it. Here the key was re-applied, the decodes scored and checked against the decipherment of the time on the facing page, and every letter built into French sentences from the decode (22–23 October 2026), with the doubtful places re-read on native-resolution images. Four letters follow decipherments of the time found in the volume. What it says Levies in Germany for the Huguenots, the death of Don Carlos and the marriage negotiation, Archduke Charles’s journey to Spain, and after Moncontour the Emperor’s offer to mediate. Still open The letter of 10 September 1569, whose reading leans on too many look-alike sign choices; phrase holes in five letters and about 90 single-word holes; a few lone codes. The transcription is AI-only. Credit Reading contributed by Harumi-Matsuba (issue #52), made entirely with AI models (Claude; OpenAI Codex and Claude Sonnet for the cross-checks). No human has checked the transcription. Their figures, 85.0–93.6% agreement between two AI transcriptions and a shuffled-key control, measure consistency, not sense. Key by Satoshi Tomokiyo.

Scipion de Fiesque, a Genoese in French service, was Charles IX’s envoy at the court of Maximilian II from the autumn of 1567, when the King’s marriage to the Emperor’s daughter Elisabeth was being negotiated. BnF Français 15919 (formerly Harlay 238) holds 174 folios of his letters to the King and to the Queen Mother. Most open and close in clear and carry the sensitive part in cipher. Satoshi Tomokiyo noted that many are partly in cipher and reconstructed the key so that the passages with no decipherment of the time could be deciphered. The letter of 15 November 1567 to the Queen Mother: the clerk’s docket in clear, then the cipher. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15919 f. 18r (Gallica view 22), via Gallica. Harumi-Matsuba’s page list (44 pages) runs from October 1567 to 4 November 1569: eighteen letters to the Queen Mother and five to the King (15 February 1568, 4 September 1568, 10 September, 20 October and 29 October 1569). One is dated from Speyer (2 December 1568), the rest from Vienna. The per-page table, with view numbers, sign counts and a one-line summary, is in contributed/docs/PAGES.en.md in the repository folder.

Tomokiyo’s table (Cryptiana, “French Ciphers for German (and Eastern) Affairs”) gives each letter two to five signs: digits (4 = b, 1 and 8 = i, 9 = n), letters used as signs (a and o = e, x = f, p = l, u = o), and invented forms (Δ = i, ϕ = m, ⊢ = q, ⊣ = r, ß = r). There are signs for doubled letters (ee, ff, ll, mm, nn, rr, ss), word codes (que, qu’il, et, vous, pour, le Roy, l’Empereur, and Φ for Saxe) and groups of clear-looking letters ( par , moy , bro ) that are nulls. The contributor named the signs ( key.tsv , 95 entries) and inferred 23 values the table lacks, among them 16 = ce, ρ = e and the pair ꝑꝑ = ff. All 44 pages are in this one key.

Harumi-Matsuba opened issue #52 on 20 October 2026 and extended it twice the same day, with the work in a public repository (data CC BY 4.0, code MIT). The account was created on 19 October. Their own description of the method: First transcription by Anthropic’s Claude, from line crops of the BnF’s full-size images. Disagreements with OpenAI Codex transcriptions shown on enlarged crops to Codex and Claude Sonnet; a sign was corrected only where both agreed. Afterwards, fresh Codex transcriptions made without sight of the first: 85.0–93.6% agreement by value per page (the lower run where there are two). For every page, 1,000 keys with the letter values shuffled: none scores as French-like as the true key. Line-by-line readings of five letters, most lines marked as inferred (word division, supplied spelling, the choice between s and p for one looped sign); mechanical decodes of all 44 pages. A person chose the target and decided to publish; no person checked the transcription. Agreement between two AI readers measures their consistency, and a shuffled-key control shows the key is right, but neither shows how much of the text reads as sense. This project’s bar for a complete reading is 95% of the cipher read as sense, measured. So the result is recorded here as a contributed result with a partial extent.

The contributed key was re-applied to every transcription with this project’s own decoder ( measure.py ): 29,627 of 29,707 signs take a value (99.7%). That is the share of signs with a value, not of text read: see the note after this list. Under the project’s period French model ( fr-1530-despatches ) the decodes score −2.37 to −3.42 per character; the best of 200 shuffled keys per page scores −4.38 to −5.31, and none of the 8,800 reaches the true key. Clean French scores −1.64 on the same model. Split into words of a period French lexicon, 81.0% of the decoded letters fall in words, against 27.6% for shuffled keys and 90.3% for clean modern French with the spaces removed. Pages range from 68% (view 8 left) to 90% (view 155 right). The key is right and the decodes are mostly French, but between a fifth and a tenth of the text is not yet words, which matches the contributor’s own marking of most lines as inferred. Reading audit, 22 October 2026. Read as sentences (George Lasry’s test: can the text be built into sentences and translated?), only two pages hold: f. 79r and f. 94r in the contributed readings, on Archduke Charles’s journey to Spain, with scattered holes. The readings of ff. 39r–v, 100r and 158r have holes in most lines, and the 44 mechanical decodes are unspaced with wrong letters (0–17% of sentences clean). So that day 21 letters, and the other pages of the two, were decoded, not read: about 6% of the signs read, against the 99.7% that take a value. The re-reading that followed is in section 06.

The volume holds one decipherment made at the time: view 23 right, headed “deschiffré de la precedente”, is a clear copy of the letter of 15 November 1567. The contributor found it but did not use it, because AI readers of its cursive agreed only 51–55% with their decode. It was transcribed here by eye from a 2,600-pixel image, as far as the end of the cipher on view 22 right ( calib_v023r.txt ). The decipherment of the time: “Madame, j’ay puis le partement de mons r de Lignerolles qui fut le cinquiesme de ce moys…” Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15919 f. 19r (Gallica view 23), via Gallica. Of its 1,193 letters, the contributed decode of view 22 right matches 1,000 (83.8%), and 98 of its 182 words of three or more letters come out whole ( calib.py ). The sense runs the same throughout: Lignerolles has left for the Duke of Saxony, it is rumoured that horse and foot are being raised in Germany for those who have taken arms against the King, the Emperor expects his mandates to stop it, he has written “de bonne encre noire” to two princes. Two places differ in content. Where the copy has “au pays du duc de Wirtemberg et du conte palatin”, the decode has the Φ code for Saxe and no palatin . And the looped sign that serves for both s and p gives desuis , sarteiment for depuis , partement . This reading of the cursive is itself not checked by a second reader. The same check found a gap: the cipher of this letter continues on view 23 left (f. 18v), which is not in the contributed transcription. Its text is on the decipherment page, from “de son pays d’Austriche” to the signature. View 23 left was transcribed and decoded here on 23 October 2026 (13 lines, 446 signs) and checked against the decipherment, which abridges it.

On 22 October 2026 every letter was built here into French sentences from the key decode and translated ( read/<date>_reading.md and _en.md ); four letters (15 November 1567, 4 June, 21 August and 6 November 1568) follow decipherments of the time found in the volume, on view 23 right and in the margins of views 65, 103 and 125 right, three of them not recorded before. On 23 October view 6 right (the first cipher page of 11 October 1567) and view 23 left were transcribed from native-resolution crops, the sign Dz was settled as con , and the single-word holes of seventeen letters were worked through on the images (161 bracketed holes down to 90): this hand writes the number codes with z for 2 and i for 1 (“zo” = 20 pour , “i4” = 14 estre ), which closes many of them. Twenty-two letters now build sentences. The letter of 10 September 1569 stays decoded, not read: its reading clears the sentence test, but 4.1% of its letters rest on look-alike sign choices that nothing outside confirms. Square brackets mark supplied letters or open codes, [?word] a doubtful word, [...] an unread place. 14 August 1568, to the Queen Mother: clear opening, then cipher on why the Emperor sends Archduke Charles to Spain. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15919 f. 94r (Gallica view 99), via Gallica. 6 March 1568, to the Queen Mother (f. 39r): j'ay entendu que le duc Jehan Guillaume [de] Saxe, qui est allé en France pour vostre service, a amené avec luy six prescheurs qui sont d'une secte qui s'appelle Flacciani . 4 September 1568, to the Queen Mother (f. 100r; docketed “au Roy”, but the cipher addresses “Madame”), on the marriage: Il m'a dict qu'a ceste heure il n'y a plus aucune difficulté que le mariaige [ne se] face, car le prince d'Espaigne estoict mort; mais que [pp] desiroict d'estre mediateur [de] ce mariaige . The lone code pp is the King of Spain by sense. 29 October 1569, to the King (f. 158r), after Moncontour: Lequel m'a dict qu'il ne s'est meu a mettre en avant ce party que pour une sincere affection et grand desir qu'il a de [vous] veoir delivré de ceste guerre intestine . The mechanical decodes of all 44 pages are in contributed/data/decoded_*.txt , the contributor’s line readings of five letters in contributed/docs/READING.en.md .

10 September 1569 : decoded, not read, for its look-alike sign choices (the y-shaped s/p signs and others); the partial reading is in read/1569-09-10_reading.md . Phrase holes after the image checks, each re-read on native crops: f. 79v lines 1–3 and f. 80 lines 1 and 8 (17 July 1568); f. 100r line 18 and three words in lines 24–26 (4 September 1568); view 38 left line 17 (15 February 1568); f. 39r lines 8, 22–23 and 29 (6 March 1568). No decipherment of the time covers them. Under the 95% bar. Measured on the words of the readings, six letters that build coherent sentences stay under it: 6 March 1568 (93.3%), 12 June 1568 (94.8%), 17 July 1568 (94.4%), 4 September 1568 to the King (94.0%) and to the Queen Mother (94.3%), and 20 October 1569 (94.4%). About 90 single-word holes in the seventeen letters checked on 23 October, each with its figures in the reading logs. View 6 right (11 October 1567): two words in lines 5–6 and about ten doubtful words; view 23 left (15 November 1567): the bearer’s name (nine signs) and about seventeen signs that the decipherment of the time abridges. Lone signs and codes whose values are not settled: ϖ (the Emperor or the King, eleven places), ∞ alone, =ii, pp (the King of Spain by sense), the group ffx-3y and a few more; 16 is ce or vostre . Transcription : the contributed transcription is AI-only and no person has checked it; the pages transcribed here are single AI transcriptions checked against the key. Untranscribed cipher was found on views 7 left, 110 right, 34 and 49.

I begged His Majesty to do me the favour of telling me his will, so that I could inform you. He told me it was true that, seeing so many disorders, he could do no less than complain [?bitterly] of the condition of the times, and that he put this [?misfortune] down only to the disunion of the Christian princes, who are more inclined to their private interest than to the public good, [v007l] and blinded by their own interest, have [?made] the evil known so far that for his part he will spare nothing in his power to restore Christendom to good peace and union; and he praises this good will [?greatly], of which he has always been well assured, saying that you have governed yourself so wisely that the King and his kingdom remained in good peace and quiet; and he thanked God for this good inspiration He has given you, to be willing to apply yourself to so good a work. And because the matter is of great consequence and there will be many difficulties, he wishes to think about it and take counsel, and afterwards he will give me an answer. I told him I am sure that if he would set about it [?in earnest], on this side you will show that it will not be for want of you that good order and union are put [into it], and that I hope it could come to a good conclusion, given that the greatest forces of Christendom are [?under] the hands of him, the King and the King of Spain; that there is no doubt the rest will fall in with whatever they [?agree], and that His Majesty, that it would profit him more than the others, for if by his means the said [v007r] [were] helped in their need. He told me he had well understood all that, and that God knows how he has always wished to see Christendom in good union, and told me again that he would think about it and soon give me an answer. It seemed to me that he has taken a liking to the proposal; still we can say nothing until such time as his answer has come, and so I have kept back the courier to send you the decision, and have written you this letter so that you are not troubled by so long a delay. Since then he has told me that he would have cause to complain of the King, of the bad offices his ambassador does against him at Constantinople, but that he does not complain of it [?at all], for he will not believe it. I told him that what he had just said to me, the other time I was here, people were spreading the same rumour, that the King's ambassador was pushing the Turk at Constantinople to come and do harm to His Majesty, which thing was very far from the truth; and that I begged him to do me the kindness of not believing the ill-disposed, and that there are people in the world who seek nothing but disunion between him and the King, showing him by several reasons [v008l] and that he could well know that [ϖ] and you have always shown him good affection. And he told me it might well be that this ambassador had done these bad offices of his own accord without [?your] knowledge, further; that he had been informed that an ambassador whom you are sending to Constantinople had passed through Venice. I told him I did not know that you were sending one there, but that I was quite sure you would negotiate nothing to his prejudice, and that if that were done it would be contrary to the good will you have to work for the said union; and I begged him to believe that you proceed in it with the best and most sincere friendship that is possible. Il n'est survenu autre chose, sinon que le bruict couroit en ceste ville qu'il se levoit beaucoup de gens de pied et de cheval en Allemaigne pour aller en France en faveur de ceulx qui ont prins les armes contre le Roy. Et sur ce que je luy disois que au pays du duc de Wirtemberg et du conte palatin se faisoient ces amatz, il me dict qu'il a escript a ces deux particulierement de bonne encre noire, et qu'il espere qu'ilz ne vouldront contrevenir a leur foy ne a ce qu'ilz ont juré, et que je m'asseurasse de ce qu'il m'a dict tant de fois, qu'il veult que par experience vous congnoissiez la bonne envye qu'il a d'entretenir bonne amitié envers le Roy, et qu'il y chemine du bon pied; dont je l'ay remercyé, et prié croire et s'asseurer que le Roy et vous n'auriez aussi moindre affection envers luy. Il me demande tousjours comme vont les affaires de France, mais je ne luy en sçay que dire, et les nouvelles que nous avons par deça disent la plus partie [?le] moyen de Chantonnay. L'empereur tient ce jourd'huy une diette [v023l] de son pays d'Austriche, qui n'est pour autre chose que pour avoir de l'argent; et apres qu'elle sera achevée, il s'en va a Prague. [?Et] je vous envoye ceste lettre par le [?chemin] de Flandres, [?par] [?ce] [?que] [?c'est] le plus court; et [?que] je n'ay eu responce de celles que vous ay envoyées par Suisse. [?Que] sera la fin, apres avoir prié Dieu vous donner, Madame, en perfaicte santé tres longue et tres heureuse vie, avec l'entier accomplissement de vos desirs. De Vienne ce quinziesme jour de novembre mil cinq cens soixante sept. Claude de La Guiche, bishop of Mirepoix, writing from Rome during the Parma war, with cipher runs that have no decipherment anywhere. The key, a simple substitution of 22 invented symbols, was recovered from the ciphertext alone: 429 of 431 symbols have a value, and the passage gives Dom Diego and the Sienese envoy, and the Count of Santa Fiora ready to come over to the king. The struck-through opening reads only in fragments. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (87% of the cipher) · On the map ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (87% of the cipher) The letter Claude de La Guiche, bishop of Mirepoix, to Montmorency, Rome, 22 November 1551, with about thirteen lines of cipher inside clear text; no decipherment exists. Where BnF fr. 3138 no. 22, f. 60v–61r (Gallica btv1b90601662 ). The page also checks two letters of Noailles (1558) and Seure (1558) in the same volumes. The cipher 406 symbols, 22 distinct, one for each letter of the period’s 22-letter alphabet. How it was read Simulated annealing over permutations, scored against a model of French despatches 1530–1600, recovered the key. What it says Dom Diego has had a Sienese imprisoned; the Sienese envoy has left Rome with him; the Count of Santa Fiora is “mal satisfaict” and might return to the King’s service. Still open One name and the two struck-through opening lines. Noailles’ letter already has the court’s decipherment in the margin; Seure’s six letters (about 2,000 symbols) are left as their own target. BnF fr. 3138 f. 60v (Gallica btv1b90601662, view 65): La Guiche’s first cipher lines, the first two struck through, then clear « Informer led. S r cardinal du contenu en icelluy ». Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3138 f. 60v, via Gallica btv1b90601662 view 65.

La Guiche → the duc de Montmorency , Rome, 22 November 1551, fr. 3138 no. 22, f. 60v–61r. The clear text is about cardinals and the Pope’s intentions during the Parma war. It is interrupted by cipher runs, 431 symbols in all (406 in the first transcription, the rest added on 30 September 2026). There is no decipherment on the leaf, in the margin or on the following leaf. Catalogue item 10 also listed letters of 1558 by Noailles (Venice) and Seure (Lisbon); this page was split from them on 14 October 2026 because each uses a different cipher, and each has its own page ( Noailles 1558 , Seure 1558 ).

The reading in the letter’s spelling ( texts/laguiche1551_reading.md ). The deciphered passages are in italics and the clear words of the letter in roman; [?word] marks an uncertain reading, […] symbols or words not deciphered, [::] the open code symbol. The two lines the writer struck through are deciphered only in fragments, so the letter counts as partial. [Struck through by the writer:] […] Die[…] […]constituer prisonnier en ceste [?ville] […] un [?Senois] […] croy q[…] […] adverty le [L2] procès duquel i'ay trouvé moien de veoir , affin de informer led. Sr cardinal du contenu en icelluy, pour selon cela mettre tel fondement qu'il advisera, à la pratique qu'aves entendu. Et aussi pour dire aud. Sr cardinal les propos que [?Mignet] a tenus à l'ambassadeur de Senes qui estoit icy, lequel est party pour s'en retorner à Senes avecq [Dom Diego] […] . Et pour ce que ledict Sr cardinal a commancé à vous escripre de ceste affaire, je m'en remettray à ce qu'il vous en escripra. J'entendz que le conte Saincte Fiore est mal satisfaict de [::], et que facilement se reduiroi[t] au service du ro[y] […] de la Seance […] le servi[ce] […]. Car ledict personnage qui estoit icy tractant avec moy l'affaire du sieur Barnabe Adorne […] la responce qu'a[…] […] vous informer du service que le roy pourroit avoir du dict sieur Barnabe, et aussi des conditions qu'il demanderoit. “Dom Diego” is Diego Hurtado de Mendoza, Charles V’s ambassador in Rome and the power behind Siena until the Sienese rising of July 1552. The count of Santa Fiora is Sforza Sforza (1520–1575), a grandson of Paul III, who had gone back into Charles V’s service after that pope’s death. The letter shows La Guiche sounding him out for the French side eight months before Siena turned to France. “Barnabe Adorne” is presumably a Genoese of the Adorno family; he is not identified further. Filled 30 September 2026. The run after “qu’il advisera” (24 symbols, missed by the first transcription) gives a la pratique qu’aves entendu with the key unchanged (grade H for the key, C for the reading). The plain cross without a bar is a symbol of its own, b : it gives l’ambassadeur and, twice, Barnabe , where the barred cross is r in the same word and in Adorne (grade M: a value found on three words). The pair ff + c is ss in both places it occurs ( ambassadeur , aussi ; M). In “du service” the image has the barred p ( s ) where the first transcription had the double-barred #. After “mal satisfaict de” stands a single four-dot symbol (::), a code for a person that occurs nowhere else; “l’Empereur” is a conjecture from context (grade I): “se reduiroit au service du roy” says the count was serving someone else, and in 1551 he was in the Emperor’s service (the Pope, whose general he had been, is the alternative). The clear words were transcribed from the image (Gallica view 65).

The cipher was transcribed symbol by symbol from full-resolution crops of each line ( guiche_ct.txt ). The counts pointed to a simple substitution: 22 distinct symbols, one of them at 16%, the rate of French e . An annealer that allowed several symbols per letter converged on a degenerate i/x solution. A permutation annealer with swap moves, scored with a French 5-gram model without word spaces ( fr-1530-despatches ), produced le conte sainctefiore est mal satisfaict on its best restart. Four symbols were then fixed from context (qu, p, y, v), and the rest re-annealed. Key: 3=e, t=r, #=i, θ=u, the stemmed 4=t, barred p=s, hook=a, f=d, d=n, open 4=o, curled d=o, p=c, Ⅲ=l, ff=qu, overbarred d=m, φ=y, the circle=v, hooked q=f, ∞=p; added 30 September 2026: the plain cross=b, ff followed by c=ss, and one four-dot code symbol (::).

La Guiche: the four-dot code symbol (::) after « mal satisfaict de », read by conjecture as « l’Empereur » (grade I); one rare symbol (5, in the struck lines) unassigned; the name read as « Barnabe Adorne » since 30 September 2026 (the plain cross is b , the barred cross r ); the struck-through first two lines deciphered only in fragments; the Ⅲ symbol is l everywhere but gives g in « Diego ». Key grade C; the text is grade M where marked. Two letters of the peace commissioner and a Middelburg report (BL Harley MS 287 ff. 70–72), catalogued with no sender or recipient. The cipher is a simple substitution in graphic signs; the key was recovered from the clear English around the cipher runs. Most runs are deciphered: Parma’s new canal to Sluys, a weak garrison, and Cobham’s refusal of “an irreligious peace”. the passage is dangerous and subject to interception ∪ = a · 7 = e · z = o · + = b · ∞ = d · V = r Ostend → Walsingham · substitution cipher of graphic signs within clear English · 20–22 March 1587/8 Lord Cobham at Ostend to Walsingham, 20–22 March 1588 from Lord Cobham → to Francis Walsingham Go to the transcriptions ↓ British Library, Harley MS 287 ff. 70–72 (DECODE R8482–R8487), catalogued as seven ciphertexts of an unknown sender to an unknown recipient. They are two signed letters of William Brooke, Lord Cobham, written from Ostend during the 1588 peace talks with Parma, and a cipher enclosure from Middelburg. The cipher is a simple substitution in graphic signs. No decipherment was found on the leaves or in print; the key was recovered from the clear English around the cipher runs, and most runs are deciphered. About a third of the runs on f. 70r and a few names stay open. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (verification) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial The letter Two letters of Lord Cobham from Ostend, 20 and 22 March 1587/8, with an intelligence report from Middelburg between them. Cobham was one of Elizabeth’s commissioners for the peace talks with Parma. The addressee is not named; the volume and content point to Walsingham. Where Harley MS 287, ff. 70r–72v: six of the seven DECODE records of catalogue item 132, which listed no sender, recipient or decipherment. The cipher A simple substitution in graphic signs, with a few homophones and the words divided, in runs inside clear English. A few dotted numbers and a square are nomenclator signs. How it was read No decipherment on the leaves or in print. The clear words supplied cribs (“commaunded to attend”, “that bearer hath”, “under colour thereof”). What it says Parma’s new canal from Ghent by Eeklo to Sluys, “within 15 days navigable”; his build-up at Oudenburg; a garrison “too weak by the half”; the prisoners Pigot and Barney; Cobham’s refusal to be “a means to conclude an irreligious peace”. Still open Nomenclator: 15 is Parma, the square the States, .7. probably the Queen; 42 is not identified. The seventh record (f. 11) is a different letter in a different code and is not deciphered. f. 70v, 22 March 1587/8: “This preparation, together with the reinforcing of his garrisons hereabout”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 287 f. 70v, via DECODE R8483.

DECODE Folio What it is R8482–R8483 ff. 70r–70v Cobham, Ostend, 22 March 1587/8. R8484 f. 71r Intelligence “from Middelburgh”, another hand: Grenier’s schemes, a Latin tag, five lines of cipher. R8485–R8487 ff. 71v–72v Cobham, Ostend, 20 March 1587/8, signed on f. 72v. R8477 f. 11 An undated, unsigned intelligence letter in English about a Spaniard and the Spanish agent, with one line of numeral and letter code groups. A different system; not read. The Commission (Derby, Cobham, Croft, Dale, Rogers) reached Ostend in March 1588. The letters name Mr Controller (Croft), “Mr Doctor Rogers” being sent to the Duke at Bruges, and a servant of Lord Burghley, all in clear. The Calendar of State Papers Foreign calendars Cobham’s letters of 22 and 24 March to Burghley, from the State Papers, but not these. The key on f. 187 of the same volume (R8497, Bodley, 1590) is a different system.

Each run replaces the letters of English words with signs, one sign per letter and the words kept separate. A few letters have two signs (a: ∪ and ⊥; w: two dots and a dotted x; g: a barred x and a 3), and a colon after a letter stands for u. The signs of one family (l, p, h, m, all drawn as a crossed or looped stem) and the two carets for s and t are close on the scans; they were settled word by word. a b c d e f g h i l m n o p r s t u/v/w y ∪ ⊥ + 8 ∞ 7 H̅ Ӽ 3 ϵ ⊥ ϕ ∝ †† z ϕ V ∧ ∧ .. ẋ ɣ The key was rebuilt from the clear words on either side of each run. A session working on Cobham’s May–June letters in the same volume then found the same values in the contemporary glosses of f. 89 (R8493).

Grades as in the README: (C) supplied from context, (M) uncertain; the rest is high. 22 March, ff. 70r–70v What effect this message will work I know not, but doubt the worst, and therefore do wish and think it expedient that some of .7. ships were commaunded to attend on this coast for all events , for I am persuaded 15 will never yield to send 42 hither . Some provision also for vittailes would be necessarily thought upon, for □ have no megasines here, nor mind to have any. That the same here is but from weeke to weeke as the bilanders do voluntarily bring it … there is any money stirring here. The present garrison will be found too weake for the defence of so large a circuit by the half at the least. The last supply of money will not [keep them] from the presentes wantes of the souldiers above five weeks longer, as the governour tells me. … The Duke is expected within a day or two to be at Bruges. The newe ditche from Gaunt by Eecloo unto Sluce is said to be almost ended, and will be within 15 dayes navigable for the float boates and vessels he hath ready prepared, being some of them fraught with stones and fagottes . This preparation, together with the reinforcing of his garrisons hereabout, Stanley’s repair unto Turnhout (M), make such [at] Oudenburgh with eleven companies of footmen , and the Duke’s coming to Bruges doth threaten somewhat (C). And in mine opinion this town is fit to be stopped (C) through some attempts upon the haven ; which being once stopped, the town being already abandoned of succour by land , cannot make resistance against the enemy many days (C) together. My greatest grief is that in all this town I am not furnished of any one spy to employ abroad for the more certainty of the enemy’s proceedings . And from Flushing I hear very seldom by reason that the passage is dangerous and subject to interception . … By my servant William I wrote in my private letter a special motion for our remove to Flushing (C), where we might better stand on terms for her Majesty’s honour. Middelburg report, f. 71r In my opinion the ships would be well guarded (C), and when all ships of charge as well of the [fleet] as merchants be at sea (C), there would be 2 or 3 pinnaces appointed to [watch] and direct the channel (C). [Bastune?] the Jesuite is within these fewe dayes sent post into Italy (surname M). R. tould me in talke with him that 15 ha[th] [in]sted his sonne (being under 17 years of age) in the government of his patrimony in Italy. 20 March, ff. 71v–72v There are new companies lately added to the old garrison of Oudenburgh, our near neighbours (C), which were very strong before. This drawing of his forces by land so near, and the provision of stone and fagots to come from Eecloo by water (C), make us suspect some attempts against this town and haven : we think it therefore expedient that some of the ships did continue upon this coast, to be ready for service upon occasions . Also we pray your honour (C) would remove us hence or dismiss us to some other place of more surety (C). This bearer hath laboured his own dispatch and would fain have had instructions , but I, fearing that under colour thereof he would proceed in his charge , did let him understand what we had generally written unto my Lord … As by the [words] of your own hand in your letter of the 16 March I perceive you oppose yourself still against such resolutions ; for mine own part I would think myself most unhappy to be a means to conclude an irreligious peace . Touching Pigot and Barney , if they shall be delivered over to the States , I am of another opinion … things standing as they do, □ will ranson them , and then what dishonour and disfavour will it be for her Majesty. Pigot is a martial man , and hath means and will to deserve his prise (C).

The two names after “Touching” on f. 72r and the name on the following line; they do not fit Flushing, Brill, Ostend or Bergen. About a third of the runs on f. 70r, including what “42” stands for, and the last cipher line of f. 71r. There is no symbol-by-symbol transcription. R8482-R8483, Lord Cobham to [Walsingham], Ostend, 22 Mar 1587/8 (ff. 70r-v) Henry Brooke, Lord Cobham, one of Elizabeth's peace commissioners at Ostend in spring 1588, asks that ships be sent to attend on the coast, warns that the garrison is too weak and short of money and victuals, and reports Parma's new ditch from Ghent by Eeclo to Sluys, nearly navigable for his float-boats, and the threat to the town and haven. No sign-level transcription exists: the cipher runs were read word by word from crops of the DECODE images. A cipher letter of P. Jafet to Francesc Climent, Benedict XIII’s agent, 15 September 1400. Canon Puig y Puig, who deciphered Climent’s cipher letters in 1920, printed only one deciphered sentence of it, in a footnote: some of Climent’s letters had been intercepted that day and recovered. No image of the cipher exists; it was split from Benedict XIII’s own letters because nothing shows it used his key. Francesc Climent, called Çapera, was Benedict XIII’s chamberlain and treasurer and later bishop of Barcelona; he left his papers to the cathedral chapter. Among them Sebastián Puig y Puig found fourteen letters partly or wholly in cipher, deciphered them, and printed them in the appendix of Pedro de Luna, último papa de Aviñón (1920). This is one of them: P. Jafet to Climent, 15 Sep 1400 (appendix XXXVII n. 2, pp. 477 n. 2; doc. 1043). Puig prints about 14 deciphered words. Only one deciphered sentence is printed, in a footnote: some of Climent’s letters sunt intercepte hodie et recuperate , were intercepted that day and recovered. The originals are not digitised, and the archivist Josep Mas noted that Puig studied many of the Schism papers at home in 1920–30 and did not return them all. Puig’s print may be the only witness.

Puig never printed a key, and the only image of any of these ciphers is his facsimile of one page of Benedict XIII’s own letter of 22 June 1400. From that page the key of Benedict’s letters was rebuilt here: a plain substitution, one sign per letter. Puig writes of “la clave o claves”, the key or keys, he recovered, and nothing shows whether this letter, from another writer, used the same one. So it has its own entry. Benedict XIII’s letters are on Benedict XIII to Climent, 1399–1403 (a different or unverified cipher, with its own page); the other letters of his circle each have their own page for the same reason: Santa Cruz to Climent, 1399 , Exea to Climent, 1408 , Comuel to Climent, December 1415 , Comuel to Climent, June 1416 .

The ciphertext. No image of the letter exists, so its cipher, its key and Puig’s reading cannot be checked. Blocker: needs the original in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona. The rest of the letter (doc. 1043), which Puig cites but does not print. Blocker: needs the original. Not printed; the ACB original is not digitised, and may be among the papers Puig did not return.

DECODE R366, eight pages: Ferdinand’s letter to his envoy at the Porte, mostly clear Latin with about three pages in a homophonic cipher of graphic signs whose nulls include Latin words. The key is on DECODE at the same shelfmark (R367) and was applied; the work was transcribing a difficult hand. All five ciphered passages are deciphered, 509 of 514 cipher words (99.0%) measured as Latin sense after a re-reading from the full-resolution images: the politics (the French working against the Habsburg–Ottoman peace), the envoy’s pay (4,300 ducats and a credit of 3,000 more), the troops on the border and the captives.
