Ab. Guiccioli, Madrid”. Where Spagna 423 in the Vatican (index i. 1025); ten DECODE records, catalogued with contents unknown: “what the cipher hides is not known.” The cipher An undivided digit stream. Two-digit elements stand for letters, syllables and short words; 7 is a null; 166 distinct four-digit nomenclator groups begin with 1. How it was read Every record carries George Lasry’s key “ASV - S423” (24 October 2020) and his decipherment of all eleven items, so the letters were deciphered before this project looked. What was added His key covers only the two-digit elements. 46 nomenclator groups were recovered from context alone, covering 424 of the 708 tokens, keeping a value only when it gives sense at every occurrence. Spagna 423 is described in the Vatican index (i. 1025) as “Lett. originale e ciffre della Segretaria alla nunziatura, dal 7 gennaio 1736 al 29 dicembre 1736”. The catalogue took its “7 Jan 1736” from that heading, but the ciphered items run from 14 July to 22 December 1736 . The clear dates on the transcriptions are 14 and 21 July, 4 August, September, 29 September (two), 6 October, 15 and 22 December. The dockets name the addressee as “Sig. Ab. Guiccioli, Madrid”. There are eleven items (423/1–11) across ten DECODE records. Each record carries three attachments: the item’s raw digit transcription (Matt F and NiLan, 2015–17); Lasry’s key, “#KEY: reconstructed · ASV - S423 · George Lasry · October 24, 2020”; and a single file holding his decipherment of the whole dossier, the ciphertext split into elements with the plaintext aligned underneath.

An undivided digit stream. Two-digit elements stand for letters ( 05|20|26 = a, 03|49|65 = e) and for syllables and short words ( 93 quel, 52 per, 40 non, 60 gli). The digit 7 is a null, except inside a nomenclator group. Four-digit nomenclator groups begin with 1 (1130–1985). The corpus uses 166 distinct groups. R179, Rome, 21 July 1736, the top of the page: below the dateline, an undivided stream of digits in which two-digit elements, 7 as a null and four-digit nomenclator groups beginning with 1 run together without separators. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 423 f. 294r, via DECODE R179.

Lasry’s aligned decipherment was parsed into 9,001 tokens, and each unvalued group was listed with every context it appears in. In 1718 the nomenclator ran alphabetically and the neighbouring values bracketed each gap. That does not work here: 1222 is -mente , 1245 -zione , 1882 Spagna , 1935 V.S. , in no order. So each value had to be inferred from its contexts, and it was accepted only when it gave sense in all of them. The frequent groups are anchored many times over: 1222 in 44 places (somma-, diffusa-, pari-, facil-, destra-, minuta- mente ), 1655 = N.S. in 21 (“N.S. è rimasto sommamente amareggiato”, “le giuste istanze di N.S.”).

Molina, scordatosi degli obblighi di Vescovo e Regolare, si unisca in questa congiuntura ancora dei tumulti contro la S. Sede, e per iscusa di una condotta al giudicio di ognuno tanto irregolare, che si ponga costì in vista l’affare del Donghi e delle sodisfazioni accordate all’Imperatore. Voglio prescindere che le altrui violenze non dovrebbero mai servire di esempio … His Holiness is “most bitterly grieved” that Molina, forgetting his duty as a bishop, joins in the tumults against the Holy See. Gaspar de Molina y Oviedo, Bishop of Málaga and Governor of the Council of Castile, led the Spanish side of the 1736 dispute. The earlier decode had left open the groups for scrivo , risposta , otto and congiuntura and had maggior for necessario .

In spring 1736 Spanish recruiters took men by force in Rome and the Papal State (“arrolamenti”, “ingaggiature”, “arrolatori”), which set off riots in Trastevere and at Velletri. Spain and Naples broke with Rome. The despatches deal with the tumults “contro la S. Sede”, Cardinal Acquaviva, the Duke of Montemar, Bishop Molina, the expulsion of the nuncio and the pensions at the Court of Naples. From October they turn to the Dataria, the royal padronato over benefices (“codesta giunta del padronato”), the “Regalista” doctrines of the Madrid junta, Briefs to the King and Queen, and the nomination to cardinals’ hats (“col maggior numero di cappelli”).

Nine nomenclator groups seen once in letters that read : 1200, 1335, 1960, 1985 (423/2), 1232, 1469, 1698, 1942 (423/7) and 1636 (423/8). With its four, 423/7 reads at 92.6% of its words, under 95%. No copy of those three letters is among the DECODE attachments; the copies or the minutes would have to be found in Spagna 423 itself or in the archive of the Madrid nunciature. In 423/1, the groups 1268, 1765 and 1847 (and the pairs 21, 91) occur once each; the words are carried by the clear copy, but the group values are not fixed. The three open spots of 423/9 and 423/11 were cipherer’s slips, seen on the images; the copies read “Si danno”, “l’esame de’” and “bene maneggiata”. 423/2, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10 rest on the figures with the key as corrected (grade B); the clear copies of 423/4, 6 and 10 are among the attachments but have not yet been transcribed.

R118 is six lines of figures from the Spain nunciature, dated 15 October of 1576 or 1577. Ajaydas Devadas’s reconstruction of the nunciature’s ordinary cipher reads every sign in Italian: the nuncio has told Secretary Pérez what Rome wrote in the cipher of 19 September. The clear note on the leaf is the contemporary decipherment, minus the dateline; we had misread it as a plain message. R117 is a clear memorial and has no cipher. 20 7̇ 0̇5 3 0̇7 40 · 4̇ 2̇ 0̇8 · 15̅ … scrita ali 15 di otobre · il nuntio a comunicato col secretario Perez … read · every sign Madrid → Rome · numerical cipher · 15 October 1576 or 1577 Ormanetto and Clementino, Spain nunciature, 1576–77 to Tolomeo Gallio Go to the full text ↓ ASV Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 10 (DECODE R117, R118). R117 ( ASV_i1025_SdS_Spain_10-1 , two pages). Copia del Memorial dado por parte del obispo de Pamplona : the see fell vacant on 27 January 1573 at the death of Diego Ramírez. The Pope held back the bulls of the new bishop, Antonio Manrique, for nine months, and the memorial argues that those months’ fruits belong to the bishop. The right-hand column repeats the sums in Roman numerals with the Spanish thousands sign ( xbnUdn L-ix , xxxbjUdn — m ). Those sums are what DECODE catalogued as “ciphers within cleartext”. R118, f. 365: the figures, and below them the Italian note in another hand. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 10 f. 365, via DECODE R118. R118 ( ASV_i1025_SdS_Spain_10-2 , one page). The figures are undated on the leaf. The note below the figures reads: Il Nuntio ha trattato col Sig.r Perez tutto quello che V.S. Ill.ma scrive con la cifra di 19 di sett.re, il qual Sig.r ha promesso di buoni uffici al Re, et di procurare risposta, de la quale V.S. Ill.ma sarà poi sabbato avvisata. The nuncio has discussed with Signor Pérez everything Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes in the cipher of 19 September. He has promised his good offices with the King and to obtain an answer, of which Your Lordship will be told on Saturday. The letter therefore dates from the autumn of 1576 or 1577, not from 9 January 1576, which is only the start of the volume’s date range.

Every sign of R118 reads. Spelling is as enciphered (no h , no doubled letters, u for v ): scrita ali 15 di otobre. Il nuntio a comunicato col secretario Perez [tutto] [quello] [che] [V.S. Ill.ma] scrive con la cifra di 19 di setembre; il [qua]le segretario a promeso di darne conto al [Re], [et] di procurarne risposta, de la [qua]le [V.S. Ill.ma] sarà poi subito avisata. (six null signs: s t c z p l) Written 15 October. The Nuncio has communicated to Secretary Pérez everything Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes in the cipher of 19 September. The Secretary has promised to report it to the King and to obtain an answer, of which Your Lordship will shortly be advised. Bracketed words are code groups: 6̇11 tutto, 2̇44 quello, 66 che, 9̇11 V.S. Ill.ma, 3̇44 Re, a lone 3 for et , and 5̇2̇2 for the syllable qua . The figures 15 and 19 are written as numbers under an overline. The clear Italian note on the leaf is the same text: Il Nuntio ha c[om]unicato col Sec[reta]rio Perez tutto quello che V.S. Ill.ma scrive con la cifra di 19 di sett.re, il q[ua]l Sec[reta]rio ha promesso di darne conto al Re, et di procurarne risp.ta, de la q[ua]le V.S. Ill.ma sarà poi subbito avvisata. It is the Rome decifrato, and it leaves out only the dateline, scritta alli 15 di ottobre . The year is not in the cipher. Ormanetto died on 18 June 1577 and his successor Filippo Sega reached Madrid on 11 October 1577, so “il Nuntio” on 15 October is Ormanetto in 1576 or Sega four days after he arrived. The third person suggests that nunciature staff wrote it for the nuncio; DECODE’s “Clementino” is not identified.

The key is the Spain nunciature’s cifra ordinaria , of which Meister (1906, p. 265) prints only the rules. Ajaydas Devadas reconstructed it from the images on this site and the ciphertext files on GitHub, with Claude, and emailed it with a report on 1 October 2026. It is a homophonic cipher with two signs for each letter: letter signs letter signs letter signs a 40, 4̇ i 3, 0̇8 r 0̇5, 8 b 4, 0̇2 l 80, 2̇ s 20, 9̇ c 50, 7̇ m 2, 0̇1 t 0̇7, 9 d 0̇4, 7 n 90, 6̇ u/v 10, 1̇ e 60, 5̇ o 0̇3, 6 z 0̇9 f 0̇6, 5 p 30, 8̇ g 7̈, 3̇ A dot over a lone digit is part of the sign. 0̇x is a dotted zero followed by x; x0 is x closed by an undotted zero. Three things made it hard to see. First, the unit of the cipher is not the digit: an undotted 0 closes the digit before it and a dotted 0 opens the next one. Second, the cross-stroke on a 2, a 4 or a 5 is a word-end mark ; the earlier transcription wrote it as a 4 or a barred 4, and the crib aligner of 21 September counted it as a letter. Third, the note under the figures was misread: trattato , Sig.r , buoni uffici and sabbato are abbreviated forms of comunicato , Secretario , darne conto and subbito . With the strokes as word breaks and the dotted zeros as openers, the figures give Italian words immediately.

The scan. Lines 1–3 and 5 of the leaf were compared sign by sign with the token list: 20 7̇ 0̇5 3 0̇7 40 is scrita , 3 80 | 90 10 6̇ 0̇7 3 0̇3 is il nuntio , and the overlined 15 and 19 are on the page. Lines 4 and 6 were not compared by eye. Each line decoded. The script dec118.py decodes the six lines from the key and compares them with the reading: 12 lines of the table agree, none differs. The sibling. The same key reads R116 (1573) , an independent ciphertext of more than a thousand signs, as Italian. A key fitted to one short text would not do that. The leaf. The reading matches the contemporary decifrato word for word, apart from the dateline.

The year, 1576 or 1577, and who wrote it. The register of the Cardinal of Como’s ciphers to Spain, or the Spagna 10 index, would settle both. The transcription ( r118_cipher.txt ) is digits only and cannot carry the key. A dotted transcription of all six lines, from the image, is still to be made before a read fraction can be measured here. R117 needs nothing: a clear Spanish memorial.

Catalogued on DECODE as an unknown sender’s letter of 1587, this is Catherine de Médicis writing from Chenonceau, with one cipher block on Anjou, the Low Countries and the embassy to England. Tomokiyo’s reconstructed key was applied and extended by twelve values; all 289 signs are accounted for, and the last line he left open is the end of “d’Angleterre” plus padding. The cipher A homophonic substitution on Greek letters, digits and invented signs, with a small nomenclator (de, le, la, que, nous, mais, Angleterre …) and nulls. Credit Satoshi Tomokiyo (the key reconstruction).

Villeroy, secretary of state, was in Guyenne with Bellièvre and the duc d’Anjou, carrying out the peace of Fleix (November 1580). Catherine writes from Chenonceau about the chamber of justice for Guyenne, the money for the troops, the handing back of Mende, the quarrel between the dukes of Montpensier and Nevers, and the embassy that was to go to England for Anjou’s marriage to Elizabeth. The cipher block is one sentence in that last part: why the court is not pressing the prince Dauphin, Montpensier’s son, to go to England. DECODE R4157, “Non-decrypted”, 9 pp., sender and recipient unknown, 5 Feb 1587 Actually Catherine de Médicis → Nicolas de Neufville, seigneur de Villeroy, Chenonceau, 7 (and 8) February 1581; BnF fr. 15564 ff. 30–34, Gallica views 40–44. DECODE image P7 (f. 38, “Madame…”) belongs to another letter. Cipher f. 33r, eight lines, 289 signs; deciphered at the time in the left margin and on three lines under the block In print Lettres de Catherine de Médicis , ed. Baguenault de Puchesse, t. VII (1899), pp. 349–353, “Orig. fonds français 15564, f° 30” The docket (f. 30 verso of the cover leaf, Gallica view 40): “Double de la lettre de la / Royne mere du Roy / a Mr de Villeroy / du v[ii]e febvrier 1581”. DECODE’s “5 Feb 1587” comes from this line. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15564 f. 30v, via Gallica (btv1b9064027v, view 40).

BnF fr. 15564 f. 33r, lower part (Gallica view 43): the clear text ends “se dizant par deçà qu’il”, then eight lines of cipher. A second hand wrote the decipherment in the margin (“doibt aller en flandres recevoir le serment de fidelite…”) and went on under the block (“et fera tout ce qu’ilz pourront pour le service…”). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15564 f. 33r, via Gallica (btv1b9064027v, view 43). The cipher is a homophonic substitution on Greek letters, digits and invented signs, one to three signs per letter, with special signs for mm and ss . A small nomenclator covers de, le, la, que, qui, pour, nous, mais, faire, tout, avec, dict, prince and Angleterre , and it is used for syllables as well: fi[de]lite , [de]mourer , Con[de] , [le]gation , mon[dict] . An overbar marks several of the codes. Nulls pad the start of the block, the end of line 4 and the end of the last line.

One line per manuscript line; codes in brackets, nulls in braces. The clear text before the block is “car, à ce que j’entends, nous n’i gaingnerions rien, se dizant par deçà qu’il”. {3 nulls} DOIBT AL ER EN FLANDRES RECEUOIR [LE] SERMENT [DE] FI[DE]LITE [DE] CEULX [DE]S {null} PAIS BAS [POUR] MON FILZ ET [QUI]L Y DOIBT [DE]MOURER ET [QUE] [LE] [PRINCE] [DE] CON[DE]E DO IBT MENER [LE]S FORCES [QUI] S’ASSEMBLENT ET [FAIRE] [TOUT] CE [QUI]LZ [POUR]RONT [POUR] [LE] SERUICE [DE] MON[DICT] FILZ [QUI] SE [DICT] AUSSI Y [DE]BUOIR ALER {3 nulls} AU TEMPS [QUE] [NOUS] AUEZ ESCRIPT ET NON [DE]UANT [MAIS] [NOUS] NE LAISSER ONS [DE] [LE] NOMMER [AVEC] [LE][DICT] SIEUR [DE] MONPENSIER AU[DICT] POUOI(R) [DE] [LA] [LE]GATION D’[ANGLETERRE] {20 signs of padding} Normalised: “…se dizant par deçà qu’il doibt aller en Flandres recevoir le serment de fidélité de ceulx des Païs-Bas pour mon filz, et qu’il y doibt demourer, et que le prince de Condé doibt mener les forces qui s’assemblent, et faire tout ce qu’ilz pourront pour le service de mondict filz, qui se dict aussi y debvoir aller au temps que nous avez escript, et non devant; mais nous ne laisserons de le nommer avec ledict sieur de Montpensier audict pouvoir de la légation d’Angleterre.” In English: “…since it is said here that he [the prince Dauphin] is to go to Flanders to receive the oath of fealty of the people of the Low Countries for my son [Anjou], and to stay there, and that the prince of Condé is to lead the forces now gathering and do all they can for my son’s service, who says he means to go there too at the time you wrote to us, and not before. But we shall not fail to name him, with the said lord of Montpensier, in the commission for the embassy to England.” The contemporary decipherment and the 1899 edition give the same text, except that they lack et before non devant and de before le nommer . The edition also spells the name Montpensier where the cipher has Monpensier .

The DECODE images are Gallica openings of fr. 15564 ff. 30–34 and a crop of the block. The docket and the content (Anjou in the Low Countries, Condé’s troops, “Chenonceau”) pointed to 1581. The letter is in volume VII of Catherine’s letters, not in volume IX where a 1587 date would have put it. The block was transcribed from the Gallica native scan, one label per sign. A first attempt without the key, aligning the signs with the printed text (one sign per letter plus nulls, by EM and annealing), failed. The printed passage turned out to be only half of the plaintext: the rest of the decipherment is on the lines under the block, which at first looked like the letter’s clear continuation. Tomokiyo’s reconstruction for “BnF fr. 15564, f.33” (Cryptiana, French ciphers during the reigns of Charles IX and Henry III ) decrypted the block as soon as the labels were mapped onto it. A second pass at double magnification split signs that the first labels had merged: forked ψ = n and curled ɣ = t; filled ᴀ = z and Δ = f; ϖ = g, the looped u = s and the &-shape = z; ɦ = u and б = e; small v = e and capital V = tout ; bold ʒ = avec and barred Ʒ = e; ɤ = ss. Values missing from the published table were fixed from the text: 18 = dict (four times: mon[dict] filz , se [dict] , le[dict] sieur , au[dict] ); C̄σ = mais ; ß̄ = la ; ō = Angleterre ; 4/b = nous , not vous ( que nous avez escript , mais nous ne laisserons ); ℬ = p, ꝏ = u, ꝑ = t, F̣ = i, ϑ = l, d = x.

After “[de] [la] [le]gation d” the last line has an overbarred ō and then twenty signs. The decryption takes ō as the code for Angleterre and the twenty signs as padding: the contemporary decipherer, who had the key, ends at “de la legation d’Ang[leter]re” and writes nothing more; f. 33v opens in clear with the next sentence, “Nous adviserons, aiant oy ledict La Fin…”; the tail contains Tomokiyo’s declared null Z7 twice, and the same signs (Ʒ with a dagger, the double f, a small raised hook) that pad the start of the block before “doibt”; the few tail signs that have letter values give “a l mm a que”, which is not French. So Tomokiyo’s “the first d” is the d’ of d’Angleterre , and the rest is padding.

ō = Angleterre occurs once and is fixed by the decipherer’s “d’Ang…re” and the edition, not by a second occurrence: grade M. The Latin e after the de code in Condé is either an e (for é) or a null: grade M. “pouoi” at the end of line 6 lacks its r. Either the encipherer left it out or the Z that opens line 7 was meant for both r and de . Everything else decrypts with a key value (H from Tomokiyo’s table, or C against the contemporary decipherment).

A letter-book copy (Harley MS 260 f. 419, DECODE R8364) of Burghley’s letter about the ship sent for the Duke of Alençon, in clear English with name codes and two short cipher runs. A Folger chronology of 1573, pointed out by a reader, names the people: Davison is Maisonfleur, Hall the Queen, Glasgow the Duke. The six-sign place name recurs, with different homophones, in four letters printed by Digges in 1655; comparing the five copies with a French letter in Walsingham’s file gives VALERY (St Valery). The nine-sign run and the name codes need the 1571 key, which is not online. a Shipp sent to 2 0 ‡ H 6 1 · the ship may stay at 2 ɔ ǂ 6 r y · the Port of 2 0 ǂ 6 ɔ Δ · = VALERY Westminster → Paris · homophonic letter cipher and name codes in a clear letter · early 1573 Burghley to Walsingham, 29 January 1573: the ship sent to St Valery from William Cecil → to Francis Walsingham Go to the transcriptions ↓ BL Harley MS 260 f. 419r–v (DECODE R8364, catalogue 122), listed as “Unknown sender to …, Feb 1572”. It is a copy in Walsingham’s embassy letter-book of Burghley’s letter of 29 January 1573 answering Walsingham’s of 20 January. The letter is in clear English except for name codes and two short cipher runs. It is part of the plan to bring the Duke of Alençon to England. The six-sign run is a place name that Digges printed in four letters of the same winter. Comparing the five copies, which use different homophones, with Walsingham’s file gives VALERY, the Channel port of Saint-Valery-sur-Somme. That word is the only cipher text recovered by a key (6 of 26 cipher tokens). The people behind the name codes come from a different source: a Folger chronology of 1573 that summarises this letter (below). Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on plaintext from external sources · Extent: partial (23% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Adam Wright (pointer to a source) external text At a glance Key from external plaintext · partial (23% of the cipher) The letter Burghley to Walsingham, 29 January 1573, copied in a fair-copy letter-book. It concerns the attempt by the Duke of Alençon’s agents to bring him to England on the understanding that Elizabeth might marry him. Where British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 419r–v; DECODE R8364, two pages. Printed by Digges (1655, p. 327) with the cipher left as signs. The cipher Homophonic letter cipher in two runs, plus boxed and numeral person codes: 26 cipher tokens, among them a six-sign place word and a nine-sign run. How it was read The six-sign word is read VALERY, the port of Saint-Valery-sur-Somme: the same word recurs in four letters of the winter, with the same first and third signs, and Walsingham’s file mentions a ship kept waiting there (grade M, probable). What it says From a Folger chronology summary: “Davison” is Maisonfleur, “Hall” the Queen, “Glasgow” and the boxed 9 the Duke. These are read from a summary, not a key (grade I). Still open The nine-sign run is unread and only H is known. Person codes 3 and II, and the exact values of tt and [9], rest on a summary. No key material is online. Credit Adam Wright pointed out the Folger summary on 1 October 2026.

Harley MS 260 is a later fair copy of Walsingham’s Paris correspondence of 1570–73, one letter after another with their addresses, under running heads by month. Folio 419r opens with the end of Walsingham’s own letter of 6 February 1572 (old style), in which he asks to be relieved. Then comes the address “To the right honorable Mr Fraunces Walsingham Esq, the Queenes Maiesties Amba[ssador] in Fraunce”, and the letter beginning “Sir I have receaved yor lres of the xxth of this month with the tickett after yor accustomed manner contayning [9]”. The copy breaks off at the foot of f. 419v with a struck-out “finis”. Digges printed it from another copy, with the rest of the letter (Worcester’s dishonour off Boulogne, the French libel against Burghley, Walsingham’s letters of the 24th), under the running head “The Lord Burleigh to Fr. Walsingham”. DECODE’s sender (“unknown”), recipient (“…”) and date (February 1572) come from the letter-book’s old-style year and the address line. The letter is Burghley’s, to Walsingham, and is dated 29 January 1573 by the Folger chronology (after Conyers Read), which also says he wrote “partly in cipher”.

The names in clear are cover-names or real names of the affair of Alençon’s intended crossing, November 1572 to February 1573: Glasgow, Davison, Hall. Who they are is in section 04. Digges printed the cipher of Walsingham’s correspondence in cipher type; the earlier attempt had taken it for figures. A search of all 457 page images of his volume, first by the OCR’s word confidence and then by two page-by-page scans, found about 45 ciphered passages in the letters of 1570–73. Four of them are the same word, in letters about the one ship: Letter Context Digges Harley 260 Burghley, Westminster, 11 Nov 1572 (p. 301) “he hath required me to provide a passenger to attend at Harwich. Le the Port of …” 2 0 ǂ 6 ɔ Δ Walsingham, Paris, Nov 1572 (p. 303) “he desireth that the ship may stay at … 9 or 10 days” 2 ɔ ǂ 6 r y Walsingham, Paris, 20 Jan 1573 (p. 313; R8363 ) “a Gentleman of [9] departed hence to … with intention to imbarque there” 2 ) ⌘ Ꭾ ) 4 2 1 ⌘ ε 9 4 Burghley, early 1573 (p. 327; R8364) “by Davisons writing of a ship sent to …” 20 ǂ H Ꭾ ) 2 0 ‡ H 6 1 Every copy has six signs. The first is always 2 and the third always the same crossed sign (ǂ, ⌘ and ‡ are the founts’ and the copyist’s versions of it). The other four places change from copy to copy. That is what a homophonic alphabet gives when one word is written several times. The place is a French port where a ship waits for passengers bound for England, with Harwich on the English side. The Nov 1572 letter has Walsingham ask that the ship may stay there nine or ten days. Cotton MS Vespasian F VI, the volume of Walsingham’s letters and drafts of 1572–73, holds at f. 197 “A French letter; earnestly desiring that a ship might be kept in waiting at St. Valery. Dec. 11”. VALERY has six letters, and Digges’s copy of the Walsingham letter even ends in a plain “r y”: V = 2 · A = 0, ɔ, ), 1 · L = ǂ, ⌘, ‡ · E = 6, Ꭾ, H, ε · R = ɔ, ), r, Ꭾ, 9, 6 · Y = Δ, y, 4, ), 1 A few signs turn up under two letters (ɔ/) under A and R, 1 under A and Y). They are the places where Digges’s type and the letter-book copyist blur distinct manuscript signs, which the Digges and Harley copies of the same letters show. The reading does not depend on them. Dieppe, the other six-letter port, needs a different sign for each of its two Ps and two Es in every copy, and nothing in the sources points to it. Harwich, Dover, Calais and Dieppe are all written in clear elsewhere in these letters. Grade M (probable). No source gives the alphabet; the length, the fixed signs, the “ry” and the St Valery ship in Walsingham’s file all point to this word. With it the passage runs: I see there was a great mistaking of our doings, for by Davison’s writing of a ship sent to [St] Valery, [tt] imagined that Hall had a meaning to provoke Glasgow to come hither; whereupon this last gentleman came to enquire of Hall some assurance, if [3] should so do, to enquire […]. This you must think must needs appear very strange. Read for sense, the sentence is about an invitation. The people in it are identified in the next section. The port is the one in the French letter of 11 December 1572 in Walsingham’s file, and in Walsingham’s letter of 20 January ( R8363 ) a gentleman “departed hence to [St] Valery with intention to imbarque there”.

On 1 October 2026 Adam Wright wrote that the Folger Shakespeare Library’s Elizabethan Court Day by Day (the 1573 volume) summarises this letter under 29 January, partly in cipher, and cites Conyers Read, Lord Burghley and Queen Elizabeth (1960), pp. 94–95. The summary names the people where our copy has cover-names and codes. Set side by side, clause by clause, it gives: Harley 260 f. 419 The summary says So “the partie … sent from [9] ” the party sent from Alençon [9] = Alençon “hee spake with Glascoe 3 and Davison with him” he spoke with the Queen, and Maisonfleur with him Davison = Maisonfleur; “Glascoe 3” stands where the summary has the Queen “ tt ymagined” Alençon imagining tt = Alençon “ Hall 3 had a meaninge to provoake Glascoe [9] to come hither” the Queen had a meaning to provoke him to come hither Hall = the Queen; “Glascoe [9]” = Alençon “the laste gentleman came to enquier of Hall 3 some assurance yf 3 shoulde soe doe” this last gentleman came to enquire of the Queen for some assurance, if Alençon should do so, that she would marry him this last gentleman = La Mole; the lone 3 = Alençon “to enquier ^ 4 d H m 11 11 I J ” (the marriage?) the nine signs may carry the marriage; unread The people are the Duke of Alençon (François, the French king’s youngest brother), his agent Maisonfleur, who had a ship sent to bring him over, and the Sieur de la Mole, who was secretly at Whitehall on 23 January. The same chronology, under 22 January, says a ship sent for the Duke “waited in vain off the French coast for 23 days”. That is the 23 days of Burghley’s letter of 24 January ( R8362 ), and the ship sent to St Valery of this one. The Archbishop of Glasgow is not in it: “Glasgow” is a cover-name, here for the Duke. An earlier version of this page, and of R8362, took it for James Beaton on the strength of the name alone. What this does and does not give. These identifications are read from a modern summary, not from a key, so they are grade I. We do not know where Read had the plain text of the cipher. Two points do not fit one meaning: the digit 3 follows Glascoe and Hall where the summary has the Queen, but stands alone for the Duke, so it is left unread. And the clear name Glascoe is the Queen in one clause and the Duke in another, according to the digit that follows. The boxed 9 now looks like a code for the Duke rather than a bare marker: “the ticket concerning [9]” (R8363’s of 20 January), “sent from [9]”, “the ruin of [9]” and, in R8363, “a gentleman of [9]” all read well as Alençon. That is an inference from five contexts, not a proof.

The key. Hsuan-Ying Tu’s thesis on Walsingham’s intelligence (York, 2012) cites the key itself: TNA SP 106/2 f. 141A, “Sir Francis Walsingham Cipher, 1571” . She gives the Harley 260 letters of 1570–73, among them f. 399 (R8363), as examples of its use. DECODE has eight keys from SP 106/2 but not f. 141A. The nearest in date, SP 106/2 f. 50 (R343), names Moray, Cardinal Châtillon, Dover, Dieppe and Calais and belongs to Norris’s embassy of 1568–70. Its homophones give neither VALERY nor sense in the Digges runs. SP 106 is online only in the subscription State Papers Online. The sent letter. Cotton MS Vespasian F VI holds Burghley’s originals to Walsingham of 14 October 1572 (“with many cyphers”), 3 and 7 November 1572, and, at f. 245, a letter of 1572–3 from Somerset House that is probably this one. It also holds Walsingham’s drafts in clear of his letters of November 1572 to February 1573. The volume is catalogued “partly in cipher” and is not digitised. The Calendar. CSP Foreign vols. ix and x were searched for letters “partly in cipher, deciphered” that could be paired with Digges’s cipher. Walsingham to Smith of 10 August 1572 (no. 527) is deciphered, but Digges prints that letter without its cipher sentence. Burghley’s letters to Walsingham are not in SP 70, and this one is not calendared. The nine-sign run. Of its signs only H is known (= E, from the place name). Cribs such as passport, safe conduct, “the Queene”, “the Regent” and “Lord Seton” do not fit the shape. The Burghley–Walsingham runs of 1572–73 in Digges give only about 80 signs, loosely typeset, and too few overlap with this run to fix it.

The nine-sign run “^ 4 d H m 11 11 I J” (f. 419v l. 2): no key material (the key and the original are not online; one sign known). Person codes 3 and II, and the exact value of tt and [9], which rest on a summary and not on a key. 3 is left unread because the summary does not give it one meaning. No key material. The boxed [9] ×5 (read as Alençon, grade I) and the 3 after Glasgow and Hall (unread). Of 26 cipher tokens, the six of the place name have a value (23%, grade M). SP 106/2 f. 141A, or a photograph of Cotton Vespasian F VI ff. 172–247, would probably give the rest of this letter and of its siblings R8356 , R8358 and R8361 , together with the 45 passages in Digges.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (97% of the cipher) Credits · ry-xu (solution, identification) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (97% of the cipher) The letter German, to Duke Wilhelm V of Bavaria, dated 12 June 1583 (new style), three weeks after his brother Ernst was elected Archbishop of Cologne. The writer, at Ernst’s court, signs with a mark only. Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 ff. 274–275; DECODE R9424, part of catalogue entry 161. The cipher A simple substitution on Latin letters with a few invented signs; a slash doubles the letter before it, and a few signs at word edges are nulls. One sign, a barred o-o, stands for a name. How it was deciphered Ryan Xu recovered the key from the repository’s transcription alone, from word endings and short words, and tested it against shuffled keys. Every word was then checked here on the archive photographs. What it says Rivalry among Ernst’s councillors, “Si.” ruling alone at court, and a plan to bring “Susanna” down to Cologne or Liège that would cause great scandal. Still open The barred o-o sign (three times), a name or title in line 21, two letters after “ghen” in line 22, and one word glossed “Aichstet”. Credit Key and first decryption: Ryan Xu ( ry-xu ) with Claude Opus 5.5, 23 October 2026 ( issue #89 ; his write-up ). Until 15 October 2026 this letter was filed on one page with thirteen other ciphertexts of the same key volume; they are different ciphers, each with its own page ( System A′ , the “Post Scripta” dot cipher ). Attempted here on 21 September 2026, it gave no text; Ryan Xu broke it on 23 October.

The first page (f. 274r) opens in clear German and changes to cipher at line 8, with clear words left inside the cipher (“Zwisch Ho. Fe. und Ni. sein”, “Si.”, “quam”). The second page is clear German only. On f. 275r single cipher words stand inside clear lines, and a second hand wrote the meaning over some of them at the time: der, thumbrobst, Wirtzburg, Hildesheim, “den nonnen haben”, Aichstet. The letter is dated “Den 12 Junij Ao. 83 Stilo novo”. The photographs are not in the public domain, so this page shows none.

Each plain letter is written with one Latin letter or sign: r = a, w = b, d = c (dD = ch), z = d or r, k = e, i = f, u or v (i/ = w), 3 = g, D = h, o = i, s = l, n = m (also n, u), a = n, 4 = o, t = p, c = t, m = z. A slash doubles the letter before it (s/ = ll, c/ = tt, e/ = ss). The signs g, y, b and p, and some d, m and n, stand at word edges as nulls. Ryan Xu noticed that the values form chains (p→t→c→d→z→m→n→a→r): each plain letter is written as the next letter of a scrambled sequence, so each sign should have one value. The two values of z are two glyphs under one label of the transcription. On the photograph the z for d has a hooked or tailed top and the z for r is a flat-footed 2; zizoD (durch) shows both in one word. In the words aligned with the key, z stands 37 times for d and 37 times for r; 6.8% of the letters rest on a label that covers two glyphs, about 1% once the two z forms are kept apart.

In the writer’s spelling; clear words in ⟨ ⟩, […] unread, [?word] uncertain, letters in [ ] supplied, [#] the unread name sign. ⟨wöll in⟩ […] geistlichen [?als] auch den kriegswesen in grosser confusion befinde. ⟨Zwisch Ho. Fe. und Ni. sein⟩ grosse dissimulationes und cunctationes, will kainer den andern nachgeben, ieder für sich selbs das veldt regiren, sy versthen den handl alle drey nit genugsam. (zu hof regirt ⟨Si.⟩ allain cum [?magna] indignationen tam coloniensium ⟨quam⟩ leodiensium.) es sein noch zur zeit gar wenig cöl[ni]sche bey hof, man wartt aber teglich etlicher fürnemen, die beschriben. summa, ich findt den gresten mangel an guetten treuen leuthen. es ist ain suspition vorhanden, als wöll man die susanna lassen herab chomen; die soll […] von freising mitt seim [?weihb.] herab belaitten, wais aber nit obs ghen […] oder ghen lüttich soll gefurt werden. [#] welen darauf gedacht sein, wie dis mitt fueg zuverhindern, dan es wurdt diser orthen ain gr[o]ss scandalum geben, und vil guetherzige so woll als von ⟨Ca.⟩ alienirt werden. wehrs muglich, ire [#] von disen und dergleichen, darein ehr durch bese leuth gefuhrt, mit beschaidenhait und glimpf abzehalten, so soll man disem sti[f]t chain andern herrn [?wünschen]. In English: … that I find both the spiritual affairs and the war in great confusion. Between Ho., Fe. and Ni. there is much dissembling and delay; none will give way to another, each wants to rule the field for himself, and all three understand the business too little. (At court Si. alone governs, to the great indignation of the people of both Cologne and Liège.) There are still very few men of Cologne at court, but some notables who have been summoned are expected daily. All in all, I find the greatest want of good, loyal people. There is a suspicion that they mean to let Susanna come down here; […] of Freising is to escort her down with his [?suffragan], but I do not know whether she is to be taken to […] or to Liège. [#] should consider how this might properly be prevented, for it would give great scandal in these parts, and many well-meaning people, as well as those of Ca., would be estranged. If it were possible to keep [#] from these and similar things, into which he has been led by bad people, with tact and gentleness, then one could wish this see no other lord. On f. 275r the cipher words give “der thumbprobstei wirzburg”, “son phillip zu resigniren”, “so wurdt Si. zu freising die maisten f[r]uctus darvon einnemen, und Si. allain den namen haben” and “hildeshaim”: the Würzburg cathedral provostship was to be resigned to a son Philipp, with the revenues going elsewhere.

21 September 2026, here: the volume’s keys R9420–R9422 did not fit, and annealing in German, Latin and Italian gave no text. 23 October 2026, Ryan Xu: from the transcription alone. The ending -ka closes 32 of 174 words, so k = e and a = n; then -kz = -er, zka = den, rwkz = aber, zok = die, i4a = von, noc = nit. Long words came out whole: zoe/onisrco4ake dissimulationes, oazo3aco4aka indignationen, wkedDrozkaDroc beschaidenhait. 146 of 169 cipher words read directly, 15 more after a one-sign emendation. His controls: 65% of cipher words of four signs or more decode to a word of a sixteenth-century German lexicon (Deutsches Textarchiv), against a median of 8% for 40 shuffled keys. A from-scratch annealer with a sixteenth-century German model recovered 11 signs (70% of the sign tokens) with no cribs; an unconstrained one collapsed into e/n/r text, as ours had. 23 October 2026, here, on the photographs: of his 15 emendations, 9 are what the image shows (a looped d read as s or o in auch, confusion, nachgeben, durch; an s-form read as e in muglich; an r-form read as z in allain; w, not c, in befinde; a cross mark, not 4, before belaitten). One was withdrawn: the image gives suspition , with no letter missing. The rest are kept as supplied letters. The writer’s own spellings were restored (regirt, ghen, gefurt, muglich). “Sl” on f. 275r is the clear abbreviation “Si.”. The contemporary glosses on f. 275r agree with the key: der, thumbrobst, Wirtzburg, Hildesheim. Over zka marnka the gloss reads “den nonnen”, where the cipher gives namen .

The barred o-o sign, three times (ll. 23, 27, f. 275r): a name sign. Its table is not in the photographs; the f. 273v nomenclator fragment is only half visible. Line 21, izriafzia/kz : a name or title of the escort from Freising (f-r-a-u-n-?-d/r-u-nn-e-r). One sign has no value. Line 22, eo after “ghen” (Cologne expected), and the two signs before “geistlichen” in line 8: too short to value. f. 275r zodDcw3 , glossed “Aichstet” at the time, does not decode with the key. Uncertain words: [?magna], [?weihb.] (Weib or Weihbischof), [?wünschen], and the supplied letters in gr[o]ss, sti[f]t, cöl[ni]sche, f[r]uctus. With these counted as holes, 92.8% of the words read as sense, under the 95% bar for a full reading.

Nine code passages of the Orangist envoy in Berlin to the Hereditary Prince and Princess Wilhelmina (KHA A35-1232, A32-549), with no decipherment. Neither Van Reede’s 1789–92 code nor the 1795–96 Euler list fits the glossed letters. His own “Explication” of a letter of 15 August 1796 shows the “Chiffre Littéral” to be a book code: seven groups for a whole sentence, keyed to a printed text that is not named. 12.15.72.45.92.171.319 · 13 · 73 · 2 · 39.97.16 “envoyé à Ivoy un mémoire pour établir & justifier les principes d’une nouvelle coalition …” 91 = Ivoy · 72 = le Duc · 13 = Athlone · 73 = Portland · 2 = de Luc Berlin, Blankenburg → the Hereditary Prince of Orange · book code and numbered lists · 1796–1807 · attempted, not solved Arend Willem van Reede to the Hereditary Prince, 1796–1807 (KHA A35-1232, A32-549) to Hereditary Prince William Nine code passages from the Orange family’s envoy in Berlin were left undeciphered; his own key to one letter shows a book code whose book is not named, so they stay unread. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 26 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letters Arend Willem baron van Reede, the Orangist envoy in Berlin, to the Hereditary Prince Willem Frederik (1796–1807) and to Princess Wilhelmina (1797–1801), in French with runs of numbers; several are written over a letter in invisible ink. Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, A35-1232 (scans 143592, 143603, 144339, 144352, 144361, 144448–49, 144507) and A32-549 (171667, 171744). Not on DECODE. The cipher In 1796 a “Chiffre Littéral” in which a short run of numbers stands for a whole sentence, with dotted groups such as 39.97.16: a book code keyed to a shared printed text, beside a short list of numbers for names. From 1797 a larger numbered list with prefixes and superscripts. How it was tried All nine passages and four glossed letters were transcribed at full size. Van Reede’s 1789–92 code and the Euler word list of 1795–96 were tested on the glossed runs; neither fits (3 of 13 and 3 of 32 decoded words in the run’s own gloss). Why it resists The book of the 1796 code is not named anywhere in the file, and the later list has only about fifteen glossed values. 15 August 1796: name numbers glossed above (91 Ivoy, 72 du Duc, 13 Athlone, 73 au Duc de Portland, 2 de Luc) and the run marked (1.), “12.15.72.45.92.171.319”, explained on the next page. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, A35-1232 (image 144358), via Koninklijke Verzamelingen.

The pairing of all 300 scans of A35-1232 and 139 of A32-549 (research files pairs_A35-1232.tsv , pairs_A32-549.tsv ) left nine code passages with no decipherment: Image Date Groups Note 143592 Jan–Feb 1796 78 in 14 runs black letter over brown invisible ink 143603 Feb 1796 50 rows of figures over an invisible-ink letter 144339 P.S., Jan 1796 54 the “petit chiffre”; warns not to confuse “valeurs réelles” with “indicateurs” 144352 Blankenburg, 5 July 1796 19 144361 “Précis” of 29 July 1796 127 sent in cipher because the letter was too long 144448–49 c. Dec 1801 73 between lines of invisible ink 144507 c. 1806–07 35 over invisible ink 171667 1797–98 about 98 to Wilhelmina; fractions and plus signs 171744 Berlin, 5 Dec 1800 or 1801 46 to Wilhelmina; “Votre chiffre primitif”

“Explication des chiffres employés dans la lettre; chaque trait indique que la phrase est finie, & qu’il faut passer au chiffre suivant.” Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, A35-1232 (image 144359), via Koninklijke Verzamelingen. The letter of 15 August 1796 carries its own key. Its run (1.), seven groups, is explained as “envoyé à Ivoy un mémoire pour établir & justifier les principes d’une nouvelle coalition basant sur la reconnoissance de Louis XVIII comme seul moyen d’inspirer de la confiance à la Prusse”; run (3.) as “qu’il n’y avoit rien à faire dès que l’Angleterre n’adoptoit pas en plein la marche proposée”. Seven groups for some two hundred letters cannot be a letter cipher or a word code; with the dotted groups in the text (“39.97.16”, “29.17.19.37”) and Van Reede’s words, “Je me sers, Monseigneur, du Chiffre Littéral usité pour ma correspondance particulière avec Elle”, the system reads as a book code, each group pointing into a printed text that both men held. The text is not named in the file. The Prince’s own drafts in the same folder (Berlin 11 June, 2 July 1796 and others) are the clear texts of letters he sent in cipher to Van Reede; the enciphered versions are not here.

Transcription. The nine passages and the glossed letters of 15 August 1796, 27 September 1796 (the Prince’s draft, meanings in parentheses), 19 May and October–November 1798 were transcribed at full size with every mark ( runs_a.txt , runs_b.txt ). Known keys. test_keys.py decoded every run with Van Reede’s 1789–92 code to Wilhelmina ( targets/reede1789 ) and with the Euler word list of 1795–96 ( targets/wilhelmina1795 ), and scored both on the fifteen glossed runs: 3 of 13 and 3 of 32 decoded words stand in the run’s own gloss, against 2 and 0 in another run’s. The glossed values contradict both (13 is Athlone here, “difficile” in the Euler list; 6/52 is Haugwitz in 1798, where the Euler list has 52 = une). Print. Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken II and III, searched in full text, print no letter of Van Reede to the Prince.

All nine passages, about 580 groups: unread for lack of key material. A reading of the 1796 passages needs the book; the Explication gives plaintext for one letter only, too little to identify a book by itself. The 1797–1801 list (groups to 1951) has about fifteen glossed values in the file.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letters Two numerical-code letters of 13 pages, attributed by DECODE to W. F. Röell: R1469 (7 pages, dated 9 February 1809) and R1470 (6 pages, undated). They are neither addressed nor signed. Röell’s despatches in the archive are in clear Dutch. Where Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 1.02.04 legatie Turkije inv. 804; DECODE R1469 (images 6681–6687) and R1470 (6688–6693). The cipher 2,585 groups, 931 distinct, none reaching even 1% of the text, so common words have many equivalents. Frequent groups are spread over the whole range, so it is not alphabetical. How it was tried It is not the legation’s 1788–93 code (only 30–33% of each crib’s groups occur here, against 28% by chance) and not the ministry’s codes of 1804 and 1808. DECODE and print give no key. Still open No group has been decoded. The trailing marks on some groups were not re-transcribed. A key could come from the legation codebook, Croiset’s 1808–09 letters to Röell, or a clear copy of a despatch in this code. R1469, first page (image 6681): “Monsieur”, then code. Line numbers 5, 10, 15 run down the margin. Some groups carry a small trailing mark (735ʼ, 895ʼ) that the DECODE transcription mostly leaves out. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 1.02.04 legatie Turkije inv. 804, image 6681, via DECODE R1469.

R1469 (images 6681–6687): opens “Monsieur” and ends on p. 7 with a paraph. 1,297 groups, 622 distinct. R1470 (images 6688–6693): a docket on p. 1 read by DECODE as “? 69 Fermer? no? 9?”, then code. 1,288 groups, 707 distinct, the highest 3264. DECODE already doubts the address: Van Dedem was on his way home when the letter was sent.

Frequencies. The commonest groups are 1390 and 460 (12 each in R1469) and 804, 75, 357, 296 and 394 (10 each in R1470). In a French text de alone is 4–5%, so a group rate of about 1% means heavy homophony. The frequent groups run from 35 to 2920 with no clustering, which excludes a one-part code whose alphabetical ranges could be predicted. The legation’s 1788–93 code ( Van Dedem 1788–99 ), for which French (R1947, R2053) and Dutch (R2121) decipherments exist. It is a different code. Only 30–33% of each crib’s distinct groups occur here, against 28% by chance, and just 0–5 of each crib’s 30 commonest groups are among the 200 commonest here. The ministry’s other codes of the period , Van Spaen 1808 (plain groups to 1339) and Fagel 1804 (syllabic groups with clear endings). These are different systems. Keys and print. The DECODE metadata dump has no key record for this legation or ministry. Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken V (1806–1810) gave nothing by web search. The inventory of Röell’s papers (NA 2.21.008.78) lists letters from F. G. van Dedem and from S. F. Croiset, both 1808–09, but no cipher.

Both letters in full; no group has been decoded. The trailing marks on some groups are not in DECODE’s transcription and were not re-transcribed. They may be part of the code. What could supply the key: the codebook in the legation papers (NA 1.02.04, near inv. 804), Croiset’s 1808–09 letters to Röell (NA 2.21.008.78), or a clear copy of any despatch in this code. Henk Boon, Onze man in Constantinopel (2012), was not checked.

Twenty cipher letters from the Spanish envoys in London and at Nijmegen (Brussels SEG 2559, DECODE R966–R984, R1001). The Balbases 1677 key, from the same volume, was applied unchanged: 88% of 23,463 groups decrypted, and the sixteen contemporary marginal decipherments confirmed. The four letters with no decipherment are decrypted in gist; the residue is mostly transcription noise. eg . 470 . 42 . 28 . 73 . xoy . 140 . 21 . 71 . 24 . xi . 78 he [.] vi s to co n [.] a te n ci on one key for London, Stockholm and Nijmegen · the Balbases 1677 table London and Nijmegen → Copenhagen · syllabic nomenclator · 1676–78 Bernardo de Salinas and Pedro Ronquillo to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, 1676–78 from Pedro Ronquillo Go to the full text ↓ Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559 · DECODE R966–R984 and R1001, twenty letters · sixteen with a contemporary decipherment in the margin, four without The Balbases key applies unchanged to all twenty: 88% of 23,463 groups get a value, including the two letters that DECODE lists with no decipherment; eighteen carry a contemporary decipherment in the margin, and with it all twenty now build sentences and are translated, with a few holes Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · partial (100% of the cipher) The letters Twenty ciphered letters from Spanish envoys in Fuenmayor’s papers: eight from Bernardo de Salinas in London (August 1676 – March 1677) and twelve from Pedro Ronquillo at the Nijmegen congress (December 1676 – March 1678). Where Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559; DECODE records R966–R984 and R1001. DECODE lists two of them as “non-decrypted”. The cipher The Spanish nomenclator of Balbases , shared by the northern envoys; Carpio in Rome used a different one. How it was read The Balbases key, rebuilt from his margins, was applied unchanged and gives values for 88.4% of the 23,463 groups. Sixteen letters have a marginal decipherment, which the key output confirms; six transcriptions had no group boundaries and were divided against the key’s vocabulary. What it says The four letters with no margin (R970, R973, R982, R984) are decrypted in gist only: the congress, English parliament and Charles II, subsidies, and the fall of Ghent. Still open 11.6% of groups have no value, nearly all transcription noise. The four unmargined letters stand at R970 77%, R973 86%, R982 71%, R984 86%; their transcriptions still need correcting from the images. Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen, 26 February 1678 (R984, p. 1): the first cipher block, with no decipherment beside it. The reading has He visto con particular atencion quanto V.S. me participa en sus referidas cartas en lo tocante a las materias que se an tratado en esa asamblea de los aliados del Norte . Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, p. 1, via DECODE R984.

R982 and R984 have no margin and were deciphered on the images with the key. R970 and R973 do have a margin, which DECODE recorded only in a comment; their readings follow it. Quotations are from the readings of 22–23 October 2026. Ronquillo, Nijmegen, 26 February 1678 (R984) Ronquillo replies to Fuenmayor’s reports on the assembly of the northern allies. Everything depends on the resolutions of the English parliament, and on whether Charles II will really break with France. Ronquillo, who knows that court, doubts it: [?no] me atrevere a hacer todavia juicio fijo ni de la paz ni de la guerra mientras no tuvieremos apariencias mas ciertas y seguras de las deliveraciones de Su Magestad Britanica . The Danes complain about subsidy remittances and say they can do nothing. The Elector of Brandenburg is in Pomerania. At the end, the Duke of Hanover’s intrigue, "esta trama", runs through his kinship with Madame. Ronquillo, Nijmegen, 19 March 1678 (R982) This comes ten days after the fall of Ghent. DECODE’s transcription is poor (full of "?"); re-transcribed from the soft scan, the letter reads with holes: the congress, Flanders taken by surprise, the two months that are lacking, the Brunswick princes, Con que de todas maneras estamos muy mal , and Ronquillo’s own melancolicas reflexiones . Salinas, London, 15 September 1676 (R970) Ya V.S. se hallara noticioso del fatal suceso de Mastrique : the fall of Maastricht, “quiso la fortuna cerrarnos esta puerta”. The discourses at the English court turn towards a peace, and the "progresos" on Fuenmayor’s side weigh on them. The minister has taken the news calmly. There is mention of the Danish fleet. Salinas, London, 2 March 1677 (R973) The English have made a beginning, no siendo tan malos principios quando los dan en negocio que tanto nos importa como retirar las tropas de Francia, en que me prometo persistiran . The preparations of recent months show that everything is in earnest. Talk treats the peace as good as made.

The Balbases key was used, with the four values added for Hernán Núñez (167 Suecia, 161 resolución, os para, 6+ o). It was applied without changes to DECODE’s transcriptions of all twenty records. Six records (R971, R974, R978, R979, R983, R1001) are typed character by character with no group boundaries, and at first gave 0%. Each line was rejoined and divided into groups by dynamic programming over the key’s vocabulary: fewest groups, with one-character groups penalised. They then decrypted at 90–94%. R970 and R973 write one sign as "Infinity" (∞), which is c before a vowel. R970’s transcriber also writes 5 where the key has a and b for que . These conventions account for most of its groups without a value. The margins were compared with the key output. They agree. Re-reading, 22–23 October 2026: every margin transcribed from full-resolution crops of the DECODE images (DECODE’s margin transcriptions checked against them) and aligned word by word with the key decode; the decode cut into words page by page ( spaced.py ); R982 and R984, and the transcriptions of R966–R970, R973, R976 and R977, corrected on the images ( txi/ ). About 60 code values from the margins entered the key ( keyx.py ; coverage 93.6% to 95.4%). The readings first written in modern spelling were restored to the writers’ own from the key decode ( tomavan , assi , haver , Magestad ), with no word changed.

R983, the first page: the margin is faded almost to nothing on the DECODE scan, and groups l, c, 1q, L2, pA, 11 and 300 are not in the key, so its first passage has many holes. R982 and R984, without a margin: the opening groups of R982 and about a dozen phrase-level holes, and about a dozen code groups in R984 (138, 91, 113, 460, 600, 109 and others) that no margined letter glosses. R982’s scan is soft; with these holes R982 reads at 91.9% of its words, under 95%. Single words in R966, R967, R968, R971/R972, R976, R977, R979, R981 and R1001, where the margin is faded or blotted and the figures alone do not settle the word. Grades: A for R966, R968–R975, R978–R981 and R1001; B for R967, R976, R977, R982, R983 and R984.

R966, Salinas, 21 Aug 1676 Salinas to Fuenmayor, London 21 Aug 1676: Charles II tells Salinas that an invasion of France would harm the peace and that the Maastricht and Philippsburg sieges will end the campaign; the King is in a bad humour over German successes; on the passports he favours the Münster precedent against the princes' new claims (Lorraine); no treaty talk until the campaign ends. For they are already at the beginning of the turmoil, so they await the Parliament, where great things will be seen; though I foresee that, if it comes in furious and the King sees no light of obtaining anything, he will prorogue it before they have room to go further. To which I have replied that I had already given an account of mine to His Majesty, so another form is being sought, in the meantime of which I suspend sending [the] answer, though I will do it one way or another so that Your Lordship may see it, towards one or towards all. And because I already knew this way of acting, and that they tried the same with the lord Count of Molina, it has seemed best to me to hold firm with a little spirit; for if we let ourselves fall everywhere, these will despise us more than anyone, because they are prouder than all. Words in ⟨ ⟩ are in clear in the letter. --> # R970, Salinas to Fuenmayor, London, 15 Sep 1676 ⟨... I shall let Your Lordship know, so that you know where your orders are to find me, and meanwhile I beg you not to deny me here any that may serve you.⟩ Your Lordship will already have heard of the fatal event at Maastricht. So that no resource should be left to our hopes, fortune chose to shut this door on us, leaving us as our only relief the disillusion of how little can be expected of the Prince of Orange and of the armies he may command. This knowledge, added to pressing necessity, will carry us at a great pace to peace, which is what these people want and the end to which they direct these moves. So today the talk of it is renewed, and every day they shoot arrows at me, which I must parry until clear orders arrive to guide us to the right course. The progress on your side moves these minds no less, for, as Your Lordship knows, they neither wish for it nor is it in their interest. I advise them to press hard, because the soup cannot last them, as I see our affairs and the mood of the Dutch, whose minister at this court has obtained by this event what he wished, both from his ill will to the Prince and from his great longing for peace. I keep him well in view, and so as not to make him distrustful, so that he does not slip away from me, I humour him, and I hold him back so that he does not fall into some rashness. The minister of that King fears him greatly, and Bergeyck no less, because he knew him here; so his coming has alarmed him, since it is certain that the two together will do something rash. So he tells me that he has written to His Danish Majesty to remedy this blow and to make representations so that I stay here, which I did not know until he told it to Manuel de Fonseca. Pero aun no es este todo el mal, pues si se encaminaran esos oficios por la senda derecha de la honra, pudieramos esperar un buen ajuste para todos; pero temo, y no sin grandes fundamentos, que entre este Rey y holandeses nos han [?proyectado] la paz que nos quieren dar, y que ha sido menester vencer al de Orange y ajustar sus intereses; con cuya negociacion, y la prisa que se dan estos en Nimega para llegar a la sustancia, pasando sobre tantos inconvenientes y formalidades de disgusto para las partes, van de carrera a la conclusion, y se prometen aqui conseguirla antes de la canpaña, por lo que le importa a este Rey y por lo que lo desean holandeses. En cuyo proyecto temo siempre que nos quitan la Borgoña, porque, habiendose pasado grandes discursos conmigo sobre esta materia, en que me vieron firme y asentar por primer fundamento de la paz la restitucion de esta provincia, se han recatado de mi; y por ultimo andan grandes demandas y respuestas de aqui a Paris. Sobre que hable dos dias ha al Rey, y me dijo que la paz se habia de hacer, que el ni estava en estado de entrar en guerra ni la queria, que Flandes habia de quedar con fronteras, que no nos lisonjeasemos con el Parlamento, porque este no le obligaria a este empeño. En que dire a V.S. que las disposiciones que tenemos para este tribunal no pueden ser mejores, pero por la misma razon temo que ha de haber tanta confusion que ha de obligar a este Rey a disolverle o prorrogarle, con que nos quedaremos como nos estamos. No obstante, no pierdo de vista todos los oficios que puedan fomentar las esperanzas; y para el punto principal, y que nos mira tan de cerca, el de las levas y reclutas para Francia, he proseguido mis quejas sin rendirme al temor que me quisieron poner con la respuesta disparatada que se me dio, en que no obstante se logro a lo menos el que en el reino de Inglaterra cesasen las reclutas; pero prosiguiendo en Escocia, escribi el papel de que va copia adjunta al secretario de Estado, cuya respuesta vera V.S., tambien con la carta que Su Majestad Britanica mando escribir a los estados de Escocia. Vi lo que V.S. me participa del discurso que le tuvo Monsieur de Amerongen, y es lastima que una respuesta tan discreta y prudente como la de V.S. se emplease en aquel sujeto, porque no es de los mas clasicos de Holanda, aunque es de los de la mala intencion. Words in ⟨ ⟩ are in clear in the letter. --> # R971, Salinas to Fuenmayor, London, 26 Jan 1677 ⟨... and that all my obedience to your service wishes to deserve it.⟩ I do not wonder how awkward that residence must be for Your Lordship, having to deal with such different humours and interests, and particularly with the Bishop of Münster, whom I take for a quibbler and, as they say, something of a cheat; but let Your Lordship console himself that there is trouble everywhere, and let him turn round to the north and he will see how [?our] lyre plays, what is happening at Nijmegen and what is happening here, the disorder proceeding from the pilot who steers the helm, for which, the voices of the people say, there is another who alone can remedy it; on which the letters from Madrid will undeceive Your Lordship. Don Pedro Ronquillo has been anxious these days, with motives to spare; and although my reports will not have freed him of it, he will nevertheless proceed with more light, for since his fears came from the journey of Ambassador Temple to The Hague, which gave him and everyone cause for suspicion, I have tried to discover all the ground I could, and I have found that everything was aimed at bringing the Prince of Orange round to lend a hand to the peace, and that it has succeeded; for since this last post from Holland this King is better pleased and satisfied with the said Prince, and Ambassador Van Beuningen no less, with his inclination so barefaced to this end. But even this is not the whole evil, for if those offices were directed along the straight path of honour, we could hope for a good settlement for all; but I fear, and not without great grounds, that between this King and the Dutch they have [?planned] for us the peace they mean to give us, and that it has been necessary to win over the [Prince] of Orange and settle his interests; with which negotiation, and the haste these men are making at Nijmegen to come to the substance, passing over so many difficulties and formalities displeasing to the parties, they are running to the conclusion, and they promise themselves here to obtain it before the campaign, because of what it matters to this King and because the Dutch desire it. In which project I always fear they take Burgundy from us, because, great discussions having passed with me on this matter, in which they saw me firm and laying down as the first foundation of the peace the restitution of this province, they have kept themselves guarded from me; and lately there are great demands and answers going from here to Paris. On which I spoke two days ago to the King, and he told me that the peace had to be made, that he was neither in a state to enter a war nor wanted it, that Flanders had to remain with frontiers, that we should not flatter ourselves with the Parliament, because it would not oblige him to this engagement. On which I will tell Your Lordship that the dispositions we have towards this tribunal could not be better, but for the same reason I fear there must be so much confusion that it will oblige this King to dissolve or prorogue it, so that we shall remain as we are. Nevertheless I do not lose sight of any offices that may foster our hopes; and on the main point, which touches us so closely, that of the levies and recruits for France, I have pursued my complaints without yielding to the fear they tried to put in me with the absurd answer I was given, in which nevertheless it was achieved at least that the recruiting ceased in the kingdom of England; but as it continued in Scotland, I wrote the paper of which a copy goes enclosed to the Secretary of State, whose answer Your Lordship will see, together with the letter His Britannic Majesty ordered written to the Estates of Scotland. I saw what Your Lordship tells me of the discourse Monsieur d'Amerongen held with you, and it is a pity that so discreet and prudent an answer as Your Lordship's should be spent on that person, for he is not one of the most classic men of Holland, though he is one of those of ill intention. His opinion does not agree with that of Van Beuningen, who is here, for the latter is not of the opinion for the truce, because he is more [?thrifty], and he thinks that maintaining the allies might cost them some expense, so that he is heading with all haste towards the peace; and, as Your Lordship says, any [peace] will be better than a truce. But what I believe is that, if time were lacking here at the opening of the campaign to conclude the peace, this King, urged by this minister, might propose some suspension of arms for two or three months, but no more. What I can assure Your Lordship is that within a month the abscess must burst, and that of everything that occurs I will give you a more punctual account, always seeking [Your Lordship's] orders for your service. Pero aun no es este todo el mal, pues si se encaminaran esos oficios por la senda derecha de la honra, pudieramos esperar un buen ajuste para todos; pero temo, y no sin grandes fundamentos, que entre este Rey y holandeses nos han [?proyectado] la paz que nos quieren dar, y que ha sido menester vencer al de Orange y ajustar sus intereses; con cuya negociacion, y la prisa que se dan estos en Nimega para llegar a la sustancia, pasando sobre tantos inconvenientes y formalidades de disgusto para las partes, van de carrera a la conclusion, y se prometen aqui conseguirla antes de la canpaña, por lo que le importa a este Rey y por lo que lo desean holandeses. En cuyo proyecto temo siempre que nos quitan la Vorgoña, porque, haviendose pasado grandes discursos conmigo sobre esta materia, en que me vieron firme y asentar por primer fundamento de la paz la restitucion de esta provincia, se han recatado de mi; y por ultimo andan grandes demandas y respuestas de aqui a Paris. Sobre que hable dos dias ha al Rey, y me dijo que la paz se habia de hacer, que el ni estava en estado de entrar en guerra ni la queria, que Flandes habia de quedar con fronteras, que no nos lisonjeasemos con el Parlamento, porque este no le obligaria a este empeño. En que dire a V.S. que las disposiciones que tenemos para este tribunal no pueden ser mejores, pero por la misma razon temo que ha de haber tanta confusion que ha de obligar a este Rey a disolverle o prorrogarle, con que nos quedaremos como nos estamos. No obstante, no pierdo de vista todos los oficios que puedan fomentar las esperanzas; y para el punto principal, y que nos mira tan de cerca, el de las levas y reclutas para Francia, he proseguido mis quejas sin rendirme al temor que me quisieron poner con la respuesta disparatada que se me dio, en que no obstante se logro a lo menos el que en el reino de Inglaterra cesasen las reclutas; pero prosiguiendo en Escocia, escribi el papel de que va copia adjunta al secretario de Estado, cuya respuesta vera V.S., tambien con la carta que Su Magestad Britanica mando escribir a los estados de Escocia. Vi lo que V.S. me participa del discurso que le tuvo Monsieur de Amerongen, y es lastima que una respuesta tan discreta y prudente como la de V.S. se enplease en aquel sujeto, porque no es de los mas clasicos de Holanda, aunque es de los de la mala intencion. Su dictamen no confronta con el de Van Beuningen, que esta aqui, pues este no es de la opinion de la tregua, porque es mas [?menagero], y le parece que el mantener los aliados les pudiera causar algun gasto, con que este se encamina con toda precipitacion a la paz; y, como V.S. dice, cualquiera sera mejor que una tregua. Pero lo que yo creo es que, si faltase aqui a la abertura de la canpaña tiempo para concluir la paz, pudiera este Rey, instado de este ministro, proponer alguna suspension de armas de dos o tres meses, pero mas no. Words in ⟨ ⟩ are in clear in the letter. --> # R972, Salinas to Fuenmayor, London, 26 Jan 1677 ⟨... and that all my obedience to your service wishes to deserve it.⟩ I do not wonder how awkward that residence must be for Your Lordship, having to deal with such different humours and interests, and particularly with the Bishop of Münster, whom I take for a quibbler and, as they say, something of a cheat; but let Your Lordship console himself that there is trouble everywhere, and let him turn round to the north and he will see how [?our] lyre plays, what is happening at Nijmegen and what is happening here, the disorder proceeding from the pilot who steers the helm, for which, the voices of the people say, there is another who alone can remedy it; on which the letters from Madrid will undeceive Your Lordship. Don Pedro Ronquillo has been anxious these days, with motives to spare; and although my reports will not have freed him of it, he will nevertheless proceed with more light, for since his fears came from the journey of Ambassador Temple to The Hague, which gave him and everyone cause for suspicion, I have tried to discover all the ground I could, and I have found that everything was aimed at bringing the Prince of Orange round to lend a hand to the peace, and that it has succeeded; for since this last post from Holland this King is better pleased and satisfied with the said Prince, and Ambassador Van Beuningen no less, with his inclination so barefaced to this end. But even this is not the whole evil, for if those offices were directed along the straight path of honour, we could hope for a good settlement for all; but I fear, and not without great grounds, that between this King and the Dutch they have [?planned] for us the peace they mean to give us, and that it has been necessary to win over the [Prince] of Orange and settle his interests; with which negotiation, and the haste these men are making at Nijmegen to come to the substance, passing over so many difficulties and formalities displeasing to the parties, they are running to the conclusion, and they promise themselves here to obtain it before the campaign, because of what it matters to this King and because the Dutch desire it. In which project I always fear they take Burgundy from us, because, great discussions having passed with me on this matter, in which they saw me firm and laying down as the first foundation of the peace the restitution of this province, they have kept themselves guarded from me; and lately there are great demands and answers going from here to Paris. On which I spoke two days ago to the King, and he told me that the peace had to be made, that he was neither in a state to enter a war nor wanted it, that Flanders had to remain with frontiers, that we should not flatter ourselves with the Parliament, because it would not oblige him to this engagement. On which I will tell Your Lordship that the dispositions we have towards this tribunal could not be better, but for the same reason I fear there must be so much confusion that it will oblige this King to dissolve or prorogue it, so that we shall remain as we are. Nevertheless I do not lose sight of any offices that may foster our hopes; and on the main point, which touches us so closely, that of the levies and recruits for France, I have pursued my complaints without yielding to the fear they tried to put in me with the absurd answer I was given, in which nevertheless it was achieved at least that the recruiting ceased in the kingdom of England; but as it continued in Scotland, I wrote the paper of which a copy goes enclosed to the Secretary of State, whose answer Your Lordship will see, together with the letter His Britannic Majesty ordered written to the Estates of Scotland. I saw what Your Lordship tells me of the discourse Monsieur d'Amerongen held with you, and it is a pity that so discreet and prudent an answer as Your Lordship's should be spent on that person, for he is not one of the most classic men of Holland, though he is one of those of ill intention. His opinion does not agree with that of Van Beuningen, who is here, for the latter is not of the opinion for the truce, because he is more [?thrifty], and he thinks that maintaining the allies might cost them some expense, so that he is heading with all haste towards the peace; and, as Your Lordship says, any [peace] will be better than a truce. But what I believe is that, if time were lacking here at the opening of the campaign to conclude the peace, this King, urged by this minister, might propose some suspension of arms for two or three months, but no more. What I can assure Your Lordship is that within a month the abscess must burst, and that of everything that occurs I will give you a more punctual account, always seeking [Your Lordship's] orders for your service. Y con efecto, cuando los diputados en La Haya vinieron en quitar aquella palabra "separada" en sus plenipotencias, resolvieron al mismo tiempo que no se consintiesse la expresion de la mediacion del Papa. Los franceses respondieron que no han de alterar el contexto referido, que tiene aprovacion de su amo; pero dicen tambien que esperan dentro de tres o cuatro dias respuesta a otra carta que han escrito; y si, como dicen, quieren entrar derechos y obviar los inconvenientes al tratado de la paz, no dejaran de hallarse medios terminos para esto. Antes de anoche me dijeron los holandeses que los mediadores instaban mucho en que se permitiesen los correos ordinarios para Suecia; y aunque a mi me icieron la salva de que justamente Su Magestad danesa lo contradecia por no haber querido conceder esto mismo en su pasaporte, no obstante alzavan el grito por su comercio, que estava envarazado por no poder tener correspondencias los mercaderes para las letras de cambio y los avisos. One must confess that they are good [?Swedes], in which the English concur no less. The excuses Count Kinsky gives of a sciatica that has come upon him in Cologne they scorn. Nevertheless they have agreed that we should not hand over our full powers until a minister of the Lord Emperor arrives; and it is no small thing that they have understood that it would cause more trouble to present those of the allies one by one than all together; but it is certain that, by putting forward all the objections together, the course that is taken will be more effective. They have handed their full powers to the French and Dutch mediators. In that of Holland there was a small objection, which the States have already ordered removed. In those of Sweden the [?haughtiness] cannot be tolerated, nor the declaring that they were provoked into the war by the breach of the Peace of Westphalia; the French have thrown in similar clauses of arrogance. But the two that seem intolerable in their full power are: the one, the King of France saying that he has condescended to send his ambassadors to the congress through the expedients the King of England has supplied him, and hopes he will obtain the release of Prince Wilhelm of Fürstenberg, which the Lord Emperor will in no way consent to; the other is raised by the Dutch and all the Protestant princes, namely the one containing the mediation of the Pope, saying that the instrument of the full powers is the foundation of the firmness of the contract of peace to be made, and that it must not contain a clause contradicting religion, which is the basis of the public law of the State. And indeed, when the deputies at The Hague agreed to remove that word "separate" in their full powers, they resolved at the same time that the mention of the Pope's mediation should not be allowed. The French answered that they will not alter the said text, which has their master's approval; but they also say they expect within three or four days an answer to another letter they have written; and if, as they say, they mean to deal straightforwardly and remove the obstacles to the peace treaty, middle ways will not fail to be found for this. The night before last the Dutch told me that the mediators were pressing hard for the ordinary posts to Sweden to be allowed; and although they made me the excuse that His Danish Majesty rightly opposed it for not having been willing to grant this very thing in his passport, nevertheless they raised an outcry over their trade, which was hampered by the merchants being unable to keep correspondence for bills of exchange and news. To overcome this point the mediators offer us that France will allow us the free dispatch of the posts, though by a roundabout way; an offer I have not wished to answer positively, but it will always suit us to have the passage free, although they also believe that if they attach conditions, they will be the same ones we grant them. From the withdrawal of the minister of Münster, and the excuse of the Wolfenbüttel one for not wishing to negotiate on that account, one infers what Your Lordship reasons, that they act in concert; and I believe they will aim at having this matter brought before the general congress, because they must understand that they are to be helped by the Dutch more than others, and that the Dutch have no great wish that Denmark and Brandenburg should keep advantages in the duchy of Bremen, since they would sooner compensate Sweden from the spoils of these princes than from those of Celle and Münster. No minister of these princes, nor of Lorraine, appears here, because the King of France makes it well understood that he is not minded to grant them the jus legationis. And although he treats Lorraine with more decency, and agrees that, there being a precedent of some ambassador of the Duke having been covered, he will grant the passports in the same form; and two having been presented to him, he now says they should justify them, when the King of France has carried off to the last item the archives of Nancy; to the princes of the Empire he says he wishes to know what the Emperor and Spain will do, but he does not defer to what they may do. I should wish some course were taken in this, for I foresee that on the very day the text of the full powers is settled we shall have to enter on the main points of making proposals, and it would be of great harm if by then ministers of Lorraine, Celle and Münster were not here; and on this matter I dare not speak, because in Madrid they have not answered on this particular, and Your Lordship knows that at our court no one is covered unless he be of a crowned head, or of the republics of Venice or Holland. ⟨Your Lordship forgive the length of this letter ...⟩ R976, Ronquillo, 10 Apr 1677 Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen 10 Apr 1677: the negotiations worsen; the Dutch handed the mediators new full powers; rumours of separate Spanish talks and royal marriages worry the allies; Saint-Omer and Cambrai expected as the first article of an armistice; the Brunswick guarantee; Hanover to mediate a separate treaty with Sweden and Denmark.
