Y estoy en animo de hacer las nuestras al mismo tiempo, aunque no concurran los demas, no solo por caminar unido con esta gente, sino tambien porque, conteniendo una clausula sobre la satisfaccion de los aliados, no respondan franceses que no hemos pedido nada. Yo veo a estos hombres muy ansiosos por la paz; y aunque no me atrevere a afirmar que la hagan separada, por las seguridades que cada dia me dan de que no nos avandonaran y que nos asistiran en la guerra, no obstante temo mucho que prorrumpan en obligarnos a firmar un tratado intempestivamente, dandonos la ley que quisieren. Yo los procuro sosegar, y me an ofrecido que, aunque retarden cuatro o cinco dias mas el presentar sus pretensiones, aguardaran a que concurran a un mismo tiempo las nuestras; y procuro no dejarlos un punto de la mano, porque no se arrojen a mayor desesperacion. Repito a V.S. mi agradecimiento por las noticias que me participa de lo que ahi ocurre y por los papeles que me remite. La declaracion que ha hecho el conde de Windischgratz de parte del señor Emperador es muy buena en lo general, porque es dar a entender que quiere parte en las conquistas, o que los aliados acudan a garantir sus dominios de la Alsacia; pero esta materia es menester tratarla con mucho tiento y maña, porque no nos sea de perjuicio. Y ya V.S. habra entendido que el Principe de Orange se ha declarado en que no se movera mientras el ejercito del señor Emperador no obrase lo proyectado en La Haya. V.S. puede considerar cual me hallare con todas estas cosas, estando solo, y tan solo que aseguro a V.S. que ni de Madrid, de Flandes, ni de otra ninguna parte no me ayudan, ni aun con noticias; y en medio desto se esta en Bruselas don Manuel de Lira, que era el unico que me podia ayudar desde La Haya; pero tambien reconozco que la misma razon que justifica su ida de Holanda justifica igualmente el que no vuelva, sin remedio; y en verdad que seria de gran conveniencia su asistencia en aquella corte. ⟨Dios nos asista, y guarde a V.S. muchos años como deseo. Words in ⟨ ⟩ are in clear in the letter. --> # R978, Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen, 10 Feb 1677 (signed for him by Bernardo Navarro) ⟨... in which to discharge my obligation.⟩ The settling of this devil of a draft of full powers keeps us more embarrassed every day by the disputes and objections raised at every moment; and although on our side, and the Dutch side too, and I believe on that of the Lord Emperor, this point could have been finished, since the drafts we have presented to the mediators agree and there is nothing to catch hold of, nevertheless a gasconade of the Danish plenipotentiary keeps this dispute alive. It consists in his maintaining and stubbornly insisting that, if the French hand him their full powers in Latin, he will hand over his in the same language; but if it is in French, he will draw up his master's in Danish; in which dispute it is plain that much of it is obstinacy. The Dutch have already handed in their signed power and are trying to do the same with their claims; and to this is added the uproar raised among the plenipotentiaries of Holland because Count Kinsky let slip to the mediators that all the drafts handed in were to be brought back to the conference of the allies so that they might be signed and the objections found be examined; which, in the Dutch hurry, seems to them a great deal of delay; and this morning they were with me hurling thunderbolts and sparks, and finally burst out saying that there was to be no more conference; that although it is true that in all business it was well to proceed by common accord of the confederates, they did not wish to be bound so as to be prevented from making their own particular moves. And I am minded to make ours at the same time, even if the others do not join, not only so as to keep step with these people, but also because, if it contains a clause on the satisfaction of the allies, the French cannot answer that we have asked for nothing. I see these men very eager for peace; and although I would not dare affirm that they will make it separately, given the assurances they give me every day that they will not abandon us and will assist us in the war, nevertheless I much fear they may break out into forcing us to sign a treaty out of season, laying down for us whatever law they please. I try to calm them, and they have promised me that, even if it delays the presenting of their claims by four or five more days, they will wait for ours to come in at the same time; and I try not to let them out of my hand for a moment, lest they throw themselves into greater despair. I repeat to Your Lordship my thanks for the news you impart of what happens there and for the papers you send me. The declaration Count Windischgrätz has made on behalf of the Lord Emperor is very good in general, for it gives to understand that he wants a share in the conquests, or that the allies should come to guarantee his dominions in Alsace; but this matter must be handled with great care and skill, so that it does not harm us. The Dutch will approve the first, because they are of the opinion that the share of the conquests against Sweden should serve as an exchange for our losses in Flanders; but the second they will not face, and the Lord Emperor will regain the reputation he has had of not wanting peace and of looking only to his own particular interests; and this will be the more recognised the more he marches along the upper Moselle and is employed in working for the common cause. And Your Lordship will already have heard that the Prince of Orange has declared that he will not move as long as the Lord Emperor's army does not carry out what was planned at The Hague. Your Lordship may consider how I shall find myself with all these things, being alone, and so alone that I assure Your Lordship that neither from Madrid, nor from Flanders, nor from any other quarter do they help me, not even with news; and in the midst of this Don Manuel de Lira, who was the only one who could help me from The Hague, is staying in Brussels; but I also recognise that the same reason that justifies his leaving Holland equally justifies his not returning, there is no help for it; and in truth his presence at that court would be of great advantage. ⟨God help us, and keep Your Lordship many years as I wish. Nijmegen, 10 February 1677.⟩ R979, Ronquillo, 9 Jan 1677 Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen 9 Jan 1677: backs Fuenmayor's proposed course; the Emperor aims at Breisach and Alsace, not Flanders; the English mediators passed on the Franco-Swedish draft; the Dutch are eager for peace and Kinsky does not grasp Spain's plight. El pretexto de reconocer el animo de los principes no es satisfactorio, porque, en mi entender, ellos seran buenos como los paguen, particularmente los de Brunswick. In short, from what passes there and what I can see here, I see more clearly every day that all will aim solely at their own advantage. The pretext of sounding the mind of the princes is not satisfactory, because in my understanding they will be good as long as they are paid, particularly those of Brunswick. Pero por lo mismo que nosotros contradeciremos lo que nuestros enemigos desean, se valdrian ellos para no admitirla; y assi me parece que este punto no podra tener ajuste, y que sera menester pensar solo en la guerra. Y volviendo a la paz separada que holandeses desean hacer con Suecia, que aunque en el congreso no se ha llegado a hablar abiertamente, es fijo que en La Haya se hara con grande ahinco, dire a V.S. que esta proposicion ha sido hecha por los mismos suecos, añadiendo que en caso que el Rey de Francia no quisiese venir en ella, la ajustarian ellos por si solos y se declararian contra el Cristianisimo. Es cierto que los holandeses anhelan como siempre por la paz con Suecia, diciendo que no ay otro remedio para la paz general sino compensando con las perdidas de Suecia las nuestras en el Pais Bajo; pero al mismo paso que este ajuste nos podia ser de gran conveniencia haciendose en una paz general, nos exponemos al precipicio si la de Suecia se hace separada, pues es fijo que perderemos los aliados del norte, que el Rey de Suecia no nos podra ayudar, y que, teniendolos tan cercanos a nuestros dominios, nos pueden hacer una mala burla tomando el partido de Francia, particularmente en coyuntura que son tan grandes las sumas que les devemos. Con que, si este negocio no sigue a la paz universal, encuentro muchos inconvenientes en entablarle aora; con que devo suplicar a V.S. se sirva de participarme lo que ay entendiere, para que este prevenido quando se llegare a hablar de este particular en el congreso. Todo ha sido boberias y batallar en borracheras quanto hasta aora se ha tratado en el, haviendonos envarazado el tiempo el Conde de Kinsky con sus alemanadas, muy preciado de que venia con maximas y reflexiones italianas, con que la mayor parte del tiempo se ha gastado en conponer sus pendencias. El punto del proyecto de la plenipotencia comun esta resuelto, y en la conferencia que tendremos mañana los aliados creo que vendra aprovado por los enemigos; y no doy parte a V.S. de los reparos que se han ofrecido porque le enviare copia de el quando este acavado de ajustar. Solo dire a V.S. que al paso que por nuestra parte se procura facilitar el acomodamiento de los preliminares, en que no puedo negar enpleo mi mayor solicitud, dan a conocer franceses la poca gana que tienen de paz, cuyo dictamen le tienen ya descuvierto; y aseguro a V.S. que todo ha sido menester para desvanecer las voces que nuestros enemigos habian esparcido, y habian hecho comprehender en todo el mundo, que nosotros no queriamos la paz, dilatando los medios que podian conducir a ella. Veremos lo que resulta de la conferencia de mañana, y de todo dare parte a V.S. ## Notes - The margin decipherment runs beside every cipher line on ff. 1-6 and is written on beyond the last cipher line of each page across the foot of the leaf (so each page's margin ends with the first words of the next page's cipher). Words in ⟨ ⟩ are in clear in the letter. --> # R980, Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen, 27 Jan 1677 ⟨I thank Your Lordship with all the gratitude I owe for the news you are pleased to give me of what is happening there,⟩ and from it I see that the Princes of Brunswick and the Bishop of Münster are already thinking of withdrawing the negotiation from that assembly, judging by the delays their ministers put in the way of meeting. I come to believe that this will not only be on account of the proposal of the Imperialists, whose sting, Your Lordship tells me, they keep very much in mind, but even more particularly because they must have heard something of the Dutch treating to make a separate peace with Sweden, which must touch them to the quick, for they will see how harmful this novelty will be to them. And I hold to this view all the more as I see the openness with which the matter is already spoken of, which I do not doubt will have come to Your Lordship's notice, since even from England they write it to me. This talk has much reduced the rumours that went about of a suspension of arms, and the argument Your Lordship made on this point to Monsieur Amerongen is so prudent that I can say with much pride that I have used the same reasons Your Lordship gives on the occasions that have arisen to speak of the matter. It now carries less weight, as I told Your Lordship; but I would think that, in the state we are in in Flanders, so wretched that I spare myself repeating to you the gloom that the letters from Brussels will cause you (if it is with Your Lordship as with me, we may count their brevity well spent, so long as they do not add to our distress at greater length), it would be of great benefit to us to agree a suspension of arms until the end of June, and on the contrary of the greatest harm if it were to be for four years, as Amerongen argued, for the reasons Your Lordship weighs and I understand. But for the very reason that we shall contradict what our enemies want, they would use it to refuse it; and so it seems to me that this point cannot be settled, and that we shall have to think only of the war. And to return to the separate peace the Dutch wish to make with Sweden: although it has not yet come to be spoken of openly in the congress, it is certain that at The Hague it will be pursued with great insistence. I will tell Your Lordship that this proposal was made by the Swedes themselves, adding that if the King of France would not agree to it they would settle it by themselves and declare against the Most Christian King. It is certain that the Dutch long, as always, for peace with Sweden, saying that there is no other remedy for a general peace than to offset our losses in the Low Countries with Sweden's losses; but while this settlement could be very convenient for us if made within a general peace, we expose ourselves to the precipice if Sweden's is made separately, for it is certain that we shall lose the allies of the North, that the King of Sweden will not be able to help us, and that, having them so close to our dominions, they can play us a nasty trick by taking the side of France, particularly at a juncture when the sums we owe them are so great. So if this business does not go along with the universal peace, I find many drawbacks in opening it now; and so I must beg Your Lordship to be pleased to let me know what you hear there, so that I may be prepared when this matter comes to be discussed in the congress. Everything that has been dealt with in it so far has been foolishness and drunken squabbling, the Count Kinsky having taken up our time with his German ways, very proud of coming with Italian maxims and reflections, so that most of the time has been spent in settling his quarrels. The point of the draft of the common full power is resolved, and in the conference we allies shall hold tomorrow I believe it will come approved by the enemy; and I do not tell Your Lordship of the objections that have been raised because I shall send you a copy of it when it is fully settled. I shall only tell Your Lordship that, while on our side we try to ease the arrangement of the preliminaries (in which I cannot deny I employ my greatest care), the French show how little wish they have for peace, an attitude they have already revealed; and I assure Your Lordship that all of it was needed to dispel the rumours our enemies had spread, and had made the whole world believe, that we did not want peace and were delaying the means that could lead to it. We shall see what comes of tomorrow's conference, and I shall report everything to Your Lordship. Dios nos de buen suceso en la conferencia de [?Wesel], que si en ella el Elector de Brandeburgo puede mas Stetin que las persuasiones de los demas, es menester estar alerta. Y en amistad dire a V.S. que el Elector tiene miedo de que el señor Emperador no le consienta el que se quede con la Pomerania, y es justo, porque mas le importa al señor Emperador que posean aquellas provincias los suecos que no el Elector de Brandeburgo, y con razon es induvitable. Y sobre esto he tenido algunos ratos no tan gustosos como el de una comedia, porque el domingo en la noche estavan resueltos los brandeburgueses a pedirla derechamente en sus proposiciones, y los imperiales precisados a contradecirlo, porque se alvorotara el Imperio si no sucediera esto, y el Emperador no lo podia consentir; porque, sea o por razon de conquista o de feudo caduco, es interesado: si por lo primero, ya se ve que ha asistido con cuerpo de ejercito, y si por lo segundo, que es lo mas regular, sienpre que saliese de la casa de Suecia buelve al cuerpo del Imperio y toca al Emperador dar la investidura a quien quisiere. Con este cuidado vinieron a mi los cesareos; y teniendo yo noticia de que todo nuestro partido estribaba en tener firme al Elector, se lo manifeste, con que tome el temperamento de ir yo a ofrecer montes y valles a los brandeburgueses, y que el Emperador estaba por su amo, ponderandoles al mismo tiempo que ellos mismos se perdian si pedian la Pomerania en sus proposiciones; y se ajusto el expediente de que los imperiales y ellos la hiciesen en general, y los embajadores imperiales pasaron muy buenos oficios a este fin. Y son tantos los enredos que an sido menester desmarañar, que tuviera mucho que decir a V.S., y por esta razon no estoy con sosiego. Es verdad que ha habido cartas del ministro que el Elector tiene en Madrid de buena tinta y de buenos doblones, con que deven de haberle estrenado; mostraronme oy la copia los brandeburgueses, y se me declararon con mas sinceridad en buena forma; pero Dios sobre todo. Ha tres dias que partio de aqui [?Mulle], ministro de Zell que reside en La Haya, y aunque estuvo incognito, a cada uno nos hizo una reverencia con una proposicion en dos partes: la una contiene el pedir sus pasaportes con la calidad de embajadores, y la segunda que se suspendiese la tractacion de la paz hasta que los hubiesen conseguido; que, sobre ser desvergonzada a la varva de tan grandes reyes y tan poderosos principes, es una diligencia que hace heder ya la neutralidad. Yo le respondi que hablase con los demas, que nuestro amo no seria el dificil; y ademas de esto no hablo de subsidios, que para mi es mas fatal señal. Pero si Brandeburgo tiene firme, puede ser que los Brunswick y Munster se pongan de mejor ayre, y en ese caso estare yo sosegado de que no se trata de paz separada con Suecia. Aunque tengo hechas las extradiciones de la nueva plenipotencia con Francia, todavia con los godos nos estamos asi, porque pretende Suecia que, como es en español la nuestra, ha de ser la suya en sueco; pero creo que aora caeran de su burro, viendo que ya hemos entregado los aliados nuestras proposiciones, que al fin oy a mediodia quedaron en manos de los mediadores, y presto tendremos la extradicion de las de nuestros enemigos, con que ya esta en la plaza el primer tomo de esta negociacion. Las nuestras son las incluidas, a que las acompaña la carta que va con ellas; y despues del incienso que era menester umar en el parlamento, se apunta la razon de pedir que seamos restituidos al estado del año de 65. En justicia no pueden ser mas rectas, pero en la ley de las armas y en nuestra debilidad las derivara un papirote. No he juzgado hacerlas pidiendo distintamente cada cosa de las que se encierran desde el año de 65 aca, por no hacer mayor horror pidiendo la paz de los Pirineos, que tambien contradijera al deseo de mejorar, si se puede, el tratado de Westfalia en favor del circulo de Borgoña, y que no se le dificulte al señor Emperador el asistirnos; y por no tocar esta tecla, y por dejar abierta la puerta por si Dios quisiere que entre algun buen suceso por ella, se puso el articulo sexto con aquel exordio de los daños que habia mostrado la experiencia. El segundo es tan de tabla el ponerse en las proposiciones como el no concederse en los tratados; lo mismo digo del cuarto y del quinto, pero servira esta espanpanata para nuestros flamencos. Como el caso de Mesina es de diversa naturaleza, se pone en articulo separado. Words in ⟨ ⟩ are in clear in the letter. --> # R981, Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen, 4 March 1677 ⟨... and I only miss being employed in Your Lordship's service, to exercise my obedience.⟩ In both letters Your Lordship writes at great length on the separate peace with Sweden that is being negotiated; and that it was promoted by the Dutch is certain, and God knows what will come of it. Freedom of trade is so much so that it will be a relief to the three provinces that the Swedes should have no exemption in the North; it is that too, but I do not know whether it will be worse for Denmark to have it, as will happen if she wins Scania, for she is a good [?manager], and much more so being master of both shores of the Sound; and I do not know whether the provinces would put up better with the Swedes' exemption than with the absolute dominion of the Dane. God grant us good success in the conference of [?Wesel], for if in it Stettin weighs more with the Elector of Brandenburg than the persuasions of the others, we must be on the alert. And in friendship I will tell Your Lordship that the Elector fears that the Lord Emperor will not allow him to keep Pomerania, and rightly, because it matters more to the Lord Emperor that the Swedes should hold those provinces than the Elector of Brandenburg, and with reason it is beyond doubt. And over this I have had some hours not as pleasant as a comedy's, because on Sunday night the Brandenburgers were resolved to ask for it outright in their proposals, and the Imperialists obliged to oppose it, because the Empire would be in uproar if this did not happen, and the Emperor could not allow it; for, whether by right of conquest or of lapsed fief, he has an interest: if the first, it is plain that he has helped with an army corps, and if the second, which is the more regular, whenever it leaves the house of Sweden it returns to the body of the Empire and it falls to the Emperor to give the investiture to whom he pleases. With this worry the Imperial ministers came to me; and having learned that our whole party rested on keeping the Elector firm, I told them so, and so I took the course of going myself to offer mountains and valleys to the Brandenburgers, and that the Emperor was on their master's side, pointing out to them at the same time that they would ruin themselves if they asked for Pomerania in their proposals; and the expedient was agreed that the Imperialists and they should make them in general terms, and the Imperial ambassadors did very good offices to this end. And so many are the tangles that have had to be unravelled that I would have much to tell Your Lordship, and for this reason I am not at ease. It is true that there have been letters, in good ink and with good doubloons, from the minister the Elector keeps in Madrid, with which they must have made a start with him; the Brandenburgers showed me the copy today, and they declared themselves to me with more sincerity in good form; but God above all. Three days ago [?Mulle], minister of Celle who resides at The Hague, left here, and although he was incognito he made each of us a bow with a proposal in two parts: the one contains the request for their passports with the rank of ambassadors, and the second that the treating of the peace be suspended until they had obtained them; which, besides being shameless under the beard of such great kings and such powerful princes, is a step that already makes the neutrality stink. I answered him that he should speak to the others, that our master would not be the difficult one; and besides this he did not speak of subsidies, which to me is a more fatal sign. But if Brandenburg holds firm, it may be that Brunswick and Münster will put on a better air, and in that case I shall be at ease that there is no question of a separate peace with Sweden. Although I have made the exchanges of the new full power with France, with the Goths we are still where we were, because Sweden claims that, as ours is in Spanish, hers must be in Swedish; but I believe they will now get off their donkey, seeing that we allies have already handed in our proposals, which at last today at noon were left in the hands of the mediators, and soon we shall have the handing over of those of our enemies, so that the first volume of this negotiation is now on the market square. Ours are the enclosed, accompanied by the letter that goes with them; and after the incense that had to be burned in the preamble, the case is made for asking that we be restored to the state of the year '65. In justice they could not be more right, but by the law of arms and in our weakness a flick of the finger will knock them down. I did not think fit to frame them by asking separately for each of the things included from the year '65 until now, so as not to cause greater horror by asking for the Peace of the Pyrenees, which would also run against the wish to improve, if possible, the Treaty of Westphalia in favour of the Burgundian Circle, and so that the Lord Emperor should find no difficulty in assisting us; and so as not to touch that key, and to leave the door open in case God wills some good success to enter by it, the sixth article was put in with that preamble on the damage that experience had shown. The second is as much a matter of course to put in the proposals as not to be granted in the treaties; I say the same of the fourth and fifth, but this bluster will serve for our Flemings. As the case of Messina is of a different nature, it is put in a separate article. The last is the allies', which is "here peace and afterwards glory": God give us the first as soon as possible and the second afterwards. I go on to beg you not to put down to neglect or want of friendship my not having answered with the punctuality that Your Lordship's continued favours deserve,⟩ for here we are so hampered [...] in doing nothing, as Your Lordship can [...] temporise with the [...], for here they follow the same maxims as in Bremen [...] of Pomerania, to the jealousy [...] power of Brandenburg and princes of the [...] Swedes and [...]; and the worst is that in the end the treaties make no progress, and that premature declarations [...] which are the cause of the [?losses] [...] take upon their [...]. [...] I value, as I ought, the papers Your Lordship is pleased to send me, and I shall always be glad that the plan that has been formed on the separation of that conference should go ahead. And to tell Your Lordship the truth, it [?grieves] us little that Bremen and Verden should remain Swedish [...], so long as the present [...] is pursued with warmth; which depends solely on our [...] with diligence the Baltic squadron, whose importance [...] Don Manuel de Lira and I do not cease to represent to Spain every day with the most urgent pleas. As far as I see, the Swedes stand firm in refusing to give up any of the conquests, and say that if they make any reparation it will be to Brandenburg, but that it is not to be in lands or fortresses. I believe Your Lordship knows the view I have always held on the northern alliances since the time the treaties were being [?negotiated], and I would wish us to have an army of our own in Flanders, which without doubt would set in motion the troops of [...] and of the Prince of Orange; for although we have nothing particular to [?expect] from either, after the battle of Saint-Omer, it is my opinion that things would be done differently if the Lord Duke of Villahermosa could take the field with mules that were not hired; but in the present state of things God grant we have even these, and above all the means to feed them. And since God willed that we should find ourselves embarked in the war with Sweden, we must make the last effort to carry it forward under full sail and keep those allies, not so much for the profit we should expect from them as for the harm that would come to us if France won them over, especially now that they find themselves with forces and men, and need money to keep them up or to get rid of them on good terms. ⟨At last, notwithstanding the reluctance of the adversaries, we presented on the 18th of this month our answers to the first proposals ... publishing us as infringers of the Peace of Aachen,⟩ using, to bring the English round to their view, the [?pretext] that, if they had to answer in writing, their justification on the point of the infringement [would rest] on the declaration that [?the ambassador of Great Britain] made against us after the siege the Prince of Orange laid to Charleroi; a commitment which they well knew the English would try to avoid, since this recourse would not serve the King of England well with his Parliament, which is full of the misgivings that the monstrous progress of the Most Christian King and our weakness must give it. And even after our proposals had been handed in, the English suggested that the treating should begin in the form that I myself had proposed to them, namely that, to avoid the harshness the parties' proposals may carry when handed over sealed, which would serve rather to embitter minds than to soften them, the mediators should take the verbal answers of both sides and put them in writing themselves; and for this they sent me Monsieur Jenkins, third plenipotentiary of England, who, being a devout heretic, came to preach to me what I would not receive as gospel, telling me that they still held our answers sealed and that handing them over could be dispensed with. But seeing that I held to it [...], and finding that he was making our allies and even the Imperialists waver, he asked me, convinced, with very weighty words, whether I thought peace would be made by handing over these answers; to which I replied again that [...] the King of France [...] so that he should withdraw them. In the end Ratman and I, who alone supported me, carried the point, so that they are now obliged to put our answers into the hands of the French; and it matters little to me whether they speak in writing or not, nor the cleverness of trying to involve the King of England in the blame they lay on us for having broken the peace treaties, for I trust that God will not fail us in answering them decently without offending the mediator. Now we are discussing the form in which we are to proceed from here on, so that we remain covered with our masters. "la ida del humo" = it will come to nothing (go up in smoke). - Don Manuel de Lira was the Spanish envoy at The Hague; "los Estados" = the States General. Words in ⟨ ⟩ are in clear in the letter. --> # R1001, Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen, 6 Feb 1677 ⟨... and believing that no other objections will be raised, we shall very soon be done with this preliminary,⟩ to the settlement of which it has been necessary to contribute on our side because of the haste of the Dutch and the clamour they have raised to this end, going so far as to reveal their mind publicly, and Beverningk in particular. But it is also true that when I speak to him alone I find him calmer; and all of them give me great assurances and promises that they will not abandon us, drawing as proof of this the gallantry with which the Prince of Orange has sent to Flanders the troops that were asked of him. But this does not quiet my concern that in one way or another they may play some trick on us, and so I do not let go of them, notwithstanding some news I have had (of the kind I can obtain in the absence of Don Manuel de Lira, whose absence from The Hague I cannot sufficiently convey to Your Lordship, how much harm and inconvenience it does us) that the States are attending to our interests and know that it matters to themselves. But as Don Manuel de Lira is staying in Brussels, and he is the one who could find out and discern more openly the mind of the Dutch, nothing can be believed; and so I say again to Your Lordship that my greatest concern is to watch the actions of these Dutch ambassadors and to walk together with them. So far there is strong talk of the separate peace with Sweden, as I related distinctly to Your Lordship in my last, and I told you the reasons the Dutch have for getting out of the war, directing their policy in this to our benefit. But I try to make Beverningk, who is the one who talks most about it, understand that it can by no means be so unless this settlement comes within a general peace; and Your Lordship will have seen the reasons I put forward. How it will end [is not known], nor has it so far been spoken of formally in the congress. I repeat my thanks to Your Lordship for the news you give me of the steps being taken in that assembly and of the difficulties Your Lordship sees in settling those matters. And as to what Your Lordship tells me, that an opening has been made for getting out of the difficulties by way of an interim, to which the Danes seem inclined, I must tell Your Lordship that, according to my information, it seems to me that the Dutch will agree to nothing that is a settlement; and that the minister of Holland has come to The Hague for this purpose, and I believe it will go up in smoke, because the States want to keep up the difficulties that arise so that the conclusion is afterwards left to their discretion. Your Lordship, who is on the spot, will know better than anyone what there is in this, and it falls to me only to praise the judgement and prudence with which Your Lordship reasons, and to beg you to be pleased to continue sending me your news. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete Contributed by George Lasry (solution) · Also credited · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter Unsigned and unaddressed, dated in clear 30 January 1586. Tomokiyo attributes the hand to François d’Espinay de Saint-Luc, governor of Brouage. The volume holds despatches to Henri III and to his secretary of state Villeroy. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 15572, f. 43 (Gallica). Not on DECODE. The cipher Invented symbols: two to five for each letter, 20 signs for common words and syllables ( que, est, tout, faire, vous, peut …), a sign that doubles the letter before it, and 10 nulls. How it was solved George Lasry transcribed the leaf in CTTS and recovered the letter table with its built-in cryptanalysis in 2022; in 2026 he resolved the last signs from context with Claude Opus 5.5 and edited the French. Re-checked here mechanically and statistically. What it says “Monsieur” has sent an agent to work on the concierge’s household. The writer proposes to win over the gardener, spoil a marriage the concierge wants, and spread a rumour to frighten her: “fear holds the old as often as reason does”. Credit Key, transcription, edition and translation by George Lasry (pull request 76). Description and attribution of the leaf by S. Tomokiyo. Still open Who the cover names stand for, and the recipient. Four doubtful words and two tentative symbol values.

The opening lines of f. 43 with George Lasry’s values in red: Si m[ons]ieur m’escrivit il y a environ deux mois ung des siens… Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 15572 f. 43 (Gallica); decipherment overlay by George Lasry. Folio 43 of Français 15572 is two pages entirely in cipher except the date line, Du xxx e Janvier 1586 . It names neither its writer nor its recipient. Tomokiyo recognised the hand of Saint-Luc’s clear letter at f. 35, and Saint-Luc wrote another letter, f. 42, on the same day. Saint-Luc’s other ciphered letters in the volume (ff. 245 and 260) use a different table (a different cipher, with its own page ), and so do the Mayenne and Matignon despatches around it: Cipher-1 , Cipher-2 and Cipher-3 . The key is a homophonic substitution. Twenty letters plus x have 51 symbols between them, two or three for most letters, five for i and four for s . Twenty more signs stand for 17 words and syllables: que, qui, est, de, et, dict, tout, faire, je, vous, lui, bien, plus, peut, pas, mal and ons (as in m- ons -ieur). One sign doubles the letter before it, one marks an abbreviation, and ten are nulls. George Lasry’s key, as reconstructed in CTTS. Image: George Lasry, CTTS key for BnF fr. 15572 f. 43.

Du xxx e Janvier 1586 [date line in clear, after Tomokiyo] English translation (George Lasry) Monsieur wrote to me about two months ago that one of his men, whom he sent here on purpose, was to be addressed to the sister of the concierge's procurator. She was loved and, being on this side, very close to her mistress, and yet always held very suspect since the summer of the said Nimier, and for that [?] fallen somewhat back in her favour. The said lady herself put the letters into my hands: they were only of general recommendation. And from then on I judged that he was intriguing at something here, by means of his old contacts, and I believed that it was either for love or for money. He , having come over, has worked hard on both the one and the other, so that on this occasion he has made [?] many friends and enemies. Perhaps with that he can make himself welcome with the gardener, whom one can win over and draw away from the attachment that he is thought to bear the stonecutters. Above all , the concierge has much at heart the marriage between the little one and the half-brother of Saint-Sulpice, who brought [him?] there again on Sunday. And if these overtures remain on the table [?], it is only to break the blow to the other [?], having added that of the courier's sister with the son of the chief of arms of Saint-Sulpice, just to give a taste of it and make them want it. I assure you that Sermelles is much feared here, and Monsieur Lue would fear much more if it were thought that Jugan was joining him. So I will tell you that perhaps it would not be amiss to have the rumour spread on purpose, to hold the concierge, since fear holds the old as often as reason does. However , the governor will judge this better than the planter. [He] begins to be on quite good terms with the concierge, who is little by little losing that first opinion she had formed: if not to think him too Catholic, at least not to think him a deceiver or one who loves bad things. The 30th of January 1586 [date line in clear]

François d’Espinay de Saint-Luc (1554–1597) was one of Henri III’s favourites. He fell from favour in 1580 and withdrew to Brouage, the salt port of Saintonge facing Huguenot La Rochelle, which he governed and fortified. By 1586 he was again serving the King in the war against Henri of Navarre that followed the Treaty of Nemours, and that year he took the island of Oléron from Agrippa d’Aubigné. Français 15572 gathers the despatches of January to July 1586 from the King’s commanders in the west. The letter is written in cover names: the concierge and her mistress, the gardener, the stonecutters, the governor, the planter, the little one. Who they stand for is not known. A few real names come through in the cipher: Nimier, Saint-Sulpice, Sermelles, Jugan, and a “Monsieur Lue” who may be one of the Daillon, comtes du Lude, governors of Poitou.

All three images are read here: 1,315 cipher signs (1,168 letter homophones, 77 code signs, 44 doubling and abbreviation signs, 26 nulls), with every sign assigned. | | | |---|---| | **From** | François d'Espinay, seigneur de Saint-Luc, governor of Brouage (attributed from the hand by Tomokiyo; the letter is unsigned) | | **To** | Not named in the letter; the volume holds letters to Henri III and to his secretary of state Villeroy | | **Date** | 30 January 1586 (date line in clear) | | **Content** | An intelligence report on an agent of "Monsieur", sent to work on the household of "the concierge", in which the people are given cover names (the concierge, the gardener, the stonecutters, the governor, the planter). | ## Summary of contents About two months earlier, "Monsieur" sent one of his men to the writer's area with letters of recommendation, addressed to the sister of the concierge's procurator. That woman had been close to her mistress but has been under suspicion since the summer of "the said Nimier". The lady herself handed the letters to the writer. He concluded that the man was intriguing to revive old contacts, either for love or for money, and had made friends and enemies doing so. The writer suggests ways to use the household. The gardener could be won over and turned from his attachment to "the stonecutters". The concierge is set on a marriage between "the little one" and the half-brother of Saint-Sulpice, and the writer wants to spoil it by putting forward a second match: the courier's sister with the son of the chief of arms of Saint-Sulpice. Sermelles is much feared, and Monsieur Lue [du Lude?] would be feared more if Jugan were thought to have joined him. The writer proposes to spread that rumour on purpose to hold the concierge, since fear holds the old as often as reason does. He leaves the decision to "the governor". He says "the planter" is now on good terms with the concierge, who no longer thinks him a deceiver. ## The key A homophonic substitution of 20 letters plus *x*, with 51 symbols. Most letters have two or three homophones; *i* has five and *s* four. A small nomenclator of 20 signs stands for 17 words and syllables (*que, qui, est, de, et, dict, tout, faire, je, vous, lui, bien, plus, peut, pas, mal, ons*). There is one sign for a doubled letter, one abbreviation sign, and 10 nulls. ![Key reconstructed with CTTS](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GeorgeLasry/cyphersolver/writeup-saintluc1586-lasry/targets/saintluc1586/lasry2022/cryptiana/images/saintluc1586_key.png) ## Reading conventions The whole letter is enciphered except the date line. **Bold** marks words and syllables written with a single nomenclator sign. Spelling is kept as deciphered. [x?] marks an uncertain reading and [ ] an editorial addition. ## The letter: BnF fr. 15572 f. 43 (images f43a, f43b, f43c; 30 January 1586) ![f43a with decryption in red](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GeorgeLasry/cyphersolver/writeup-saintluc1586-lasry/targets/saintluc1586/lasry2022/cryptiana/images/saintluc1586_f43a_decryption.jpg) ### French Si m**ons**ieur m'escrivit il y a environ deux mois ung des siens, **qui** envoya ici exprès, **qui** l'adressa à la seur du procureur de la concierge, **qui** a aimée, **est**ant deça, fort privée de sa maistresse **et** **tout**efois **tout**jours tenue fort suspecte depuis l'esté du **dict** Nimier, **qui** **de** cela [?] ung peu reculée de son credict. La **dict**e dame m'a elle mesme baillé les lettres en mes mains : n'**est**oient **que** de generale recommendation ; **et** ces lors **je** jugeai **qui** [qu'il] pratiquoit ici **que**l**que** chose, le moyen de ses antiennes intelligences, **qui** [que j'] eus opinion **que** c'estoit ou **de** l'amour ou **de** l'argent. **Lui** **est**ant venu deça, il a fort travaillé et à l'ung **et** à l'aultre, **qui** à c**est**e occasion il y a luise [?] beaucoup d'amis **et** d'ennemis. Peult **est**re **que** avec cela il se **peut** **faire** **de** f**est**e près du jardinier, le**que**l on **peut** gaigner **et** retirer de l'affection **que** l'on croit il porte aux tailleurs de pierre. Sur **tout** le concierge a fort à coeur le mariage d'entre la petite **et** le demi frère de St Suplice, **qui** mena là encores dimanche ; **et** si ces ouvertures r**est**ent proposées desast [?], c'en **est** **que** **de** rompre le coup à l'aure [?], ayant adjousté cellui de la soeur du courrier avec le fils du chef des armes de St Suplice, **de** seullement bailler le goust **et** en **faire** venir l'envie. **Je** **vous** asseure **que** l'on craint ici fort Sermelles, **et** M[onsieu]r Lue craindroit **bien** **plus** si l'on pensoit **que** Jugan se joignist avec lui, **qui** **vous** dirai **que** **peut** **est**re ne seroit il **pas** **mal** à propos d'en **faire** courir le bruit à bon esciant, **de** retenir la concierge, estant ainsi **que** la crainte retient aussi souvent les vieux comme la raison. **Tout**efois le gouverneur jugera mieulx cela **que** le planteur. Commence à **est**re assés **bien** avec la concierge, **qui** se perd petit à petit c**est**e première opinion conceue, sinon de le **est**imer trop catholi**que**, à **tout** le moins **de** ne le penser pas trompeur ni aimant les choses mauvaises. Du xxx<sup>e</sup> Janvier 1586 [date line in clear, after Tomokiyo] ### English translation Monsieur wrote to me about two months ago that one of his men, whom he sent here on purpose, **was** to be addressed to the sister of the concierge's procurator. She **was** loved and, being on this side, very close to her mistress, **and** **yet** **always** held very suspect since the summer of the **said** Nimier, and **for** that [?] fallen somewhat back in her favour. The **said** lady herself put the letters into my hands: they **were** **only** of general recommendation. **And** from then on **I** judged that he was intriguing at something here, by means of his old contacts, and I believed **that** it was either **for** love or **for** money. **He**, **having** come over, has worked hard on both the one **and** the other, so that on this occasion he has made [?] many friends **and** enemies. Perhaps with that he **can** **make** himself welcome with the gardener, whom one **can** win over **and** draw away from the attachment **that** he is thought to bear the stonecutters. Above **all**, the concierge has much at heart the marriage between the little one **and** the half-brother of Saint-Sulpice, **who** brought [him?] there again on Sunday. **And** if these overtures **remain** on the table [?], it **is** **only** **to** break the blow to the other [?], having added that of the courier's sister with the son of the chief of arms of Saint-Sulpice, **just** to give a taste of it **and** **make** them want it. **I** assure **you** **that** Sermelles is much feared here, **and** Monsieur Lue would fear **much** **more** if it were thought **that** Jugan was joining him. **So** **I** will tell **you** **that** **perhaps** it would **not** be **amiss** to **have** the rumour spread on purpose, **to** hold the concierge, since fear holds the old as often as reason does. **However**, the governor will judge this better **than** the planter. [He] begins to **be** on quite **good** terms with the concierge, **who** is little by little losing **that** first opinion she had formed: if not to **think** him too Catholic, at **least** **not** to think him a deceiver or one who loves bad things. The 30th of January 1586 [date line in clear] ## Historical context François d'Espinay de Saint-Luc (1554–1597) was one of Henri III's favourites (*mignons*). He fell from favour in 1580 and withdrew to Brouage, the salt port of Saintonge across from Huguenot La Rochelle, which he governed and fortified. By 1586 he was again serving the King in the war against Henri of Navarre that followed the Treaty of Nemours (July 1585). That year he took the island of Oléron from Agrippa d'Aubigné, whom he captured (Tomokiyo). BnF fr. 15572 gathers the ciphered and clear despatches of January–July 1586 from the King's commanders and agents in the west: Mayenne, Matignon, Biron, Malicorne and Saint-Luc. Most are addressed to Henri III or to Villeroy. Saint-Luc's other ciphered letters in the volume (f. 245, deciphered in the margin; f. 260) use a different table (Tomokiyo, "StLuc's Cipher"). The letter is written in cover names: the concierge, her mistress, the gardener, the stonecutters, the governor, the planter, the little one. The real people behind them are not identified here. Its subject is a familiar one for a governor facing La Rochelle: a party's agent working on a household through its servants, its marriages and its fears, and how to counter him. "Monsieur Lue" may stand for a member of the Daillon family, comtes du Lude and governors of Poitou (see Open points). ## How the key was obtained The three images were transcribed in CTTS (CrypTool Transcriber and Solver), and the homophones were recovered with CTTS's built-in cryptanalysis (George Lasry, 2022). In 2026 the thirteen signs still unassigned were resolved from context with Claude Opus 5.5: - 71 = *ons*, as in m-ons-ieur. - 23 = *q*, as in prati-q-uoit. - 68 = *je*. - 101 = *vous*, in "je vous asseure" and "vous dirai". - 89 and 70 = *peut*, in "il se peut faire", "on peut gaigner" and "peut estre". - 91 = *bien* and 100 = *plus*, in "asses bien" and "craindroit bien plus". - 102 = *pas* and 103 = *mal*, in "ne seroit il pas mal à propos". - 36 = *et* and 84 = *lui*, both tentative. - 97 = a raised abbreviation *r* on M, for M[onsieu]r, checked on the image. The full reading was checked against the CTTS overlays of all three images. ## Open points - 36 = *et* and 84 = *lui* fit their contexts but are tentative. - "Lue" (f43b line 11) follows a sign listed as a null; "du Lude" is possible but not established. - Unclear passages: "de cela [?]" (f43a line 7), "il y a luise [?]" (f43a line 15), "desast [?]" and "à l'aure [?]" (f43b lines 5–6). - The writer, the recipient and the people behind the cover names are not identified from the text alone; the attribution to Saint-Luc rests on Tomokiyo's comparison of hands. - The date line in clear is quoted from Tomokiyo; it is not in the transcribed images. ## Sources - BnF, Français 15572 (letters to Henri III and Villeroy, January–July 1586), f. 43: [Gallica](https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b9061879d/f1.image). - S. Tomokiyo, *Cryptiana*, ["Ciphers Solved by George Lasry"](http://cryptiana.web.fc2.com/code/GL.htm), "An Unsigned Letter in BnF fr.15572 (1586)": Lasry's 2022 solution images. - D. Siena, Concistoro 2308: the cipher letters by key Cyphersolver › Write-ups Siena, Concistoro 2308: the cipher letters by key The Archivio di Stato di Siena keeps the Sienese government’s cipher file as Concistoro 2308: fascicle 1, “Cifrari”, the filed keys (DECODE R4746–R4789), and fascicle 2, “Lettere in cifra”, the letters (DECODE R4790–R4814 and R1858), all photographed in the reading room and catalogued on DECODE as “1500–1599”. Aloys Meister counted 29 letters in 1902 and dated the first to 1421; 25 are photographed. This page used to be one entry for the whole bundle, with a table of the pieces. Following George Lasry’s consolidated report, “The cipher documents of Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2” (17 October 2026), which deciphers most of the letters and groups them by key, each key now has its own entry. The headings below are his; piece numbers are the pencil numbers on the sheets. Under headings D, G and H each piece has its own key.

Nos. 20 and 23 (R4808, R4811): a royal captain at Perugia to King Ladislaus, 30 March 1413, and two royal memoranda on the Marche campaign, about April 1413 (the years inferred from the context, not written). Read in full; key recovered from the ciphertext by George Lasry with CTTS and Claude. Seven name signs are open.

No. 12 (R4790): Naples, 10 March 1413, to Sforza: the King offers him a bride. The letter gives the day and the sixth indiction; the year 1413 is reconstructed from the indiction and the historical context. It is the earliest date in the file. Key recovered from the ciphertext by George Lasry with CTTS and Claude.
Nos. 6 and 24 (R4795, R4812): Cristofano to the Signori, on the war over Lucca. Deciphered by George Lasry from the ciphertext alone; the filed key R4755 (fascicle 1) was found to match afterwards.

No. 4 (R4793): Galgano Borghesi to Leonardo Benvoglienti, Naples, 12 May 1456. Key rebuilt here from a fragment on the letter. No. 14 (R4802): Sienese envoys to the Priori, before 1429. Key recovered here from the ciphertext, in part. No. 19 (R4807): Sienese envoys kept waiting by the S. Capitano, 9 March, 1440s. Not solved. No. 21 (R4809): “Karissimo come padre”. Not solved. No. 25 (R4813): a lord on the road to Casole. Key recovered here from the ciphertext.
No. 11 (R4800): Donato Acciaiuoli to Lorenzo de’ Medici, Rome, 13 June 1478. Key recovered from the ciphertext by George Lasry with CTTS and Claude.
No. 18 (R4806): Maximilian I and the Sienese orators, Pisa, November 1496. Key recovered from the ciphertext here and, independently, by George Lasry.

No. 17 (R4805): Bartolomeo Tantucci, 25 August 1528, the “cifra di Balìa”. Key recovered from the ciphertext by George Lasry, about 85%. No. 15 (R4803): Mario Bandini, Innsbruck, 4 January 1547. Key partly recovered by George Lasry, 75 of 240 signs; none of the filed keys fits, R4764 included. R4794 (unnumbered; earlier given as “no. 5?”): the artillery slip, sixteenth century. Key recovered from the ciphertext by George Lasry; the four number codes 44, 26, 67 and 74 are open.

No. 9 (R4798): Castiglione and the King of Aragon, 1440s–50s. Key recovered by George Lasry from the decipherment below the lines. Nos. 13 and 16 (R4801, R4804): the Pope and Bologna, c. 1527–29. Deciphered at the time (no. 16 is the clear copy); the key was recovered by George Lasry from the plaintext of no. 16. No. 10 (R4799): “presura di Montepulciano”, deciphered at the time between the lines. No. 7 (R4796): an orator at Milan to the Officials of the Balìa, 1450s. Not solved; the interlinear gloss gives nine values. No. 8 (R4797): the Milan–Ferrara league slip, c. 1440–41. The report lists it as not yet deciphered; aligned here sign by sign, the memorandum on the same sheet is its decipherment.

R4791, R4792, R4810: clear letters (R4810, no. 22, is a set of drafts in which numbers stand for key words). R4814: fragment of a key. Nos. 1 (1421), 2 and 26–28: in Meister’s count of 1902, not photographed. Only the Archivio di Stato di Siena can supply them.

The grouping by key, the readings of nos. 20, 23, 6, 24, 12, 11, 18, 17, 9, 13 and R4794, and of no. 15 in part, and their datings are George Lasry’s (report of 17 October 2026 and corrections of 18 October, sent to Daniel Bourdeau). His method: CTTS for the transcription (in full, or correcting a transcription made by an LLM) and sometimes its built-in cryptanalysis, with Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude, and with GPT-6 Astra as well for nos. 6 and 24. He solved no. 18 independently and in full. Nos. 4, 14, 18 and 25 were broken here on 24 September 2026, no. 8 aligned with its decipherment here on 18 October 2026 (and again, independently, on 20 October). On 20 October his keys of nos. 17, 11 and 5? were run on this project’s own transcriptions of 24 September, made before his work: 92.9%, 94.4% and 93.1% of our signs give his reading; our transcription of no. 20 carries his reading at 71% against 15% for a wrong-plaintext control. Nos. 7, 19 and 21 are open. Sources: DECODE records R4746–R4814 and R1858; A. Meister, Die Anfänge der modernen diplomatischen Geheimschrift (Paderborn 1902), pp. 50–51; Archivio del Concistoro del Comune di Siena. Inventario (Rome 1952), p. 366. Manuscript rights: Archivio di Stato di Siena. The collection’s key index, access notes and shared solvers: research/siena2308/ .

An intercepted Italian letter of the first half of 1625 (TNA SP 106/10, DECODE R722), half in clear and half in a three-figure syllabic code, with ten worksheets of the English codebreaker who tried to break it, all catalogued as anonymous ciphertexts. The endorsement and the clear text (Spinola before Breda, the Pope and Béthune) are read and the 420 groups transcribed; the codebreaker’s partial key and annealing do not break the code. Split on 14 Oct 2026 from sp106box10. 525 393 283 313 540 212 una di questi matine ? · ? · ? · ? · ? · vo · (clear) a Venetian secretary → the Venetian ambassador in England · three-figure syllabic code · first half of 1625 · attempted, not solved A Venetian secretary to the ambassador in England, 1625 An intercepted Italian letter, half clear and half in a syllabic code, with the worksheets of the English codebreaker who failed to break it; its clear text is transcribed, the code is not broken. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter A Venetian secretary, perhaps in the Low Countries or at Rome, to the Venetian ambassador in England, first half of 1625. The endorsement reads “Cypher of a Venetian Secretary to the Embassador of that nation”. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 193–195 (DECODE R722), with ten worksheets in the same box (R656, R661, R662, R663, R667, R684, R701, R702, R703, R720), all catalogued as anonymous ciphertexts. The cipher Three-figure groups 200–599, one per syllable, in runs of five with the vowel in the last digit (366–370 la le li lo lu ). The same syllable can have two groups. How it was tried The codebreaker’s partial key and a few cribs at the edges of the clear passages, then simulated annealing of the rest against an Italian model, in four set-ups. Why it resists About 70 groups stay free in one letter of 420 groups; every run gives different Italian-sounding nonsense. The codebreaker did not break it either. Still open The whole code text. Another letter in the same code would be needed. The letter is part of one English codebreaker’s file of Italian intercepts, which holds several ciphers; each has its own page (a different cipher in each): the “Venetian Cifer” of two earlier letters, built the same way with another table ( sp106box10 ), the two-figure nomenclator of his key sheet R725 ( sp106r725 ), and a letter-and-figure syllabary ( sp106r704 ).

R722, lines 1–3: 525 393 283 313 540 212 una di questi matine ; 283 495 541 … ; 369 280 367 464 432 … , with the codebreaker’s trial syllables above the groups, many struck out. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 193–195, image p. 2, via DECODE R722. R722 has 48 numbered lines, written half in clear Italian, half in three-figure groups, with the codebreaker’s trial syllables between the lines. The endorsement reads “Cypher of a Venetian Secretary to the Embassador of that nation in …” , with “1625” on the fold. The clear passages give its matter: Parmi che … , Io mi credo che questi siano … , Ho visto chiaramente che V. E. … , proposito che ella procurasse , di satisfattione con honor di … , il Spinola sotto Breda , di Bruselles si è inteso … , di Roma , and near the end “… soliti concetti del Pontifice il quale disse a Bethune di voler esser risarcito di 150 m[ila] …” : Philippe de Béthune, the French ambassador in Rome, and the Pope’s demand for compensation over the Valtelline forts. Spinola besieged Breda from August 1624 until 5 June 1625, so the letter is of the first half of 1625. The whole letter is transcribed: 420 code groups of 117 different values, and the clear Italian between them. DECODE and the earlier notes here had filed R722 with the letter-and-figure intercepts, following DECODE’s pointers; it was first looked at on 21 September 2026.

Ten more records of the box are the codebreaker’s sheets on this one letter, listed by DECODE as separate anonymous ciphertexts (catalogue items 58, 62 and 66). Their line-numbered fragments stand in R722 verbatim: R703’s l.1 540 212 una che is the end of line 1, R720’s l.2 280 367 464 432 is in line 3, R703’s l.6 340 367 misciendosi and R684’s l.7 … 510 al meno are lines 6 and 8, and R656’s l.12 313 541 377 238 254 is line 12. His line count runs one behind the page’s numbers in places. R703 (ff. 184–185): an index headed linea of every group 200–399 with the lines where it stands, notes such as “201 is a finall sillable after an entire word”, and glossed fragments under “Entire wordes assured by reiteration”. R667 , R684 : count grids of every group 200–577 and frequency lists (244 fifteen times). R702 p. 1, R663 : Italian–English dictionary trawls and syllable drills against numbered lines ( li.25 495 391 540 395 207 “a ta n do”). R661 , R656 : English drafts in clear (one on Spain’s treasure from the Indies, one a sheriff’s answer to the Exchequer) reused as scrap for fragments by line. R662 : a torn strip of his English memorandum on how the code is built: “series of sillables beginning …”, “the vowels a.e.i. for every consonant”, “the most frequent … di”. R701 p. 3: his partial key, below.

On R701 p. 3 the codebreaker wrote values in runs, the vowel stepping in the last digit: 209 va · 210 ve · 211 vi · 212 vo · 213 vu · 231–235 sa se si so su · 244 ra · 245 re 322–326 pra…pru · 333–336 cha che chi cho · 366–370 la le li lo lu · 375–378 da de di do · 510–514 sta…stu It is not the table of the “Venetian Cifer” (there 244 is pi , 245 po , 433–437 la…lu ), though it is built the same way. His own trial glosses conflict with it in places (244 is glossed ta on R702; 540 both una and n ). The clear text fixes a few values where a code run meets a clear word: line 24 che 525 245 541 449 lo haveva assecurato gives che il Re glie-lo haveva (525 il , 245 re , 541 gli , 449 e ); line 8 245 510 Almeno gives resta. Almeno (510 sta ); and 334 is che throughout. Where R701 p. 3 can be checked this way it is right.

The remaining groups were annealed against an Italian sixteenth-century five-letter model, allowing at most two groups per syllable and rewarding runs of five like the codebreaker’s. Four set-ups were run (free; normalised for length; R701 values fixed; R701 values fixed with a strong run bonus and no word groups), with 12 to 20 restarts of 400,000 steps each. Every restart ended in different Italian-sounding word salad, and no two agreed beyond the fixed values. With about 70 free groups over 420 tokens, one letter does not determine the code.

The code text of R722: 420 groups, 117 values, deciphered only where a clear word forces a value. What would move it: another letter in the same code (the Venetian correspondence of 1625, in Venice or among the Venetian papers at Kew, SP 99), more of the codebreaker’s run sheets among the unimaged SP 106/10 leaves, or a careful pass fixing only values forced at clear-text junctions before annealing again. The Venetian calendar (CSP Venice vol. 19, 1625–26) has not been searched for a despatch quoting Béthune’s 150,000 and Spinola before Breda.

This is a letter-for-letter substitution that uses Latin-looking letters as cipher signs, so the ciphertext looks like gibberish English. It has homophones for a, b, e, i, o and u (w is written as two u-signs) and single signs for persons: N = the Queen of Scots, W = the Queen of England, L = your Lordship, and a few others (Z, M, La, ⊔) whose referents the gloss does not preserve. Plain → cipher: a q/ħ, b r/K, c B, d ε, e α/ε, f a, g б, h c, i ∂/4, l f, m g, n ɧ, o 7/i, p k, r m, s n, t o, u p/Δ, x y, y x. The key is Tomokiyo's, and it held without change on every word decrypted here.

The clear text is in roman type and the deciphered passages in italics. [?] marks a word not securely decrypted, and a sign in brackets is a name sign. The page order is ff. 79r, 79v, 80r, 80v. f. 79r. What was intended and resolved here concerning the [N, Queen of Scots] [?] for her restauration, as for the disposition of her in marriage, your [L, Lordship] … thoroughly understand by Mr John Woodes narration. Since which time you did hear also by a letter sent from me to the Lord of Liddington in your [?] of the same matter absolutely and breefly … How your frendes which here aforesaid were of a contrarie minde for the whole, were violently constrained and by great necessitie urged to condescend and thereunto . So as now my good Lord the matter is not in state of deliberation, but rather requires expedite [?], having good opportunitie for execution . With further by all convenient means I doe wishe that you should concurre with your frendes [Z] here, who see so far into your case , and are so content for the same, as they desire nothinge so earnestlie as your Lordship's pr[ocuring] in that matter , and that to be donne in suche sorte, both for the [sign] and good affection, as it may not appear after [signs] to the [N] or to such as have interest in her , that you will doe nothinge frendly but compulsorilie, whereby the frendship, good affection borne you and thestimacion of you shalbe changed into worse conceiptes, and so gradatim your happines, tranquillitie, and anie good else, shalbe turned into turmoile, calamitie, and division, and the prosperitie of your neighbours and frendes eyther converted into greate dissention, or into a miserable transformation. Now (as matters have ben used and conducted) the protestants your frendes have credit and meanes to assure all things there and here in good termes . And suche may be your impugninge or [double?] proce[edinge] … f. 79v. … as yours and ours adversaries shall [sign] possess the instrument [?], and all other circumstances to the ruine of Religion, you, and your countrey also, and to worke the lyke effectes amongest us moost dangerouslye. You may perhaps amongest other perswasions be moved to thinke, that as you find a faction there to impugne their designe , so there shall not want Instrumentes and a party here to runne the same course . My Lorde I will not dissemble with you, and if I would you can gesse at the truthe. Some there be [sign] graunt which will to their [Z] power withstand this matter . Others will geve the lokinge on; and some will cary twoe faces in a hoode, lokinge which way the matter is lyke to wende. [M] Of all these sortes that will the end , to hasten apace, not to be lefte alone, [sign] when they shall see the ablest and the greatest runne and concurre together in the favour of the [N, M, La] for the purposes aforesaid . And albeit you may thinke [W, the Queen of England] will not so hastily favour her promotion , yet youre experience paste dothe teache you that [W] could never accord her overthrow , or be contented to see her lyfe dispossessed of her state. For I graunt, if her majestie would have runne the direct course against her, perhaps the same would have taken good successe , but this neutralitie can not stande as the worlde standeth. Some light you maye see and thereby conjecture the reste by her majesties letter written to you [sign] at that time , whereby also you may be resolved of what affections they f. 80r. they be in this matter which have the principall credit about her . [signs] I can assure your lordship there is not one, no, not one , which are of moment, that dothe not allow of this case, and maketh hast to shew his gratitude , leste he might be demed slowe. If I could by anye other course espye anye other thinge than your owne overthrowe, I would not write so peremptorilie unto you, neyther perswade you to geve place where peradventure your conscience may be combred, and some question of overprecise objections may arise to calle your honor in dowbte. We see so far to the beginninge, the middeste and the endinge, and doe forsee all dangers and eventes, as I thinke you can not, but [?] yourself to concurre with your frendes . Therefore settinge aside argumentacion, [Z, La, sign] wishe you should with speed [?] send hither the Lord of Liddington, who undoubtedly is both the wysest and the sufficientest man you may send to provide for you and all the reste substancyally and assuredly. And when you shall leave to be advised by him and to truste him, you shall procure unto yourselfe greatteste perill, and to the whole state of your countrey the grettest hazarde. No mans frendship will be more imbraced than yours, no mans estimacion more preserved. [sign] Contrarywise, if you desist or become an adverse party, you will be so incombred both from hence, from thence, and from all other places, your neighbours, as no man can advise you what to doe. Therefore God send you to directe your course for the beste. And so I commit you and all yours f. 80v. to almighty Gods counsell. At Grenew. the 20th of July 1569. Your L. to use and commande, N. Throkmorton . Address: "Lorde Regent of Scotlande".

The record came from the rule-scored DECODE part of the catalogue. Bain was checked first. His no. 1103 matched the shelfmark, the address and "in cipher deciphered", which settled the sender and the date. The four DECODE images, and Tomokiyo's key image filed on the record, were fetched with a DECODE login. The key was first confirmed on about twenty words whose gloss survives ( and, the, your, frendes, intended, resolved, concerning, restauration, disposition, aforesaid, condescend, should, Liddington ). Each cipher passage was then transcribed from half-line crops of the full-resolution scans and decrypted by hand. Where the gloss is legible it agrees with the decoding.

Name signs Z, M, La, ⊔ and the barred 4 are not resolved. The gloss around them is faded, and the key table does not list them. N (Queen of Scots) and W (Queen of England) are glossed (H). The word after the first N on f. 79r, the word after "in your" on f. 79r line 4, the word after "expedite" (the gloss has "having"), "[double?] proce[edinge]", the word after "instrument" on f. 79v, and the verb before "yourself" and before "send" on f. 80r are graded M. Everything else in italics is H or C: it decodes letter for letter, and where the gloss survives it agrees. DECODE's date of 26 July is wrong: the letter says 20 July. The docket at the foot of f. 80v, "9 of aug", is probably the date it was received.

Sixteen bundles of the Japanese Navy Minister’s records for 1932 hold about 850 intercepted American telegrams, copied as the clear text the Navy’s cryptanalysts had recovered, with no cipher groups (JACAR C05022467800–C05022469300). Brice Dudout inventoried them, transcribed eight bundles and compared 53 State Department telegrams with FRUS: about 77% of the words recovered, 45–95% by telegram, and the confidential passages not read. The wrong words are alphabetical neighbours of the true ones (63 of 137 share the initial against 6.3% for shuffled controls), which fits a one-part code and is compatible with the Gray code. Contributed by Brice Dudout. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 30 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: partial (77% of the cipher) Contributed by Brice Dudout (new cipher with solution) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · partial (77% of the cipher) The documents About 850 American messages, 29 January–28 September 1932, copied in Tokyo as typed English clear text under the American heading. About 70% are US Navy traffic, 25% State Department, 3% War Department; the rest are ship-movement bulletins. Where Sixteen bundles in the records of the Navy Minister’s secretariat (Kobun bikan, Showa 7), National Institute for Defense Studies, Tokyo, online through JACAR, Ref. C05022467800 to C05022469300, 796 images. The images are all rights reserved and not reproduced here. The cipher American, but not in the file: no cipher groups were copied, only the recovered words, with the missing ones left blank or reduced to their first letters, and notes such as “what follows: code not deciphered”. How it was read It was not read here. The Japanese Navy’s 1932 readings were transcribed (bundles 1–8) and set against the State Department text printed in FRUS, word by word. What it shows Tokyo recovered about 77% of the words of 53 State Department telegrams (45–95% by telegram). The paragraphs left unread are the most sensitive ones. The wrong words are alphabetical neighbours of the true ones, which fits a one-part code. Still open The confidential passages; which code it was (the Gray code is a compatible hypothesis, not a proof); a full transcription of bundles 9–16. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ) found the file, inventoried it, transcribed and compared it, and designed the one-part-code test, working with Claude agents; he sent it on 29 October 2026. American texts: FRUS (US government, public domain).

Each copy is typed in English under the copied American heading (sender, addressee, number, word count, date, Tokyo time), with a handwritten Japanese title and distribution stamps, among them the round seal of Commander Nakasugi Hisajō, head of the Naval General Staff’s cryptanalytic annex according to Kotani. About 70% of the lines are US Navy traffic (Asiatic Fleet, Cavite, Yangtze Patrol, 4th Marines), 25% State Department (Peiping legation, Shanghai and Nanking consulates, Tokyo embassy) and 3% War Department. Most State Department telegrams from China went over Navy radio and were intercepted in Japan, about forty at Hiratsuka; cables of the Tokyo embassy carry Japanese telegraph marks and probably came from the telegraph administration. Brice Dudout inventoried all sixteen bundles (about 850 messages), transcribed bundles 1–8 image by image, and compared 53 State Department telegrams with FRUS 1932 vol. III–IV and Japan 1931–1941 vol. I. The working notes are in French.

The American code is not seen: the file holds the Japanese result, not the cipher groups, and no copy of the State Department’s own file with its groups was available. What the file allows is a test of the code’s nature from the errors in the Japanese reading. A one-part code. Wrong readings share the initial of the true word in 63 of 137 cases (46%) against 6.3% when the FRUS words are shuffled (10,000 draws); truncations have the right initial in 95 of 119 (80%) against 6.1%; p < 1e-4 for both and in each of the four batches. Wrong words are alphabetical neighbours ( functioning becomes “fundamental”, admission “admonition”, million “military”): median alphabetical distance 0.10 against 0.30 for controls, replicated on the held-out batch d. The protocol was written before the calculation ( stats_initials.py ). Which code. Compatible with the Gray code, the State Department’s ordinary one-part code since 1918, used without superencipherment; Kotani credits Nakasugi’s office with solving it. This is a hypothesis: neither groups nor a Gray copy are available. The Japanese code book. Of 1,972 distinct FRUS words, 1,107 are always read right, 357 sometimes, 270 only replaced by another word, 181 never read and 57 only omitted ( reconstructed_book.tsv ). The errors spread over the whole alphabet.

Word for word, the Japanese copy renders on average about 77% of the FRUS text, from 45% to 95% by telegram. The four batches were measured somewhat differently (sense recovered, identical words, manual count), so the figure is an order of magnitude. Structure, figures, dates and common names are nearly always right; losses fall on small, rare or abstract words and unusual proper names. Wrong values persist for months: believe is rendered “calculate” from March to September. Confidential passages. In six telegrams the unread part begins at a paragraph break and covers the most sensitive matter: Forbes, Tokyo, 1 February; Johnson, Peiping, 12 July (“28 words Enciphered”, “251 words Enciphered”); Grew, Tokyo, 2 September, no. 223 (45 words on the Vice Minister’s confidence); Johnson, 7 September, no. 1078, on the Lytton report, where only the first paragraph is read and the nine paragraphs of political analysis are marked as not deciphered. One hypothesis is an ordinary code largely read and an enciphered confidential code for sensitive matter. US Navy. The Asiatic Fleet traffic was mostly in clear. Sixteen dispatches of late January to 12 March 1932 carry an office-number group “00” followed by a five-letter group, very probably the naval code indicator, so coded Navy dispatches were probably read as early as February 1932 (to be confirmed on the originals). Where the Japanese copy corrects FRUS. Cunningham, Shanghai, 9 February: FRUS “Rear Admiral Shimottowa [Shiozawa?]”, Japanese copy “Shiozawa”; Shanghai no. 222, 6 May: “about 24,000 men of the 3d Division” against FRUS “about 2400 men of the 14th division” (probably right). The reverse also occurs.

Confidential passages (for example Grew no. 223, last 45 words; Johnson no. 1078, paragraphs 2–10): not read in 1932, and no groups were copied, so nothing can be read from the file; the American text is known from FRUS. The code : needs the State Department file copies (NARA RG 59, decimal files in frus_pairs.md ) with their groups. Bundles 9–16 are inventoried, with the comparison against FRUS in the gaps files, but not transcribed in full; that needs the JACAR images, which cannot be redistributed. Rates are measured differently from batch to batch; the Japanese marks A.C., A.G., A.O., D.C. and G.H. are not explained; Kotani’s pages and Moriyama’s articles are known through a review and Japanese Wikipedia, not read directly.
